BABY'S VALENTDIE. Baby has a valentine Sent her through the poet. Who has sent it? Why, the one Who loves baby most. Who loves baby best of all? Is. it sister, brother? Ah! you guess the valentine Must have come from mother. —"Bo-peeP" for February. ONE DAY. We peer isto the darkness and find naught But darkness, great, impenetrable, still; Immensity past any finding out, until Each one alone into its midst be brought, Perhaps we know the fulness of it all , In one short moment. Many times a year We at our work pause awe-struck, when a call From out the Unseen bids some worker near Obey and come. This darkness will be spanned One day by light—we too shall understand. —Harper's Monthly.

_ If your wife faints, do not spoil her dress by dashing a pitcher of water over her. Loudly kiss the back of your hand. She will immediately revive and want to know whom you were kissing. Do not tell her, and she will not faint -any more. If the proposed plan of mimbering the hours from one to twenty-four is adopted, it will sound funny to hear such talk as that—" Here it is nearly twenty-five minutes past twenty two. Yesterday night it was twenty minutes past twenty-three when you came home, and the night before you never came near the house till five minutes to twenty- four. If you can't get home at half-past nineteen or a quarter to twenty, I'll let you have the house to yourself and go back to mother." A KIND DOG.—I have heard an interesting story about a large dog living in Algiers. This good creature used to be sent every morning to a baker's shop to fetch bread ; and each day he had to carry twelve rolls back. One morning it was noticed that he brought home only eleven rolls; so his movements were watched, and this is what was seen. On his way back from the baker's he had by some means found out a poor suffering dog, which was hidden, with her puppies, in a corner of the road along which he passed. So the kind creature had taken pity on her, and had given her a roll each morning. After this the baker was told to send. thirteen rolls in the basket, and the dog delivered twelve for I some days; and then he began to bring home thirteen, which was a sign that his friend was well again.—Bo•Peep. A Cumors PROBLEM.—One of our Western 'friends thinks it would be a curious problem for a woman to find out from mankind what lie really expected of her. Man adores helplessness, and complains that it ruins him. He talks about economy, and raves over spendthrifts. He de- cries frivolity, and runs away from brains. He pines alter his grandmother, who used to make good pies, and falls in love with white hands that can't. He moans over weakness, and ridicules strength. He condemns fashion theoretically, and goes for it practically. He longs for sensible women, and passes them by on the other side. Ile worships saints, but is careful to send them all to convents. He despises pink and white women, and marries them if he can. He abuses silks and laces, and takes them into his heart. He glorifies spirit and independence, but adores the little vines instead of the oaks. What would the critical lords have, if they could have it all their own way ? Christian at Work, (U.S.). GOOD ADVICE TO YOUNG MEN.--President Porter, of Yale, recently gave this sound and wholesome advice to the Students :—" Young men, you me the architects of your own fortunes; rely on your own strength of body and soul. Take for your star self-reliance. Inscribe on your banner, 'Luck is a fool, Pluck is a hero.' Don't take too much advice, keep at the helm and. steer your own ship, and re- member that the art of commanding is to take a fair share of the work. Think well of yourself. Strike out. Assume your own position. Put potatoes in a cart, go over a rough road, and small ones go to the bottom. Rise above the envious and the jealous. Fire above the mark you intend to hit. Energy, invincible determination, with a right motive, are the levers that move the world. Don't swear. Don't deceive. Don't read novels. Don't marry until you can support a wife. Be civil. Read the papers. Advertise your business. Make money and do good with it. Love your God and fellow-men. Love truth and virtue. Love your country and obey its laws."—Anierican Paper. SCOTTISH SONGSTRESSES.—The daily household toil, the motherly cares are exhausting, and against the chances of nneincated women raising above their circumstances. Our Scottish songstresses have, as a rule, been women of goad social position and education, such as Lady Anne Barnard, Lady Grizzel Baillie, Miss Elliott, Mrs. Cockburn, Lady Nairne, and others. But names of women of the humbler ranks are not wholly absent from the bead-roll; and in these times is to be added to it the honoured name of Janet Hamil- ton, who, without what is technically known as education, and in the face of daily toil and depressing circumstances, rose as naturally to the position of a genuine poetess, as inborn genius impels. I should not seek to place her in the very foremost rank of our Scottish bards, yet, in virtue of her pure spontaneous power, the force of assiduous self- culture, a fine sensibility for outward nature, and a noble human-beartedness, she has risen to the rank of a true and tender poetess, and added largely to the imperishable trea sure of our national so/lg.—Good Word.. When Webster ,4'll. 3 at the zenith of his career, a gentle- man waited upon him one day to engage him for the de- fence in an important case at law, the amount at stake in the snit being 80,000 dollars. The &maternal asked Webster what the retaining fee would be. "A thousand dollars." "A thousand dollars !" exclaimed the gentleman. " Yes. But think for a moment what I engage to do, sir. I do not only hold myself at your service in the matter, perhaps, for a month or more, but I debar myself from ac- cepting any offer, no matter how large, from the plaintiff." The applicant was satisfied with this explanation, wrote out a cheque for the amount, and gave it to the great expounder, who, after he had put it into his pocket, said—" I will now give you a bit of advice gratis. If you can compromise this business upon fair terms with the plaintiff, you had better do so." In a few days after the gentleman called upon Webster again, and told him that a compromise had been effected, and the matter satisfactorily settled. Webster drily congratulated his visitor on the result, and would have turned to other business, but the visitor seemed to have something farther on his mind "Of course," he ventured, after a pause, "I shall not require yonr services, Mr. Web- ster." "Certainly not, sir." "And—and how about the 1,000 dols. I paid you ?" faintly asked the gentleman, who was not quite reconciled to paying such a sum for services which were never to be rendered. "Oh, ah !" responded Daniel, with a bland smile. "You don'eunderstand. It is very simtee. That was a retaining fee—called in law a 'retainer.' By virtue of the contract, I also became a re- tainer. What should I retain, if not my fee?" THE INvEarron OF TID3 LIFEBOA.T.—One of the very earliest inventors of a lifeboat was Ms. Lionel Lukin, a coaeh-bnilder of Long Acre, who turned his attention to the subject in 1784, from purely benevolent motives. The then Prince of Wales (afterwards George IV.), who knew Lnkin personally, not only encouraged him to test his in- vention, but offered to pay the expenses. Lnkin purchased a Norway yawl, to the outer frame of which he: added a proj,ecting gunwale of cork, tapering from nine inches amid- ships to very little at the bows and stern. Hollow water- tight enclosures gave it great buoyancy, while ballast suffi- cient far stability was afforded by a heavy false keel of iron. On this principle several boats were constructed, and found to be as the inventor describes them, "unimmergible." The Rev. Di. Shairp, of Bamborough, hearing of the inven. ton, and having charge of a charity for saving life at sea, sent a boat to Lnkin to be rendered " unimmergible." This was done, and satisfactory aecount3 were afterwards re- ceived of the altered boat, which was reported to have saved several lives in the first year of its use. The Ad- miralty and Trinity House would have nothing to do with it, in spite of the Prince of Wales' interest in the matter. It has been said that a committee is a body without a con- science; it was true in those good old days. Lnkin re- tired from business in 1824, and went to live at Hythe in Kent, where, ten years after, he died; the inscription on his temb in Hythe churchyard says that he was the first to build a lifeboat.—" The Sea: Its Stirring Story of Adven-

tore, Peril, and Heroism." Tax FUTURE OF SINGLE WOMEN.—The mental life of a single woman is free and untrammelled by any limits ex- cept such as are to her own advantage. Her difficulties in the way of development are only such as are common to all human beings. Her physical life is healthy and active, she retains her buoyancy and increases her nervous power if she knows how to take care of herself, and this lesson she is rapidly learning. The unmarried woman of to-day is a new, sturdy, and vigorous type. We find her neither the exalted I ascetic nor the nerveless, inactive creature of former days.! She is intellectually trained and socially successful, her Physique is as sound and vigorous as her mind. The world is before her in a freer, truer, and better sense than it is be- fore any individual male or female. Her tastes are various Mind refined, her opportunities for cultivating them practic- ally unlimited. Whether it be in the direction of society, or art, or travel, or philanthropy, or public duty, or a com- bination of many of these, there is nothing to let or hinder her from following her own will, there are no bonds but such as bear no yoke, no restrictions but those of her own conscience and right principle. She feels that it is in no sense her duty, since it is not her choice, to devote herself to securing the happiness of some one individual, nor to add to our difficulties of over-population. From her strong- hold of happiness and freedom she can help the weak and protect the poor. She is fitted to fill a place which has al- ways steed empty in the history of the world, that of a loving and tender woman armed with official power to re- press the wrongs of women and children, to stand as their representative before the ration, the creator of their rights, and the shield of their weakness; those whose nature and necessities are known only to her, and to her only because she is a woman, have found in her a guardian, an advocate, and a friend. While losing none of the fun and frolic and gaiety of life, she is called by a deep religious conviction to stand f ace to face and hand in hand with suffering; it is her holy mission to grapple with some of ' the most painful pro- -I.le 713 of modern civ*lisation.— We.stminster Review. NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI- CULTURE, &c. The dairy farm of Boghead, belonging to the Duke of Hamilton, has been let to Mr. Lambie, Overtonost a rental of £375, being a rise of £ll5 on that paid by the present tenant, in the occupation of whose family the subject has been for a lifetime. Proposals have been made for:the establishment of a beet sugar factory at Lavenham, but the farmers appear rather lukewarm, and indications are in favour of the establish- ment of a factory at Ipswich instead of at Lavenham, as the East Suffolk farmers are anxious to have one in their midst. In consequence of the holding of the Royal Agricultural Show this year at Shrewsbury, it has been decided that no show of the West Midland shall be held until 1885, and the Council has voted £2OO to be given in prizes at the meeting of the Royal, and £2OO towards the fund raised to meet the expenses incurred by the local committee. What is claimed to have been the largest sale of thorough- bred stock ever made ala a private sale in any country has recently been made by Messrs. Burleigh and Bodwell, of Hallowell, Maine the Indiana Stud Stock Company. It numbered 200 head of imported Hereford and polled Aber. been cattle, and the price was £18,670. Minx FEvxm—Herr Hasselman, Zcelen, Holland, writes: In Agricultural Gazette, of February 4, you mention several cases of milk fever. As long as I can recollect, some twenty years, we never had it in our stable. I attri- bute this luck to our feeding the cows pretty liberally with mangels, cut straw, and hay, and not giving to them any corn nor cake during six weeks before calving." MR. ARTHUR _ARNOLD'S CATTLE DISEASES BILL.—Mr. Arthur Arnold's bill to amend the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act,lB7B, which has been read a first time in the House of Commons, proposes, by inserting the words "or any specified part of a country''' in the fifth schedule of the Act of 1878, to give the Privy Council power to make regu- lations affecting only part of a country, the object being to facilitate the bringing of cattle, and especially of store cattle, from the western States through Canadian ports to this country. FOOT-AND-MOUTH-,DISEASE IN THE HUMAN SUBJECT.— Three 'families in the district of Ballyvoile and Kilmae- thomas , are stated to be suffering from foot-and-mouth disease, the symptoms including profuse discharge of saliva, together with soreness of the nose, lips, and tongue. One of the most marked symptoms in the cow is a cessation in the natural ,flow of milk, and, considering the extent to which cattle suffer in this country, this circumstance is probably one reason why the disease is so rarely communi- cated to the human subject. —The Lancet. THE CART-HORSE Saow.—The fifth annual London show of the English Cart-horse Society, which opens at the Agri- cultural Hall on February 26th, will afford a striking proof of the popularity of these exhibitions among owners of animals eligible to compete for the prizes offered. The fol- lowing figures, which give in convenient form the entries (exclasive of geldings) indicate the annual increase in point of numbers. Entries nominally closed on February 2nd, but additional ones may be made on payment of double fees up till Saturday, the 9th. 1880. 1881. 1882. 1883. 1884. Stallions Mares Totals Including the Elsenham challenge cup, value 100 gs., given by Mr. Walter Gilbey, the prizes offered for competition reach a total of £624 55. THE Dun OF RICHMOND'S CATTLE DISEASE BILL.-1. This Act may be cited as the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, 1878, Amendment Act, 1884. 2. From and after the Ist day of October, 1884, the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, 1878, shall be read and construed as though the provi- sions following were inserted in and formed part of section 35 of the said Act, that is to say :—The Privy Council shall lin all cases in which it is made to appear to them, either by consular reports or otherwise, that foot and mouth disease exists or has within three months existed in any specified foreign country or in any specified part thereof, make such general or special:orders as shall be sufficient for prohibit- ing the landing of living animals brought from such speci- fied foreign country or from such specified part thereof ; and when after the making of any such order it appears to the Privy Council that any living animal brought from such specified foreign country or from such specified part thereof has been or is likely to be shipped at any foreign port not within such specified foreign country so as to evade such order' the Privy Council shall, by a special order, pro- hibit the landing of any living animal shipped at such foreign part. NATURAL ALLIES OF THE FARMER.—The Rev. C. H. Fielding, in a paper read at a meeting of the Rochester Farmers' Club on "The Natural Allies of the Farmer," con- tended that there was a chain of destruction throughout native, and that to break the chain caused serious loss. In illustration, he referred to the increase of rats, "the most mischievous and baneful of our quadrupeds," in consequence of the extermination of the badger, weasel, and hawk. At Higham he bad seen the banks filled with enormous grey rats since the hawks and owls and weasels had been frightened away. Being freed from their natural enemies, the rats made havoc of the stacks of corn in the neighbour- hoxl. He urged that man should protect the badger, the weasel, the mole, the hedgehog, and the shrew, and even his more humble allies the frog, the toad, the snake, and the blindworm, and rescue the lady-bird, the ichneumon and the dragon•fly from the dangers their race are liable to. Many birds, he also held, were natural allies of the farmers, the good they did by the destruction of insect pests being much greater than the loss they occasioned by the con- sumption of seed and fruit. FOOT AND MOUTH DISEASE.—EVADING REGULATIONS.— I The restrictive arrangements of the Cumberland and West- ,'l moreland'authorities, for the prevention of the spread of foot and mouth disease, have been excellent, but it would appear that the ingenuity of a cattle dealer has been enabled to find a loophole. Mr. Henry Johnson—or, as he is better known, Harry Johnson—is one of the best-known cattle dealers in Westmoreland. It appears that he was wishful to I move 57 animals from Yorkshire into Cumberland, so he obtained a license 'for their transport into Westmoreland. Having got them over the border of the two counties, he placed them in a field at Osenholme for a short time, and then took them on by rail into Cumberland. The authori- ties issued a summons, but the solicitor for the defence pleaded that his client had complied with the law. He ob- tained a license to remove them into Westmoreland; he did Iso remove them. No license was necessary to remove cattle from Westmoreland into Cumberland, and in so removing them Mr. Johnson had contravened no law. We are told that the magistrates reluctantly came to the conclusion that they had no option but to dismiss the information. THE LATE Ma. M. H. AlNSLlE.—Agrienithre in North Lonedale has lost a liberal and generous friend in the death of Mr. Montague Ainslie, J.P. and DL., who died at his re- sidence, Grizedale Hall, yesterday week, in his 92nd year. Head of a firm of mining merchants, Mr. Ainslie gave I largely of his wealth, especially to agricultural associations, • for independent of liberal annual subscriptions to all the societies for miles around he also regularly offered valuable special prizes for promoting the good breeding of live stock, land his loss will be much felt. When the county show was held at Lancaster, a few years ago, Mr. Rigby wrote asking permission to place Mr. Ainslie's name on the list of the local committee. The answer was characteristic. Cows' Tekrs.—At this season of the year, when so many cows are calving, and when in large dairies, through the carelessness of the milkers, many cows are permanently daraaged by the loss of what is commonly known as a quarter—in other words by the loss of 25 per cent, of the milk through the blocking up of a portion of the teat—a few words upon the subject will be instructive. The udder of the cow, with its teats, is not by any means to be played with, for the milk does not, as some farmers and cowkeepers think when they insert a straw or quill into the teat of the animal, run from the udder and through the teat in a die- tinctly defined passage. The physiological characteristice of the teat resemble a sponge in appearance, being fall of very delicate little dame or canals running the one into the other, and around them is a tissue of a fibrous and exceed- ingly elastic nature. Surrounding this is a layer of tissue, the glands of which are full of vesicles hanging on tabular ducts, whose purpose is to secrete the milk flowing into the larger ducts, where it oomes into contact with the milk de- scending from the udder. The teat, therefore, like the udder, is really engaged in producing the milk, and is not a mere channel for its passage to the pail. At the extremity only does it really differ from the udder, and there its pas- sage for the escape of the miptils very short, being no longer than the thickness of,lhaVsFlar covering. If a cow is pained by the introductieri ills, straws, or any- thing of a like description, there no, , flowing what damage may be done to her. If the membranes are jagged or torn the trouble may, be serious, while-theleast evil, next to the ' entire stoppage of the injured teat, is that she may contract her udder and give for a long period a much less quantity of milk. There may be seaeons when some article can be in- serted into it advantageously, but at all times straws and quills ought to be discarded. A quill has often been used with a wrapping of thread around its lower end, so that its insertion shall not extend beyond a certain point—the nar- row end, which is naturally rounded, being of course the one to be placed in the teat, and this after it has been filed off and the quill oiled. Silver tubes, however, made for such a purpose, are by all means the beet, and eowkeepers and owners should possess one of these instruments for use in cases of emergency.

"OUR OLD NOBILITY.", ishcd by Mr. E. L. Kibbletehite, 31, Tavistock-street, London, W.C., and reprinted by permission.] 3 dealt almost exclusively with our older nobility, have been said of the wholesale creations tbsatner last reigns. Mr. Disraeli's phrase, the "borough- mongering of our own times," is almost obsolete now; but it is_still true that the exercise of electoral influence is the surest road to the House of Lords. When the then Premier was last in c ffice several peers were created who owe their titles to political partisanship, among the number being Lords Penrhyn, Kesteven' and O'Neil. But, during Disraeli's six years of power, the large-scrod and steady-voting Tories have had a rare time of it, while superannuated or incom- petent colleagues of the Minister have been lifted into the House of Lords when offices could not be found for them. For nearly forty years, Sir John Pakington sat for what was once the pocket-borough of Droitwich ; in 1874, the people of Droitwich asserted their independence, and rejected Sir John. At once he was created Lord Hampton. Colonel Wilson Patten, another old colleague, had to be provided for, so he was created Lord Winmarleigh. Then there was the heir of "My dear Grey de Wilton," whom the electors of Bath placed at the bottom of the poll in 1874; he, too, was consoled with a seat in the Upper House. The Ormsby- Gores had done much for the Tories in Shropshire and other counties, and the late Lord Harlech had his reward in his elevation to the Upper House in 1876. The Shirts had been equally useful in Dorsetshire, and in the same year Mr. H. G. Sttlrt became Lord Alington. Mr. John Tollemache had long served the Tories well in Cheshire and Suffolk ; he had his reward the same year by being created Lord Tollemache. Mr. Guard had helped to secure South Lancashire he be- came Lord Gerard. Lord Wharncliffe had served the Tories equally well in South Yorkshire; his reward was an earl- dom. The late Lord Ravensworth and his son, Lord Ealing- ton, had fought hard for Conservatism in Northumberland and Durham ; his lordship was created an earl. The Homes, hitherto Scotch peers, were rewarded for the use of their great territorial influence with an English barony. Mr. Hylton Joliffe, whose seat for Wells was abolished by the last Reform Bill,was consoled with the title of Lord Hylton. Sir Charles Adderley conveniently retired from the Ministry not long, ago, and became Lord Norton. The Government has certainly been mindful of its friends, but its own princi- pal members have not been lost sight of. Mr. Disraeli has become Earl of Beaconsfield, Lord Cairns has become Earl Cairns, Mr. Gathorne Hardy has become Viscount Cran- brook.

These instances, drawn front the history of the last few years, will suffice to show how unscrupulously the House of Lords is used at the preeent time. The first step for a wealthy parvenu is to buy up land right and left; the second is to keep a steady pressure upon his agricultural tenants at each election; in due time he or his heir may hope for the coveted reward. Since the accession of the House of Han- over a very large proportion of the modern aristocracy— probal4 half of them—ewe one or more titles to the exercrs6 of electoral intimidation. We deal in a very curious manner with offences against the free exercise of the franchise. The bribed electors are temporarily dis- franchised, the briber obtains an office or a judgeship The ruffian who tramples on a voter's head is sent to gaol the landlord who tramples on a voter's conscience is created a peer. There have been not a few modern peers who have gained their titles by the possession of land alone, as well as a yet larger number who have gained them by the exercise of such influence as the possession of land carried with it. We must never lose sight of the fact that the House of Lords is not only a legislative body, but also a great agrarian institu- tion. We hear much, at the present time, of the artificial causes which tend to the aggregation of estates. We may do much bY destroying such of these artificial causes as are due to class legislation, or to the permission by the law of practices which are inimical to the public interest. But the House of Lords itself is the most powerful of all these artificial causes. I am not pleading for its abolition, but I bring the fact forward to show that those who dread Free Trade in Land will still have a powerful conservative force on which to rely, and to serve as an argument against the degradation of the peerage, to which we are growing accus- tomed. We are constantly told that great modern estates which have been acquired by purchase are only the results of natural causes; bat in England wealthy buyers have constantly been indueed to accumulate land, no matter at what price purchased, as a road to the House of Lords. Thus, out of one great manufacturing establishment in South Wales, during the present century, two peerages and a baronetcy have been produced; but, as a necessary pre- liminary, the wealthy ironmasters bought up land right and left. The first Mr. Loyd who came to London owned no land stall; the first Lord 0 verstone has 30,849 acres of land in eleven different counties. The Barings, Caringtons, Foleys, Denisons, and other modern families, have travelled to the peerage by the same road; and I might name a multitude who have already reached the half-way house of the baronetage. Even when a coronet has been obtained, the earth-hunger is unappeased. There are steps in thel peerage to be gained, and the noble who has not sufficient brains to become a statesman can still continue to buy up land. It is a common complaint against farmers that they have been too eager to farm more land than their capital allows them to manage properly. Unfortunately, a great many landowners have set them the example. A generation ago, the most conspicuous instance of this tendency was found in the case of one w‘c had already reached the highest rank in the peerage—ge Duke of Buckingham. Though the family was already embarrassed, the Duke went on Ibuying up land which paid him two per cent. with money borrowed at four per cent., until at last the inevitable crash came. There are not a few landlords who have recently been playing the same game, though more circumspectly. It is simply impossible for themlo do justice to the land, or to make provision for the depression that has overtaken agriculture. For my part, lam not at all surprised at the gradual extinction of the yeoman class, when we offer the highest prizes in the State to the nip who will accumulate the most land in their own hands. There are some peers who are not suffering from family greed of aggrandisement, but from past family extravagance, I pity them. They mast make no sign of distress, while the teeth of the fox concealed beneath the cloak are fixed in their flesh. Honest poverty is not hard to bear so long as it does not verge on destitution; but to a good man, assumed wealth masking actual poverty must be a constant torture. But if I pity such men, still more do I pity their lands and all that dwell thereon. If an ordinary trader cannot meet his bills, we wind up his affairs in the Bankruptcy Court; if a Duke of Newcastle, with 34,000 acres of land in a single county, is in the same position, another measure is dealt out to him. Front a sentimental point of view, it may be well that life-ownership should save an old family from destruc- tion ; but what of the interests of those who live upon the estates of a bankrupt lord? Yet another point must not be overlooked. The rent-rolls given in the preceding chapters must only be regarded as giving an approximate idea of the incomes of their owners. In some cases I believe they are greatly under the mark; in others the owners would be only too glad to put into their pockets the amounts put down. There are not a few estates, even where earth-hunger and extravagance have had but little influence—where "the dead hand" controls the living much more than most people are aware; and just now land- owners are beginning to feel this most acutely. Family encumbrances are a fixed sum; rents fluctuate. It was all very well so long as rentals had an upward tendency; it is otherwise now. One of the most beneficent results of the great uprising of the farm labourers was to quicken the zeal for improvement in the housing of the men. In some counties the expenditure must have been very large, and has been, doubtless, owing largely to the facilities afforded by Land Improvement Companies. These Companies have also done not a little in the way of agricultural improvement generally, though the inquiries of Lord Salisbury's Com- mission showed that the cost to landowners was burdensome even in prosperous times. What must it'be now, when rents are fallen on all sides 2 Of legal peerages of recent date nothing adverse could be reasonably advanced if only they were but life peerages. Such men as Lords Selborne, Penzance, O'Elagan, and Cole- ridge would be ornaments to any Legislative Assembly. The same may be said of what may be called the Civil Ser- vice Peerages. The matured wisdom and experience of such men as Lords Blachford, Hammond, and Cottesloe should not be lost to the country, or left to find vent in magazine articles, when age has necessitated their retire- ment from active duty in the less obtrusive, but none the less eminent duties of statemanship. As to our modern military peerages, I fear they are quite numerous enough to make the Service impatient of long-continued peace. Since the outbreak of the Crimean War, we have had Lords Raglan, Clyde, Strathnairn, Sandhurst, Napier of Magdala, and Airey. Against these, Literature can only place two novelists and one historian, and these would have never sat in the House of Lords had they not been also politicians.

MISCELLANEOUS. Mr. P A. Taylor, who has represented Leicester since 1862, has informed his constituents that in consequence of failing health he will not again reek re-election. The Exchequer returns from April let to February 16th show—Receipts £75,361,164; expenditure, £73,837,394 ; balances, £7,883,940. Corresponding period last year: Re- ceipts, £75,673,349; expenditure, £76,017,624; balances, £6,460,037..

The result of the polling in West Somerset was declared on Saturday at noon as follows :—Mr. Elton (G), 3,757; Lord Kilcouisie (L), 2,99 s—majority for the Conservative, 762. This was the first county election since the Corrupt Practices Act came into operation. In the Queen's Bench Division, on Tuesday, the Earl of I.4ylesford was sued for arrears of alimony alleged to be due to his wife. The Earl pleaded in defence that his wife had been guilty of immoral conduct with the present Duke of Marlborough. The Duke and the lady both refused to at- tend the court, and the case was adjourned. PAYING FOR HOSTILE Crtmemat.—At a banquet held in Paris on Monday evening there was much laughter when M. de Lesseps mentioned that on his first visit to England the publisher who brought out the report of his meetings charged, as the first item of his bill, "£5O for attacking the book in order to make it succeed." "Since then," observed M. de Lesseps, "I have been attacked gratuitously, and have got on without paying."

EXTRAORDINARY LAKES OF SALMON.—Since the opening, of the Tay and other Scotch salmon rivers the takes have been unprecedentedly large. On Monday, from the rivers North and South Esk, in Forfarshire, no fewer than twelve tons o' splendid fish were landed, and from the North Eck alone 700 were got. The rivers are literally swarming with salmon, and there is little disease. Prices are Is 4d and is 6d per lb.

• The bill for the abolition of actions for breach of promise of marriage consists of a single clause of four lines. After its passing no person is to be entitled to maintain such ac- tions, exception being made of causes commenced before the bill becomes law. The bill is brought in by Colonel Makins, Mr. Bryce, and Mr. Meldon. Should the bill reach

the stage of secled reading its rejection will be moved by Sir Hardinge Giffard. Without opposition, Mr. C. S. Read was on Wednesday elected member for West Norfolk, in place of Mr. G. W. P. Benticck, who has resigned, after continuously representing the county since 1871. Mr. Bentinck's majority at the general election was only 129; but the constituency is well known to be Conservative, and with a candidate like Mr. C. S. Read, who was sure of the support of the agricultural classes, in the field, there was little encouragement for a Liberal to provoke a contest. THE ROYAL COMMISSION ON THE DWELLINGS OF THE POOR.—We understand that the Royal Commission to in- quire into the whole question of the dwellings of the poor will include the Prince of Wales, Cardinal Manning, Mr. Broadhurst, Mr. tyulph Stanley, and Mr. Jesse Collings. Lord Salisbury has been invited to act as a commissioner. The Queen has, we believe, given her consent that the Prince of Wales should serve on the commission. We have already stated that Sir Charles Dilke will preside over the inquiry.

FinE °MINING OF THE CLARENCE.—At the Liverpeol Assizes on Monday the five boys lately detained on board the reformatory ship Clarence,- moored in the Mersey, who pleaded guilty to having set that vessel on fire, were each sentenced to five years' penal servitude. Mr. Justice Butt said the prisoners, whose de- signs were directed against property and not life, though there were over 203 persons in the ship when it was set on fire, evidently hoped to escape servirc! their terms of correction, but he could not be a party wards assisting them in that intention.

SAD ACCIDENT TO A FUNERAL CORTEGE.—About OL o'clock on Wednesday afternoon, whilst a hearse and mourn- ing coach combined were parsing along Corporation-street, Birmingham, the horse took fright. The vehicle was brought to a stop by colliding with an iron stump. The driver WAS thrown from his seat, and the horse fell over him. The two

frout wheels of the hearse were broken off the vehicle,whilst the coffin, containing the body of an infant, was broken, amidst the pitiful screams of the mother, who for some time could act be extricated from the broken conveyance. The bereaved woman appeared panic-styicken by the sad sight, and cried bitterly. A CONSERVATIVE LMADER WANTED.—The Economist says•the Parliamentary weakness of the Tory party has been revealed this week with hitherto unknown completeness. They have in the Commons no adequate leader, and they are looking round for one with an eagerness which gives a chance even to a man with the defects of Lord R. Churchill. The Tories are irritated at the want, for they are hungering for a serious straggle in a way of which the reports of Parlia- mentary debates give no adequate idea. They dislike the present regime with a bitterness which each day seems only to increase. This temper has been rising for two years,land is now so exasperated by the Franchise Bill, which all Con- servatives secretly dread, that they will run any risk rather than remain in a monotonous inaction. They only want a leader, and, whether it is Lord Randolph Churchill or not, they are pretty certain to find one. TRH Howortra DIVORCE CASE. In the Probate and Divorce Division of the High Court of Justice, on Tuesday, before Sir-James Hannen, a motion was made in the case of Howorth v. Howorth. Mr. Middleton, who appeared for Mrs Ada Howorth, of Blackpool, the petitioner, said this application to the court was for substituted service of the wife's petition for maintenance, which had been filed as long ago as the 31st October last, the decree nisi having been obtained on the 18th June prior. Since that time consider- able correspondence had taken place between the solicitors without the wife's legal advisers having been able to find out the respondent's address, and they now asked that sub- stituted service might be effected on Mr. lloworth's solici- tor, and, if the court thought it necessary, by advertisement also.—Sir James Hannen'granted the application, directing substituted service on the respondent's solicitor, and also by advertisement. Tins MURDER OP A SPANISH SEAMAN IN LIVERPOOL.— Five young men, named Duggan Campbell, APLean, Dempsey, and Ballantyne, who belong to the " rough " class, were indicted on Monday, at Liverpool Assizes, for murdering a Spanish seaman, named Muniez. That unfor- tunate mao, whilst going down to his ship, was set upon in Blackstone-street by the prisoners, without having given them the slightest provocation. He was kicked and beaten with bekts, and after enduring much illusage managed to get away. The prisoners, however, followed him for some distance, assaulted him again in a most brutal manner, and left him in a dying condition, with stabs npon his :hest, from which he expired before reaching the hospital. The jury convicted Duggan and M‘Lean, but recommended them to mercy on account of their youth. Sentence of deattrwas passed upon them, Mr. Justice Butt promising to forward the recommendation to the proper quarter. The other prisoners were acquitted. MR. GLADSTONE ON FRUIT FAHMINO.—(To the editor of _ .

he Evaminer.)—Sir, Referring to We Premier's speech at he annual rent audit at Hawarden, Mr. Gladstone is incor- rect in stating that preserves are charged from 7d to 9d a b, and that this is owing mainly to the energy of the French, Belgian, Dutch, German and American fruit growers. All the gooseberries, raspberries, strawberries, I black currants, damsons, and blackberries used by me are entirely English—no foreign whatever being used—and to prove that the quantity Is not particularly small, my usual season's make is :—Gooseberry, 300 tons. Raspberry, 300 tons. Strawberry, 200 tons. Black currant, 400 tons. Damson, 500 tons. Blackberry, 100 tons. And they can be bought retail from ready-money grocers in two and three- pound stoneware jars at the following prices :—Gooseberry, 5d to 514 per lb. Raspberry, Gd to 61d. Strawberry, 6d to ad. Black currant. 50. Blackberry, ad. Raspberry and Gooseberry, ad. Plum, 4d. Greengage, 6d. Damson, 7d. Orange Marmalade, 4d. Jars extra, one penny each. Yours, die., Wig. P. HARTLEY.—BootIe, Liverpool. ALLEGED LIBEL ON THE ATTORNEY GENERAL.—Mr. A. A. Sylvester, publisher and part proprietor of the Birming- ham Daily Gazette, appeared before Mr. Justice Denman, at Warwick Assizes, on Saturday, to answer a criminal in- formation charging him with having published a defama- tory libel concerning the Attorney General. In the journal named there appeared an editorial article imputing that Sir Henry James had been actuated by party feeling and per- sonal animus in declining, as he did, to give his fiat for certain preceedings in Chancery relating to the consolida- tion of the Birmingham Improvement Acts, and other matters. These allegations were pointedly denies! by Sir Henry James, who gave evidence for the prosecution, and who said that he was guided purely by considerations which he considered fair and equitable in the interests of the public. He emphatically contradicted the assertion that in anything he did he was "instigated by Mr. Chamberlain," as the article stated was doubtless the case. The publica- tion of the libel was not contraverted, but evidence was called to show that it was not submitted to the defendant before it was inserted, and that he had no knowledge of its preparation. The jury found a verdict of ''not guilty." An apology had been tendered by Mr. Sylvester to the Attorney General; but on public grounds the learned and hon. gentle- man decided to obtain the opinion of a jury in the matter. THE LIVERPOOL Porsospro CASE.—After a patient and exhaustivetrial, extending over three days, Mrs. Catherine Flannagan and Mrs. Margaret Higgins have been found guilty of the murder by poisoning of Thomas Higgins, the husband of the latter prisoner, and sentenced to death. The crimes charged against them were amongst the most hideous on record, and were committed for the most miserable of motives. The callous, selfish, and calculating nature of their dreadful career can only be regarded with destestation and abhorrence. For a few pounds to be foolishly spent they were ready to sacrifice the life of any person to whom they had access, and as their victims were usually their own relations, they might well be described by the presiding judge as stern, relentless, and cruel. There is little moral doubt these wholesale poisoners not only destroyed all the lives mentioned in the indictment, but others for which they were not arraigned. The justice of the verdict will be un- iversally asserted- and there can be no suggestion of mercy in such a case. It is a melancholy subject for reflection that the wretched culprits are sisters.—From the suspicious movements of the police during the past few days in a cer- tain quarter known as the "Black Spot" of Liverpool, and from information received, there are very strong grounds for believing that this case is bnly one of a number of other horrible casp which the police feel confident of shortly bringing to light. Although the utmost reticence is shown by the police authorities in the matter, it is alleged that a "bunch" of arrests of supposed prisoners will be made within the next few days from the neighbourhood so familiar to Mrs. Flannagan and Mrs. Higgins. div.p: Saturday was the anniversary of the commencement of the National Debt, which took place on February 16, 1689. It amounted in 1697 to about five millians, and was then thought to be of alarming magnitude; but owing to subse- quent wars the debt now amounts to about £786,000,000. Provost Reid, at a meeting of the Kirkwall Town Coun- cil, on Wednesday night, intimated that the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone had offered them for presentation to the town a bronze bust of himself as a memorial of his recent visit to Kirkwall. The provost accepted the offer on behalf of the town, and exhibited the bust to the meeting amid cheers. The Corporation afterwards agreed to place the bust in the new municipal buildings which are to be erected immediately by the Corporation. ME. BRAM...kJ:36H AND NORTHAMPTON.—For the fourth time Mr. Charles Bradlaugh was on Tuesday elected mem- ber for Northampton, the polling being—for Mr. Bradlaugh 4,031, and for Mr. Richards 3,663, giving Mr. Bradlaegh a majority of 363. Never before has he received so many votes, and not since the general election has his majority been so large. In 1880 he received 331 votes fewer than Mr. Labouchere, and 675 mere than Mr. Phipps, the most popu- lar Conservative candidate, Mr. BraiLlaugh's supporters numbering 3,827. In 1881, when his seat was vacated on the High Court ef Judicature adjudging that he was not qualified to affirm, he was re-elected by 3,437 votes against 3,305 for Mr. Corbet, the majority being 132. Eleven months afterward., when he had been expelled for disobel- ing the order of the Hence, he was re-elected by 3,796 votes against Mr. Corb.t's 3 655, his majority thus reaching its lowest point-108. In the two years that have since elapsed Mr. Bradlaugh's popularity in Northampton has evidently increased, and his hold upon the constituency is now firmly established.

GE GARDENING , to per] a, the ground must:be ..or trenched, to a depth of at least burying as mach half-decayed nasinuie, ea .ole. nere only a single row is to be plantokOhe bl method is to throw out a trench 3ft. to 4ft. wide and 2ft: deep, placing the Boil on both sides in equal portions. The bottom of the trench should be forked and mixed —with manure. It should be filled by alternate layers of manure and other soil, the manure to be the first layer, until the whole is replaced. It will then be found thit the ground intended for the row forms a ridge above all the other; this in time frill sink to its normal level. If we examine a rhubarb stool we find it has several crowns, from which the growth proceeds;; each of these when severed' makes a plant, but they are sometimes so close that it would be in- judicious to divide them, so we take two, and sometimes three, if small. For the purpose of separating, we find nothing so convenient as,a sharp spade, which we place be- tween the crowns and force down right through, and when we come to plant we cut some of the large fleshy roots entirely away. On ground prepared as we have described, Rhubarb should grow from 3ft. to 4ft. long, and each plant should not be any nearer than 31t. There would appear to be a waste of land in this method of cultivation, hut this is not so, for a crop of eabbage or cauliflowers may be put between the first year, as they :will be ready to be moved before the Rhubarb covers the ground, which it will do before the end of the season. Rhubarb is such a profitable crop that it well repays for the ground it occupies, and there are few crops that give so little labour in summer to keep clean. No weeds will grow under its leaves, and the drip from their edges during rains seems to deter those around from making much progress. No Rhubarb should be pulled for use the first year, unless late in the season it is found to be extra strong. A stick or two may then be taken from each root. The second year we may estimate the value of the produce at 6d. per root, or about £6O pen statute acre, and a crop that anyone almost can gather ready for market. Rhubarb plantations keep in good order for six years, and longer when they receive heavy top dressings of manure. We prefer renewing when we observe the least symptoms of debility, and if, instead of destroying the roots, they are taken up and pat on a few barrow loads of fermenting material during January and February, they will throw up a quantity of valuable staff. The roots should be covered with flour casks, or something similar; some long litter or straw placed over that will still hasten it. The roots are quite good for planting even after this light forcing. THE FRONT GARDEN.—This division of the cottager's garden will now be coming daily more interesting. The Snowdrop is now at its best, and those who have not the double form should secure it at the proper time. There are other species, such as the Crimean Snowdrop, the Spring Snowflake and Galanthus Imperati, which is perhaps the largest of any. Of Crocus we have only seen a yellow kind in flower to any extent in cottage gardens this season. This showy flower looks more effective when the blue, yel- low, purple, and white are planted in harmonising patches, or a row of each kind to form a border round the beds. The Primrose is another spring flower now expanding. The hybrid- let has given us numerous varieties of it within the past six years, so that a packet of seed might be expected to give two or three dozen distinct varieties, some of them showing a cross with the Polyanthus of the florist. Some that we have have a Polyanthus flower, with its beautiful gold laoing perched on a Primrose peduncle, or flower stalk, but no pedicels. THE WlNDOW.—Pelargoniums will now require a larger' pot. We allude to those that were pruned and potted early in the Autumn. The fresh pot should be thoroughly cleansed and nearly two inches larger than the one the plant is in, or there will be no space to add fresh soil. Thorough drainage is of the utmost importance, and the best way to accomplish this is to place a piece of crock on the bottom that will nearly cover it. A concave piece is the best, and the hollow side should loe downwards, as a piece that lays too flat will impede the passage of the water. On this piece there should be one inch of pieces about the size of small nuts. To prevent the smaller particles of soil intermingling with them, it is necessary to place a little of the rougher portions of the soil in first. Having proceeded so far, the plant must be turned out of the pot and the old drainage carefully removed so as not to break the roots; the depth of the ball measured so as show what depth of soil will be required underneath, and an allowance of half an inch to an inch to an inch must be made at the top to admit of sufficient water being held at the time of watering. Pelargoniums delight in fresh soil, such as pieces of decayed turf of a brownish colour. Three parts of this to one of leaf mould, with a sprinkling of sand, will grow them well, and if the soil is inclined to be heavy more leaf mould should be added. The soil must be well pressed round the plant with a flat piece of wood, such:as we have described on previous cocoa- Mons. The plant should be in a moist state at the time of potting; it will net be so easy to soak it afterwards.

THE RESULT OF PERFORMING AN UNLAWFUL SURGICAL OPErtkrioN.—At the Liver pool A.94Z25, on Tuesday, Sarah Mallinson, 50, of Lower Broughton, and William Smart, 28, were indicted for the murder of a young woman named Brierley, of Stalybridge. Mallinson had, at the request of Smart and the deceased, performed an unlawful surgical operation upon the latter, with the result that death occur- red a few days afterwards. Subsequently to the operation Brierley was atttended professionally by Mr. Henry Est- court, surgeon, Pendleton, who was now called as a witnese, and who, in answer to Mr. Justice Butt, admitted that he knew it was a felony to attempt such an operation as had been performed in this case. The jury found both prisoners guilty, but recommended them to mercy. Sentence of death was passed. It is most probable that the sentence will be commuted, in accordance with recent decisions of the Home Office in cases of "constructed murder."

CURING FISH IN Isum.—Fish drying in the sun is ex- tensively practised in Some parts of India, and, so far as the thinner forms are concerned, with some success. In this form the fish popularly known as the "Bombay Duck" (Harpodon whereof) is considered a luxury. The present writer believes that a modification of a hot-air process, well known in America for drying fruit, might be successfully applied to Indian fish. In some localities small fish are buried in sea sand, that they may become slightly salted; they are afterwards sun-dried. In damp moist weather such fish rapidly decomposes, while in the hot months it is attacked by insects, which soon ruin it. The reader who has followed the subject so far, may wonder why, under the circumstances, there should be any trouble. Why not salt the fish, and have done with the question ? A large quan- tity is so treated—much of it with natural or rough earth- salt, the remainder with pure salt, so heavily taxed that the fish-curer has indeed a hard time of it. The reader who is in possession of the mass of existing evidence on this sub- ject will share the writer's natural indignation. Millions of our fellow-subjects—the term is used advisedly—fellow- subjects, taken as a whole people, as gentle and law-abiding as any under the rule of our gracious Queen, are half- starved, because no Government has yet found means to raise its necessary revenue without a heavy impost on what every Englishman considers a necessary addition to his daily food. The originators of the International Exhibition will indeed have reason to congratulate themselves if they can oblige our legislators to think more upon this subject. "The fishermen,'' says Dr. Day, "are among the most patient of the races of India, and the least likely to bring their griev- ances under notice." So much the more reason why it should be done for them.—" The Fisheries of the World." THE STORY OF CRIDIE.—Two years after his marriage there occurred one of the saddest incidents that ever fell to the lot of a noble, true-hearted man. A great fraud was perpetrated on the Stock Exchange, the price of funds hav- ing been raised by false intelligence of a victory of the Allied Armies. The bearer of the news was a man named De Bourg, or Beringer; this man was seen to enter Lord Cochrane's house, and it was notorious that a relative of Lord Cochrane's made an enormous sum of money by the panic. It was a golden opportunity ler the enemies of the gallant sailor to avenge themselves; they piled up report and rumour against him, and the result was he was brought to trial. Lord Chief Justice Ellenborough was undis- gnisedly biassed in his judgment against the victim, and the charge, which was brutal in its severity, led to his being found guilty, and sentence was passed. The sentence was— te stand for one hour in the pillory in front of the Royal Exchange; to suffer a year's imprisonment in the King's Bench Prison; and to pay a fine of £1,000! The public voice was too strong to allow the first part of the sentence to be carried out, and it was rescinded; but Lord Cochrane was expelled from the House of Commons; his name was struck out from the Navy List and the roll of Knights of • the Bath; and his banner taken down from Westminster Abbey—and it is said was kicked down the steps by an offi- cial. Never was degradation more terribly coniplete. But the knowledge of his own innocence, the comfort of his brave • wife's faithful love, the sympathy of his constituents at Westminster, who immediately re-elected him, being confi- dent that he was a victim of enmity, sustained him under the trial. Upon the £l,OOO note with which he paid:his fine, and which is still retained in the Bank of England, he wrote these words: "My health having suffered by long and close confinement, and my oppressors being resolved to deprive me of property or life, I submit to robbery to protect my- self from murder, in the hope that I shall live to bring the delinquents to justice." This was written when he had completed his term of one year's imprisonment; prior to that, after nine months' incarceration, he escaped from the prison, fell from a height of 25 feet, and for some hours lay insensible. Then he crawled to the house of an old ser- vant, and in a few days presented himself in Parliament, although a reward of 300 guineas was issued for his appre- hension. He was dragged from the House of Commons by main force, and confined in a miserable cell in the prison, where he remained until his time expired. It is curious to us of this generation to know that each a state of things could be in existence only so few years ago. The men of Westminster believed him innocent, and, as we have said,l re-elected him, though still a prisoner; the great mass of the people, with whom he was popular, believed him inn°. cent; even Lord Ellenborough's mind miogave him, and his health failed, for he too, perchance, aeliev ed in his inno- cence; men of all shades of political ?pinion looked coldly upon the eminent lawyer, and for a time society shunned him. For all that, it was 45 years before Lord Cochrane had his innocence proved, and his good name and honours restored to him.—Heroes of Britain in Peace and War.

Mr. Henry Irving was one of the candidates elected on Thursday as a member of the Reform Club, London. The Pall Hall Gazette hears that Mr. Buckle, who haS acted as editor of the Times during the late Mr. Chenery's illness, has been appointed his successor. The Government have done a graceful act in presenting the well-known Arctic discovery ship Alert to the United States Government, to be employed in the search for the missing Greely expedition. The Alert is being fitted out at Sheerness.

Mr. Marriott announces in his address to the electors of Brighton that he believes he is acting in the best interests of the country by throwing in his lot with the Conserva- tives. Mr. Romer, Q.C., the Liberal candidate, has already been interviewed by the anti-vaccinators. He refused to pledge himself to vote for the repeal of the Vaccination Act.

END OF THE COTTON TRADE STRUM—Thursday morn- ing brought the strike in the cotton trade to an end. When at its height there were nearly 30,000 people affected. It began in Darwen ten weeks ago and ended in the same town with the submission of the last 5,000 strikers on Thursday morning. At first there were only five mills affected in Darwen, but for three weeks there have been 24, of which 23 were restarted on Thursday. An attack on the privileges of the House of Lords is be- ing made in a by no means revolutionary quarter. The Council of the Senate of the University of Cambridge in- tend to propose to the Senate that peers and peers' sons shall no longer be excused the general examination and required to keep only six terms instead of the nine exacted from other members of the University. Our correspondent says the proposal will probably pass unopposed. ASSAULT UPON THE PROPRIETOR OF A COMIC PAPER. —At Glasgow, on Thursday, Shaw Maxwell, secretary of the Glasgow Sunday Society, pleaded guilty to assaulting Arnot Reid, proprietor of Quiz, a Glasgow comic paper, and was fined three guineas, The assault was committed at the rooms of the Glasgow Parliamentary Debating Society, Reid being knocked down. The Speaker and other main- hers attended the court. Mr. Maxwell, in extenuation, said that the comic paper had made insinuations about the funds of the Sunday Society. A COLLIER KILLED AT Sr. HELENS.—An inquest was held on Wednesday touching the death of a collier named William Hill, who lived in Church-brow, Chancery-lane, Parr, who died on Monday from injuries he had received on the previous Thursday, at Ashton Green Colliery. While deceased had been engaged getting 'coal part of his work- ing place gave way. He was knocked down and severely crushed. Having been extricated, he was conveyed home, and, in spite of the medical aid he received, he died on Monday. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. THE MILES PLATTING RITUAL CASE.—Sir Percival Hey- wood, writing to the superintendent of the Sunday schools at St. John's, Miles Platting, states that presently the "le- gality of the sequestration will have to be decided." This, he adds, "must be done before I, as co-trustee with two of my brothers, give up the proceeds of the living (other than those contributed by the Ecclesiastical Commissioners) which have accumulated since Mr. Green resigned his claim to them." Sir Percival adds that "the legality of the Bishop's institution of Mr. Evans will also have to be con- sidered."

TORY CAUCVS.—At a Tory caucus, at the Carlton Club, on Wednesday, Lord Randolph Churchill, Sir Richard Cross, Sir Michael.Hicks-Beach, Mr. W. H. Smith, and other re- cognised leaders of the Tory party responded to Sir Staf- ford Northcote's invitation. The majority of the meeting were favourable to the election of Mr. Arthur Peel to the Speakership, and it was agreed that no opposition should be offered to his appointment. The action of the party in re- gard to Mr. Bradlaugh was, it is also understood, considered, and the concerted action that was taken in the iliouse in the evening was, no doubt, the result of the understand- ing arrived at. FATAL SCaLDIXO CASE AT Sr. HELENS.—On Tuesday, a serious scalding accident occurred at 2131, Fark.road, St. Helens, the house of a collier named Jarftes Lancaster. Mrs. Lancaster, it appears, had for a short time gone out of the house, leaving a daughter, aged 14, in charge of other two Younger children, a boy and a girl. The elder girl also left the house, and while she was out one of the children over- turned a pan of boiling water which was standing near the fire. The boiling liquid poared over both the children, scald- ing in a dreadful manner their faces and bodies. One of the children has died from the injuries it received, and the other is in a precarious condition. RIVALRY BETWEEN Nmannouns.—Robert Johnson, a young man, was fined ss. and costs, at the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday, for having been drunk and disorderly in Elephant-lane Sutton, on the previous Saturday night.—lt seemed that there is a good deal of between Johnson and a rival shopkeeper at the other side of the street. On the night in question the neighbour, who is a fishdealer, was ringing his bell, and this seems to have so raised the ire of Johnson that he went into the street and apostrophised his brother tradesmen so violently that a policeman found it to be hi duty to intervene. Johnson denied having been drunk, but admitted having taken three "two-pennyworths," besides two glasses of beer. THE ALTILIII COLLIERY EXPLOSION.—Mr. A. Morlev's official report to the Home Office in regard to the colliery explosion at Altham, near Accrington, where 68 men and boys were killed, has been issued. The hon. gentleman considers that the mine was worked witti all proper care and vigilance, and he cannot recommend the institution of pro- ceedings against any person connected with its management. On the other hand, he indicates several improvements in de- tail which he thinks it would be advisable to adopt. Speak- ing of the origin of the disaster, which was clearly traced to a Davy lamp firing "on encountering a rush of gas, Mr. Morley says this confirms what has long been recognised by scientific and practical men—that the Davy lamp, whatever its value for testing purposes, "affords under circumstances which are far from exceptional or unlikely to occur very little protection to ordinary miners engaged in their perilous occupation." EXTRAORDINARY ABDUCTION C aSE.—At Birmingham, on Thursday, summonses were applied for by Samuel Dil- lon, Birmingham, hotel keeper, against Samuel Meade, for the abduction of his daughter Florence, aged 15, and also foi perjury and making a false declaration to the registrar. Dillon's daughter a well-known trapeze performer, per- forming with an elder and and a younger brother as Lillo, Este, and Echo—has appeared at all the leading concert halls in the kingdom. Meade, who hawks evening news- papers about Birmingham, is 22 years of age. He became acquainted with Lillo by frequenting the bar attached to her father's hotel, and on the 6th inst. married her at a registrar's office without her parents' consent, stating that She was 18, and an orptan. She returned, however, after her marriage to her father's house, but not till he had made an engagement with Mr. Barnum's agent, for the children to tour in America. On the 10th inst., when Meade de- manded his wife, the affair was discovered. ENGLISH PATENTS. The following patents, amongst others, published in the Official Journal of the Patent Office, were sealed during the week ending February 9th, 1884: Thomas Kenyon, of Eccles, for an improved process for the utilization of galvanizers' flux or skimmings and obtaning ammonia and zinc prodhet therefrom; Edwin Foden, Sand- bach, improvements in the construction of threshing machines; James Smith Hargreaves, Ashton-under-Lyne, improvements in the construction of looms for weaving; William Kemp, Millers Dale, improvements in kilns for burning lime; Henry Lesser Rothband, Goodman Mandel- berg, and Samuel Mandelberg, Manchester, improvements in waterproof garments; James Edward Schofield Thornhill, Beswick, near Manchester, Thomas Fornall, Fairfield, and Edward Thornhill, Ardwick, improvements in mounting the wheels of railway carriages, Ac.; Robert Hall, Bury, and Charles Ellis, the same place, improvements in looms for 'weaving; John Heywood and Robert Craib Ross, 'Man- chester, improvements in galleys and frames for holding set up type.—List supplied by Mr. George Davies, CE., Fel. Inst., P.A., Patent Solicitor, 4, St. Ann's-square, Man- chester.

EMPLOYMENT IN THE ENGINEERING TRADES.—EmpIoy- I ment generally continues fairly steady, and the returns for the past month, issued by the trades union societies, do not show any very material increase in the number of members in receipt of out-of-work support. The Amalgamated Society of Engineers has at present on its books about 3i per cent. of the members in receipt of out-of-work sapport. This represents the average for the Manchester and Salford dis- trict, which is generally a pretty fair indication of the state of employment throughout the kingdom. Many of the large engineerieg centres in Lancashire have been injuriously affected by the recent strike in the cotton trade, and reports from a considerable number of the districts return trade as drill. The report of the Steam Engine Makers' Society states that none of the branch returns are more cheerful as to tke prospects of a revival in trade, but trade was no worse, and the present number of out-of-work members is only a little over 11 per cent. In the Manchester and Sal- ford districts trade is returned as rather flat. The r, port alludes to a further attempt to reduce wages in the Bar- row district, which it was expected the men would firmly resist.

• --THE HOME SECRETARY AND LICENSING REFORM.—OR Wednesday afternoon a deputation from Liverpool had a private interview with the Home Secretary at the House of Commons, and presented an influentially-signed memorial urging the early introduction of the measure for licensing reform. Mr. Whitley, MP., introduced the deputation, which was occompanied by Lord Claud Hamilton, M.P., Mr. Samuel Smith, M.P., and Mr. W. S. Caine. M.P. The deputation consisted of the Ven. Archdeacon Bardsley, the Rev. Robert B. Baron, Rev. R. If. Lundie (moderator-elect of the synod of the Presbyterian Church of England), Rev. W. F. Slater, and the Rev. Father Nugent, accompanied by the Rev. Canon Ellison, chairman; the Rev. J. Howard Wright, clerical superintendent ; and Mr. A. Sergeant, general secretary of the Church of Eng- land Temperance Society. It was stated, in reply to Sir William Harcourt, that the memorial repre- sented by the deputation was signed by 711 out of a total of 830 ministers of all denominations in Liverpool and the Hundred of West Derby, viz., 316 from the Church of Eng- land, including the bishop, the two archdeacons, 14 canons, and six rural deans; 188 out of 230 Roman Catholic priests, including the bishop and dean, and 207 out of 250 Noncon- formist ministers including the Moderator-elect of the Presbyterian Synod and the President of the Wesleyan Con- ference. The memorial having been read, Archdeacon Bardsley, the Rev. R. H. Lundie. tbe Rev. Father Nugent, and Mr. S. Smith, M.P., addressed the Home Secretary. The right honourable gentleman asked the views of those present upon certain special points, and afterwards expressed himself in fall sympathy with the objects they had in view. The deputation cordially thanked Sir William Harcourt for his courteous and encouraging reception. am,.
