Twenty-five convicts -c-onfinei in the gaol at Goeletta made their escape on Friday night. Immense damage has been done to the city of Arequipa and its environs by toe bursting of a waterspout. Several persons lost their lives.
In the Dominion House of Commons at Ottawa, on Saha- day a bill to incorporate the Royal Orange Associhtions of Canada was read a first time. '

A reduction of wages, ranging from five to one per cent. has been announced by a number of mill corporations at Manchester, New Hampshire. The Servian Ministers have resigned. The Ministerial difficulty has been caused by a difference between the Con- servative Cabinet and the Progressists. A letter has been published which professes to give Cetewayo's dying words, declaring his son Dinizulu to re- present the embodiment of his name and rights. A new organisation composed chiefly of Europeans and native landholders has been formed in India tinder the title of "The Indian Constitutional Association." The declared objects of the new association are to maintain the integrity of the permanent settlement, and to oppose dangerous and revolutionary legislation. A corresponding committee is to be formed in England. t,eePrince Bismarck has taken a step which is probably without a parallel even in his aggressive career. He has refused to receive the resolution of condolence which the United States House of Representatives passed with refer- ence to the late Dr. Lasker, and has sent it back to Washing- ton. The Chancellor says, in effect, that the House of Representatives had no business to express an opinion as to the political career of Dr. Lasker. A change of some interest to shipowners trading to Russia has lately been agreed to by the Department of Commerce in the Ministry of Finance at St. Petersburg. A circular has been addressed to the Customs offices, stating that, in accordance with the Finance Minister's proposal, sanctioned by the Emperor, foreign vessels provided with home certi- ficates showing that they have been surveyed for tonnage measurement on the Russian system will, during the present year, not be subjected to examination on their arrival in the Baltic, Black Sea, or other ports of tha Empire. A SECT OF CIIILD MURDERERS.—The Novoje Vremja warns Russian mothers of a new religious sect, which has already given several proofs of its existence. In Rostov, on the Don, an officer engaged a middle-aged nurse for his three-year-old son. She was very attentive, and seemed to love the child, but after two months she suddenly left the situation and the town. The child began to all the very next day, lost its memory, and suffered from continual drowsiness. A week later it died without having been really ill. The corpse was placed in the ooffin, when a young Jewess burst into the house, threw hereelf upon the , dead child, and crying bitterly, said: "The same woman poisoned my child. She was my nurse before, and now she has murdered your poor boy 1" The woman spoke the truth. It has been found that in Rostov there is a society' of child murderers, who poison children by means of nar- cotics. They are instigated to do so by a fanatical woman, who says, "It is every woman's duty to spare the evils of life to as many children as possible, and to make them par- ticipate in the bliss of heaven before the earth has con- taminated their souls." SURRENDER OF MEI/V.—The news of the surrender of Mery to Russia is confirmed by the Russian Official Ga:ette. The semi-official Russian press is instructed to state that "English public opinion has now abandoned its former pre- judices against Russia with regard to Merv." We are told that although Mery has been absorbed, Sarakhs "wilt never be occupied by Russia," and that another " under- standing ' between the two Empires is necessary to enable them to carry out their "civilising mission." " A' Persian statesman of the highest eminence" has sup- plied the Vienna correspondent of the Standard with some observations on this event. The advance to Mery is univer- sally regarded as another step in the deliberate design of Russia to absorb all the countries which lie between her. possessions and our Indian Empire' and if Mr. David Urqu- hart had been living now he would have told us to expect, as the Persian statesman does, a "demonstration "on the Indian homier whenever England and Russia are on bad terms through the conflict of their interests in Europe. In the opinion of the Persian statesman, tbe Turcoman tribes could, if they were supplied with modern weapons by Russia, bring to their feet one Indian province after another. Persia, "repulsed from Herat and betrayed by England.", has no alternative but to "seek an understanding witk her mighty neighbour, whose advances England seems unable or =willing to prevent.'
IMPERIAL __PARLIAMENT._

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. LORD ROSSMOBE.—Lord DUNHAVEN brought forward his resolution, declaring that Lord Rossmore's removal from the Commission of the Peace was "not justified by the facts, and was calculated to discourage the loyal party." 'I he noble Lord declared that the fullest extent of Lord Ross- tnore's offence was an "error of judgment," and contended that extreme measures ought not to have been adopted.— Lord CARLINGFORD said the subject of the debate had for- gotten his position as a magistrate, and, remembering only -that he was an Orange Grand Master, he deliberately cast aside all warning and advice and adopted a course which led to the danger they sought to avoid. This resolution was regarded by the Government as one of censure upon the Lord Lieutenant and the Lord Chancellor of Ireland, both of whona would be placed in a very painful position if it should pass that House.—Earl CAIRNS accused the Execu- tive of having abdicated its functions and then punished , Lord Rossmore for doing what they ought to have done themselves.—The Lord CHANCELLOR Said it would have been imposible, consistent with administering justice in Ire- land, to have overlooked such a Violation of a magistrate's Plain duty.—Ultimately the motion was withdrawn in com- pliance with requests from Lord Dunraven's friends. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. COLONEL KINi3-HARMAN.—M r. TRETELYAN informed Mr. Healy, who had made inquiry about a disagreement between ColonelKing-Harman and one of his tenants, that it did appear that a tenant had been deprived of the right of free turbary for voting for a certain candidate at an election of Poor-law Guardians, and he added that in the opinion of / the Government the only remedy for such a course of pro- : ceeding was vote by ballot. MY—The PREMIER, in reply to Mr. Onslow, read two telegrams from Her Majesty'e ambassador at St. Petersburg, and said they appeared to imply the virtually complete sub- miseion of the Mery Turcomans to Russia. The Govern- ment had some information from the Minister at Teheran, but it was of a less definite and precise character. GENERAL GORDON'S PROCLAMATION.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE questioned the Premier about the proclamation posted in Khartoum purporting to be signed by General Gordon.— Mr. GrAnsrosru said he did not think it would be possible to extract the true meaning of the proclamation from the summary, but he thought it would be found in no way to derogate from General Gordon:a well-known senti- ments. THE TOTE OF CENSURE.—The debate on the vote of cen- sure was resumed by Sir JOHN LUBBOCK, who thoroughly supported the Government; but Mr. Marmon', who spoke Next, was bitterly censorious, and declared that there bad Only been consistency in vacillation, and consistency in inconsistency. "Too late," he declared to have been the motto of the Government. He believed the country had lost confidence in the Government, and to test his opinion be would as soon as he had recorded his vote apply for the Chiltern Hundreds, and go down to Brighton to see whether his constituents would not endorse his censure by re-electing him.—The debate was continued by Lord John Manners, Mr. Waddy, Mr. S. Leighton, Mr. Slagg, and Mr. Ritchie.—Mr. CHILDERS then intervened, and, observing that he did not wish to spoil sport, promised that Mr. Marriott should have the Chiltern Hundreds on application, though at the same time be warned him that the omens were not in his favour, as members who had already made an appeal to their own eonstituencies had met with a cool reception. He very happily congratulated the utember for Brighton on having shown more adheson to his Constituency than to his party, his speech having been a Singularly hostile one to proceed from a member sitting on the Government side of the House.—On the motion of Mr. ASHBIES.D-BARTLETT the debate was adjourned. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. GENERAL GORDON'S PROCLAMATION—The Marquis Of SALISBURY interrogated the Foreign Secretary with respect to General Gordon's prcclamation, and contended that com- plications were likely to arise from that portion of it bear- ing upon the slave trade.—Earl GR.ANYILLE said that General Gordon bad sent a short telegram announcing the Proclamation, but until he had seen the proclamation itself it was impossible to give any explanation on the subject. The only instructions given to General Gordon on this Matter were that he was to pay especial consideration to the question of what steps might usefully be taken to counter- act the stimulus which it was feared might possibly be given to the slave trade by the insurrection- ary movement and the withdrawal of Egyptian authority. He was certain that General Gordon kad not done anything that was likely to increase existing evils in the Soudan with regard to slavery. I THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) BILL. The Duke of RICHMOND and GORDON moved the second read- ing of the Contagions Diseases (Animals) Act, 1878, Amendment Bill. He said it seemed almost impossible to Prevent foot-and-mouth disease from being carried from the landing wharf, and it was for that reason that he thought that cattle should not be imported from'any country where the disease existed.—Lord CARLINGFORD said the object of the Government bill, the second reading of which he Should shortly propose, was restriction, while the object of the Duke of Richmond's measure was exclusion. He would not, however, trouble their lordships logo to a divi- MOM—The bill was read a second time. The Government Bill on the same subject was also read a second time. MEET—Lord ELLENBOROIIGH having asked if there WAS any confirmation of the news about the submission of the Mery Turcomans to Russia, Lord LAMINGTON said that Earl Granville had that day received despatches on the subject from St. Petersburg, and that these despatches required con- Sideration. The news, he might say, was confirmed. HOUSE OF COMMONS—TUESDAY.

GENERAL GORDON'S PROCLAMATION.—Some anxiety was evinced to become acquainted with the exact terms of General Gordon's Khartoum proclamation, but Lord E. FITZMAIIRICE stated that the precise terms had not yet been received.—Subsequently a question was put as to the sen- tence referring to uninterrupted facilities to be accorded to the slave trade, and Mr. GLADSTONE remarked that any pro- ceedings of the kind would be as much out of the purpose Of General Gordon's mission or the instructions given him as they were out of harmony with his whole nature and character. The right hon. gentleman added that he had no doubt that the key to the business lay in the distinction between slavery in the Soudan and the slave trade. THE VOTE OF CENSURE: GOVERNMENT MAJORITY.— The debate on the proposed vote of censure was resumed by Mr. ASRMEAD-BARTLETT, who suggested that an alternative Policy to that of the Government that the Mandi must be overthrown and his power broken.—Mr. HOULDSWORTIT • followed, and in a maiden speech defended the Egyptian Policy of the Beaconsfield Administration. As to the Dual Control, the hon. member contended that the present Go- vernment did all they could when they came into power to make it wore permanent than it had been before; therefore they could not now turn round on their predecessors and bola them responsible for the events which had happened. He contended that the real origin and spring of the troubles Which beset the Government in Egypt was not the Dual Control, but the fear of and shrinking from intervention, and that a policy of non-intervention, so far as England was concerned, could never be con- sistently maintained. His belief was that it was the true Policy of the country to intervene wisely and prudently, and above all in time, but never unless there was a resolution to maintain with determination, perseverance, and effect !Inch intervention.—Mr. T. P. o'Comeon having spoken in u,tvour of the proposed vote of censure, Mr. J. CowEN in- sisted that the Government had turned their backs upon the Principles professed at the time of the election when they Went to Egypt, and that they could with easy and equal unanimity turn their back on the principles they bad pro- !eased shice. It was not, he said, their sincerity but their judgment was impeached. They had been attempting the impossible. He had not yet mastered the species of political ethics that enabled a man to think one way and vote another, and he therefore meant to support his opinion by his vote—The debate was continued by Mr. I'. C. Bruce, Mr. Ecroyd, Mr. al.Coan, Mr. Chaplin, and Mr. Goscben. The latter gentleman contended that unforeseen events had arisen to upset the earlier policy of the. Government, but the Government had fully and frankly accepted the situa- tion. Polite fictions were discarded and energetic action substituted. The despatch of the 4th January had been written, and action had been titkeu upon it. This altered the situation, and justified the renewed confidence of Par- liament and the country in the Government. He urged that not sufficient account was taken of the stupendous dif- ficulties that stood in the way of the Government. Of these he particularly noted the practice of cross-examining Ministers in the House of Commons, and by pereistence eliciting from them declarations of policy which subse- quently became embarrassing and even danger- ous. Amid loud, cheers from the Liberal benches, he declared that he never remem- bered except within the last few years such a system of cross-examination and of putting questions not intended to draw information, but to set up a case for future use against Ministers. Mr. Goschen did not attempt to say that In hie opinion a more distinct avowal of responsibility at an earlier date would not have avoided much of the trouble. Amid loud cheers he ooncluded a powerful speech by oh- Serving that he had been asked to have the courage of his Opinion and give his vote to the Opposition. He bad the Courage of his opinion, but he had not the temerity to give a blank political cheque to Lord Salisbury.—Mr. GIBSON Congratulated the Government upon getting Mr. Goschen's vote and the country on getting his speech.—Shortly after Midnight Lord HARTINGTON rose, and was received with loud cheers from the Liberals. His speech was, as usual, Vigorous and more than usually animated in its delivery, and in the concluding passages, in which he carried the War into the enemy's camp, he was continually cheered.— Sir Stafford Northcote haying replied, and Sir W. Lawson having withdrawn his amendment, the House divided on the main question. 262 voted for the resolution and 311 against. The majority of 49 for the Government—and against the combined forces of the Parnellites and Conser- vatives—was hailed with pi °longed cheering from the Liberals.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. GORDON'S MISSION—The PREMIER made a brief state- Ment on the subject of General Gordon's mission, and ex- Pressed a hope that the House would not be inclined to rnragl en- e a discussion which might interfere with the de- iverY of the Egyptian forces from the Soudan. The right on. gentleman -added that the only hope of delivery was afforded by the qualities of General Gordon in the difficult task he had undertaken. THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.—Mr. O'CONNOR POWER 1109Wited the debate on Mr. Parned's amendment to the Address by declaring his disappointment with the character Of the amendment of the hon, member for Cork. He pro- ceeded to protest against the House of Commons being

called upon to devote its time to the consideration of the sectional differences which prevail in Ulster between the National League and the Orange Society. The hon. mem- ber for Cork had not in his speech made any suggestion of practical legislation of any kind, and as he and his friends were instrumental in setting aside the proposals of the Government, there was a strong responsibility on them to bring relief to the evicted tenants of Mayo and other parts of the west of Ireland who adopted a certain policy on their recommendation and had not found it as snccess- ful as.they wished. There was a point beyond which an aggressive policy must fail, and the cause of Irish nation- ality could not be furthered by a policy of exasperation. He believed the great mass of the English people were will- ing to offer to Ireland equal privileges, and to concede to that country as much self-government as was compatible with the supreme authority of the Imperial Parliament and the integrity of the empire. If they found a Government disposed to go more than half way to meet their legitimate demands, it was an unpatriotic policy to pursue that Go- vernment as if they were the enemies of the human race in general, and tha people of Ireland in particular. Notwith- standing all that had been done, he expected to see the strife brought to a close and succeeded by a permanent union such as was contemplated by Grattan and O'Connell, who, though intense in their nationalism, were still loyal to the unity and integrity of the empire.—Mr. HEALY, in a bitter attack upon the last speaker, alleged that the whole personal and political life of the hon. member was strewn with the wreck of broken friendships. He complained that the Government would neither put down the " rowdies," nor let the Irish do so, and that the law was not impartially administered in Ire- land as between Orangemen and Nationalists. The founda- tion of justice was poisoned, and all the Government offi- cials delighted in practising tyranny on the Irish people.— The debate was continued by Lord Lymington, Lord G. Hamilton, Mr. J. Wearthy, Mr. S. Smith, and Mr. Macartney, and it was adjourned on the motion of Mr. MOLLOY. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. .

THE CONTA—GI—O—U;D—I9EATRS—(ANIMALS)BILL.—The Duke of Richmond's Contagious .L.lieeMies (Animals) Bill passed throngh Committee with an antendment bringing the Act into operation immediately it passed, instead of en the Ist October.—The House then went into Committee on the Government Bill on the same subject.—The Duke of Rica- moND proposed an amendment declaring that when the Privy Council were not satisfied with the sanitary condition or laws of a foreign country in this matter they should pro- hibit importation. The bill, he thought, should be brought into conformity with Mr. Chaplin's resolution.—Lord CARLINGFORD opposed the amendment.—The Marquis of SALISBURY said it was evident that the President of the Council contemplated the admission of diseased cattle as a condition precedent to shutting out the importation. The amendment was carried by 75 votes to 45. The Duke of RICHMOND next moved the omission of the clause limit- ing the operation of the Act to two years; and after several noble Lords had expressed their views or. the point. Lord CARLINGFORD consented to the clause being struck out. THE PREVENTION OF FLOODS.—hi reply LO the Earl of Camperdown, Lord CamatßoYobr said the Government were determined to bring in a bill for the prevention of floods as soon as the state of public business would allow them to do so.

div.head: SOUDAN.
div.p: THE SOUDAN.

A meeting of chiefs who have hot hitherto taken patt in the revolt has been held at a short distance from ::nakim, and a decision was arrived at to march against Osman Digma if he did not respect their territories. The garrison of Tokhar appears to be in better heart than WAS expected. They have made a sortie and inflicted some loss on the besiegers, besides capturing a quantity of cattle. The British force is rapidly concentrating at Suakim. , The mission of General Gordon is being watched with great interest by the French Government, and it is reported , in diplomatic circles in Paris that M. Barrere has pointed out to M. Ferry that the present time affords a good oppor• tunity for France to regain the position which sha lost bY the abolition of the Dual Control.

We learn from Cairo that, acting in accordance with the representations of Sir E. Baring, the Government have de- cided to reinforce the army of occupation in Egypt by a battalion of infantry from Malta and a battery of garrison artillery. lroops will be moved up to Malta from Gibraltar to replace those which are being sent from that fortress to Alexandria.

There are, it appears, altogether over 30,000 Egyptian troops in the Soudan. Of these 4,000 are stationed on the Nile not farther south than Khartoum, about 8,000 are at Massowah and towns near the Abyssinian frontier, about 5,000 are in Darfour, 3,700 are en the White Nile, and over 2,000 are in the Equatorial provinces, seven or eight weeks' journey by steamer south of Khartoum, and there about 4,000 on the Blue Nile, the majority of these being at Sen- noar. Fully one-half of the men in these garrisons and the population that they protect depend for their rescue upon General Gordon.

Further correspondenee with General Gordon is published. Earl Granville telegraphed to him, through Sir K. Baring, four days ago, asking if he bad any suggestions to offer., The General replied from Berber that he had announced his assumption of supreme authority over the Soudan. With regard to the proposed expedition to Baakim, he said he tached great importance to the mere rumour of British in! tervention. He suggested that the chiefs should be told tO meet him in an assembly of Notables at Khartoum, to dis- Cuss the. question of . independence. The rising at Kassala was known to him, but he regarded it as merely the uprising of the people against their local oppressors. A Cairo telegram states that the Khedive has come to the conclusion that It is desirable to disband the Egyptian army forthwith, as ills not only worthless but dangerous. This decision appears to have followed the appearance of a body of Egyptian soldiers at the Abdin Palace to present a peti- tion protesting against the despatch of Egyptian troops tO the Soudan, and demanding the removal of the British officers, who, it was urged, were aliens to the Egyptian race and religion. The mutineers, who declared that they repre- sented the sentiments of the whole of the Egyptian army, were arrested, and marched off to prison handcuffed. The demonstration does not appear to have been a serious affair.

General Gordon has passed through all the dangers which lay upon his route and has reached Khartoum. Before his arrival a proclamation signed by him was posted on the houses in the city, recognising the Mandi as Sultan of Kordofan, remitting one.half of the taxes, and declaring that no restrictions would be placed on the slave traffic. This proclamation has been sent to the tribes. The reference to the slave trade is liable to misconception, as has been shown by the question put in the House of Commons. It is believed that the General only means to say that his present mission has nothing to do with the slaves, and that his latest declaration is for no other pnr- pose than to save the beleaguered garrisons and clear Tur- kish and Egyptian officials out of the Soudan. In coll. firmation of this view it is pointed out that General Gordo* proposes to go round to the Congo with the object of cutting ell slavery at its source. A telegram from Khar- toum states that the arrival of General Gordon led to a "wonderful demonstration" of popular enthusiasm, and the reaction has been so great that fears are co longer enter- tained for the safety of the town and garrison. With re- ference to the famous "slavery" proclamation, it is remem- bered that Gordon, before he left England,deciared against compulsory and immediate emancipation. He was in favour of gradual emancipation. FIRING HEARD NEAR TRINKITAT.
Firing was heard early on Thursday morning in the direc- tion of Trinkitat.

The march on Tokhar will, it is hoped, begin ,on Sunday. Reports have reached Suakim that Osman Digma has sunk' mooed the tribesmen from great distances to assemble round his standard, and that he will be able to confront General Graham's column with 30,000 men. A mishap has occurred to the Neera, a hired transport which was engagsd to earrY the 19th Hussars to Suakim. The ship ran asliore near that port, but the weather was calm, the fleet was close at hand, and the Hussars were transferred to war steamers and car- ried safely to their destination. The full text of General Gordon's proclamation has been telegraphed, but much fuller information as to the state of affairs at Kharton? must be given baore the General's reasons for issuing It can be thoroughly understood.

lIFFIANISM AT PRESCOT.—At the Prescot Police Court" on Tuesday, eight young men, named David Welsh, Joh° Thompson, William Riley, John Mellior, Philip RaneY, Thomas Mulloy, William Hora, and James Nulty, Were charged with having committed breaches of the peace at Prescot on the 2nd inst. Buperintendent Barker said that from about the 25th January till the sth February gangs 0! young fellows had been going about the streets of Proc°j assaulting persons whom they met, and also shoating an,_ • making a great disturbance. Having heard of this, (Superintendent Barker) determined to put a stop to it, a? summon all whom he could find. A youth named DOI% J. Holcroft said that on the night of the 2nd instant be.w'l' in Kemble-streer, where all the defendants were also group. One of them came up to him and knocked down, when he was set upon and kicked until he wati scions. Other witnesses corroborated this statement. v defence, it was sworn that Welsh had been in the Quee4 ,1 Hotel on the night in question, and he was conserplel3o discharged. Each of the other prisoners was bound overa keep the peace for three months, themselves in one surety of £5, or in default of sureties 14 days' IMPflS°' mrnt.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-THURSDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-THURSDAY.

MR BRADLADOH.—The SPEAKER read to the House a letter he had received from Mr. Bradlaugh, stating that with the consent of his constituents be would undertake not to present himself under his new return for the purpose of taking his seat until after the hearing and judgment in the suit which the Crown was about to bring in order to test the legality of his proceedings in the House on the 11th inst.—Sir STAFFORD NORTECOTE moved to re-affirm the two resat utions made on the 11th of February, directing that Mr. Bradlaugh be not permitted to go through the form of taking the oath prescribed by the statutes, and directing the Sergeant-at-Arms to exclude him from the precincts of the House unless he shall engage not to disturb the proceed- ings of the House.—Mr. GLADSTONE agreed that it was desirable to keep the House from uncertainty as to the particular moment any further step might be contemplated by Mr. Bradlaugh, but in his opinion there had been a great change since they last heard of the matter, and he thought it desirable that they should consider ac- curately and ascertain clearly the position in which they stood, and choose one of two courses that lay before them. He proposed that the judgment of a court of law should be obtained by the Attorney General with all possible despatcb, and he thought that pending that decision they ought not to take any fresh step for the exclusion of Mr. Bradlaugh 'unless there were some strong reason for doing so. The en- gagement of Mr. Bradlaugh removed all danger of his sud- denly presenting himself at the table. He believed that no greater disservice could be rendered to religion than to plac3 it in conflict with the principles of civ " right and justice which commend themselves to all men. The retirement of the House from this contest must come at some time or other, and the question was how and when.—After some discussion the House divided on the previous question, moved by Sir J. PEASE, when there were —for putting the question, 226; against, 173. Sir Staf- ford Northcote's motion was then put and agreed to.—Mr. BRADLAUGII was requested by' the SPEexaa*to leave the House, and the hon, member said he obeyed the direction, respectfully protesting against persecution degenerating. into illegality.—The adjourned debate on the address was resumed by Mr. MOLLOEY.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO THE MEDICAL SUPERINTENDENT AT HAYDOCK LODGE.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO THE MEDICAL SUPERINTENDENT AT HAYDOCK LODGE.

On Friday evening last a very interesting ceremony took place at the Haydock Lodge Asylum. It appears that Dr. Shaw, M.D., of Queen's College, Ireland, has for a period of nearly five years held the responsible office of Medical Super- intendent of the Asylum, during which time he has gained the goodwill and esteem of all those with whom he has been brought into contact. Accordingly, on its becoming known to the officers, attendants, and servants that Dr. Shaw had accepted another engagement, and so was about to leave them, it was decided that they should offer him some tan- gible mark of their esteem and high regard. A subscription list was at once started, and the sum of £2O was soon realised. The subscribers having a desire to present Dr. Shaw with something useful as well as ornamental, it was resolved to consult his wishes on the matter. This was done, and the assistance of Dr. Watkins, of Newton-le- Willows, was then sought for, and readily obtained; and as a result a magnificent case of scientific instruments were supplied to order by a London house, and these, together with an illuminated address, were duly presented to Dr. Shaw, on Friday even- ing last. The occasion was made festive by Dr. Shaw giving the subscribers a ball, the number present being about 80. An efficient quadrille band, under tile leadership of Mr. Lythgoe, of Wigan, was in attendance, and discours:d an excellent programme of dance music to the evident delight of all. The dance commenced about eight o'clock, and was continued for a couple of hours, when, during an interval, the pleasing ceremony of making the presentation was gone through.—Mr. Thomas FORSTER, the male (head) attendant was called upon to make the presentation, and in a brief speech spoke in eulogistic terms of the affability and genial kindness which they had all experienced at his hands. In conclusion he begged the Doctor to accept the proffered to- ken of their esteem and regard. He then read the address which ran as follows :—To James Shaw Esq M.D., Queen's University, Ireland. We, the officers, attendants, and ser- vants of the Haydock Lodge Asylum, deeply regret your leaving us. We gratefully acknowledge your unvarying kindness to all of us, and many of us are specially indebted ' to you for our education and training in the enlightened and humane performance of our responsible duties. We congratulate you upon the widely recognised success of your work here for now nearly five years, and we rejoice in the esteem and regard your earnest devotion in the pursuit of your noble profession has won for you. We ask your acceptance of the accompanying scientific instruments for the work of precision and research, and trust they may prove of great value to yon in an extended field of useful- ness. We unite in cordially wishing you a happy, pros- perous and long life.—Signed on behalf of the subscribers, George Weeks, Clerk and Steward, Thomas Forster, Male (head) Attendant, Jessie Logan, Female (head) Attendant. February 15th, 1884. Dr. Saaw very feelingly acknowledged the gift and ex- pressed his gratification at the very substantial pioof which they bad given him that his services had been appreciated by those with whom be had been brought into contact. In conclusion, he thanked the subscribers for their very hand- some present, and assured them that in their use he should be pleasantly reminded of those who had given them.—The dance was then resumed and kept up with much spirit until about one o'clock, when the company dispersed, all being highly satisfied with the evening's proceedings.—The pre- sentation was valued at over £2O, and the refreshments for the party were supplied by Messrs. Thomas Prescot and C. Webster, Warrington-road.

BALL AT NEWTON—The second annual ball in connec- tion with the Earlestown and Newton quadrille class, was held in Newton Town Hall, on Friday evening last. There was a very large attendance of members and friends, who thoroughly enjoyed themselves in dancing to the strains of Messrs. Stirrup's band from Warrington. The party sepa- rated about five o'clock on the following morning. NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL BAND OF HOPE.-011 Wed- nesday evening, a very pleasant entertainment was given by the members of this society, assisted by a few friends from Ashton. The chair was occupied by Mr. R. Horridge. In the cowse of the evening J. Corless re- cited " The Traveller's Rest," W. Crompton gave "A I Queer Catch," T. Pilling (accompanied by W. Pilling) sang Tom Bowling," A. Walmsley recited "Consequence Of Disobedience," Mr. Merry recited "The Poor Man and the Friend," W. Crompton gave an amusing recitation entitled "The Pancake Night.' "Rocked in the Cradle of the Deep" was sung by A. Seddon, "Jack's Menagerie " was rung by H. Pearson, Mr. Corless recited "The Old Bell Mon," Miss Annie Naylor gave "A night with a Wolf," Mr. T. Merry read an amusing piece " Ab' o'th Yate and hie Mi-too-ral-oo," T. Pilling sang "Give me the Man of Honest Heart," Mr. Merry recited "Temperance expects I every man to do his duty,' Mr. Seddon gave "Binghen on the Rhine," Mr. James Randall mated "Every man in his own place," and Miss Rothwell very nicelyegave a song, the accompanist being Mr. T. Martindale. Mr. Jones said that he, on the part of the members, had great pleasure in thanking the friends from Ashton in coming so far to enter- tain them; and Mr. Seddon briefly acknowledged the com- pliment. THE PHENOMENA OF SLEEP.
PAPER READ BEFORE THE MdUUNGTON

LITERARY SOCIETY. A meeting of this Society was held on Thursday evening, when the following interesting paper on "The Phenomena of Sleep," was read by one of the members. the Rev. H. G. Smith, B.A. The chair was occupied by the president, the Rev. Canon Dodd. The Rev. CHAIRMAN, in introducing Mr. Smith, took oc- casion to speak of sleep and dreams from their various as- pects. He alluded to the extraordinary powers which they found themselves suddenly possessed of when asleep, and which when awake they were totally unaware they possessed. He daresay some of those present had spoken most eloquent orations and excellent poetry in their sleep whilst they were totally unconscious of being either orators or poets in their every-day life. The rapidity of thought was also very remarkable. They knew when they were awake that thoughts passed through their minds with extraordinary rapidity, and it was quite possible that in dreaming their thoughts might come with equal rapidity. Having spoken of the re- freshing nature of sleep, Canon Dodd facetiously remarked that it did not follow that because they were going to hear something about the philosophy of sleeps and dreams that therefore the subject was a "sleepy" one, or that any member of the present audience would be justified in going to sleep during its delivery. (Laughter.) The Rev. H. G. SMITE read as follows:—" Half our days we pass in the shadow of the earth, and the brother of death exacteth a third part of our lives," says Sir Thomas Browne, in words that have been often quoted. Every night, under ordinary circumstances, we pass into a state which, if known to men only once in a century, would be regarded is a mystery without parallel; a state in which, as Dale Owen says, "we enter another world, where we see, but not with our eyes; where we hear, when our ears con- vey no perception; in which we speak, in which we are spoken to, though no sound pass our lips or reach our organs of hearing. In that world we are excited to joy, to grief we are moved to pity, we are stirred to anger; yet these emotions are aroused by no objective realities. Our judg- ment is usually obscured, and our reasoning faculties are commonly at fault; yet the soul, as if in anticipation of the powers which the last sleep may confer upon it, seems emancipated from earthly trammels. Time has lost its landmarks. Oceans interpose no barrier. The past gives back its buried phantoms. The grave restores its dead." It is not strange, then, when one comes to think of it, that so little investigation has been made into the character of this remarkable phenomenon? We may say that practically nothing has been added to our knowledge of the subject since the days of Aristotle, upwards of two thousand years ago. However, it must be allowed that this subject in particular, like all the departments of mental philosophy in general, is very difficult to approach on account of our incurable ig- norance as to what mind is, and as to the connexion between mind and matter. Here is a scientific investigation in which no new scientific apparatus is needed, and no new scientific method applicable. All that is wanted is careful and minute observation of one's own thoughts. Anyone present this evening, by keeping a good diary of his own sleeping and waking thoughts, has as much opportunity of enlightening the world aboot this most peculiar problem as the greatest psychologist who ever lived. But though from the nature of the subject it is difficult to obtain results beyond what have been obtained already, one cannot help being astonished that there has been so little interest in the matter. Encyclo- paedias that devote long pages to an account of the writings and life of Joanna Zonaras, or to the natural products of the Revillagigedo Islands, are silent on such a hum.drum subject as sleep. " All knowledge," says Aristotle, " springs from wonder in the first instance." Because sleep occurs every night there is nothing wonderful about it, just as the Pyramids are nothing wonderful to the Egyptians, or Niagara to the Americans, or Mount Everest to the Indians, or Vesuvius to the Neapolitans. If I shall succeed to-night in exciting in anyone this wonder which leads to knowledge, or suggest to anyone any line of inquiry on which the subject can be ap- proached, I shall be more than satisfied. Of information on the subject little can be given, for the very simple reason that no one has ever succeeded in getting to know much about it. Now what is it that we all expect te do when we go to bed to-night? Well, I suppose the first thing we shall do will be to put the light out. What is the reason of that? Evidently to prevent our sense of sight from being stimulated. In the next place we endea-vour to hear no sounds, either by the precaution of being in a quiet room or by covering our heads with the bed clothes if the street is noisy. Evidently we do this to revent our sense of hear- ing from being excited. Again, we lie in soft beds; it is very hard to go to sleep upon boards. This must be to pre- vent the sense of touch from being excited more than is necessary. Thus we see that, generally, it is a condition of going to sleep that the senses mast not Oe under excitement. Another important condition is that we should not employ our minds in reasoning out any subject, or anxiously follow- ing out any line of thought. A man with a troubled mind cannot go to sleep. The best condition of mind is to cease to exercise our will over our thoughts, and simply let them run on and on, connecting themselves by any link of asso- ciation that they please. Many people, especially children, are brought into such a state of mind by some monotonous or crooning noise, or some gentle and easy motion, like rocking; a sharp and quick noise on the contrary, however regular, is too exciting; as, for instance, the ticking of a clock. A child may be sung to sleep, while a man may be thrown into sleep by a posture of the head, by a full stomach, by a dull or difficult book, or by a long sermon. When these conditions are satisfied, people in a state of health, and after some amount of fatigue or nervous exhaustion, usually begin to relax gradually the muscles of their bodies, the blood begins to leavrethe lerain, and in a short time they are what we call asleep. Their vitual functions still go on, their digestion is not impaired, their blood circulates, the circulation in the brain only being diminished ; and their breathing, though slower, is more regular. If we took the trouble to watch a sleeping person all night, we should find that his bodily temperature sinks towards morning. If the person bad been so unfortunate as to lose a part of his skull-bone and dune meter, thus expos- ing a corresponding part of his brain, we should see his brain lying apparently motionless within the cranium if he were in what we call a sound sleep, but moving and pro- truding from the aperture if he were dreaming, just as it would move and protrude if awake and actively engaged with mental occupation, but not quite to the same extent. This phenomenon was actually observed by Dr. Perquin, a French physician, in a patient of his, a female of 26 years of age. This motion and protrusion of the brain, it was noticed, did not occur in jerks alternating with recessions, as if caused by the impulse of arterial blood. It remained steady while the agi'ating cause lasted. So we see there are three separate m :ILA states, with corresponding action of the brain: the waking state, in which the brain gives signs of full activity; a state called dreaming, of which I shall have something to say anon, during which there is still brain action, though in a diminished degree; and a third state exhibiting no outward proof of dreaming, and leaving be- hind no remembrance of dreams, and during which no brain action can be seen. At the same time it is a great assump- tion to declare, as some do, that in this third state there is no brain action and there are no dreams. All that we can logically say is that during this state of apparent functional inactivity, brain action is much diminished, and dreams, if there are any, are disconnected by memory or otherwise from the wakeful period of our existence. The question whether we can sleep without dreaming is as old as Aris- totle. If under dreaming are included all chains of thought, however weak, I believe that future investigation will answer in the negative—that we never sleep without dreaming in some degree. For it is a question, surely, of degree, not of kind, when a person is in a light state of sleep the slightest sound, a touch, or a small increase of light disturbs and makes him restless in his sleep, even if it does not awake him. If lie is rather more sound asleep some effort is needed to shake him, or a loud noise must be made; if be is very sound asleep he will perceive none of these sensations. But if you tickle his toes you will make him wince. And he still goes on breathing, and all the other parts of his constitution carry on their functions. Now such actions as winking when the eye is dry, drawing away the feei when tickled, and so forth are cases of what is called reflex action; that is, the sensation which the dry- ness of the eye or the tickling of the feet conveys to the brain is not always mentally recorded, nevertheless an exer- tion is made and a bodily function is called into play to remedy the want without the necessity for any effort of the will. Now no constitution, however healthy, can carry on all its functions without there being some slight irritation in some part. As soon as irritation occurs it be- comes noticeable and unconsciousness ceases. In sleep such irritation affects the mind, i.e. has its reflexion in the mind, I as it were ; a strong example of this is nightmare in case of indigestion. "The cucumber" you "ate and don't digest" presents an awful spectacle reflected in your mind's mirror. . Of course, I do not wish to imply that dreams arise only from functional irregularities, more or less slight. But I contend that if no other topic engages the mind the body is always ready to supply the want in some degree of vivid- ness. Another reason why I demur to the theory that in sound sleep the mind is a perfect blank, is, that the argu- ment "I can't have dreamt, for I don't remember my dreams," involves an assumption which can easily be shown in most cases to be in disagreement with facts, when a per- son says " I never dream," what he really means is, "I never remember what I have dreamt about." But if you watch him when asleep, you will very likely at times either hear him mutter something or see him move his lips, which he could not possibly do if his mind, were a blank. Even sonmambulists seldom, if ever, know when they wake up, that they have been doing anything bat sleeping quietly. Again, if you take the trouble to observe the moment you wake up, what a train of thought your mind is following out, you will perceive that you must have been dreaming , even if you cannot well remember all your dreams. Or get someone to wake you suddenly and ask you some question immediately on your waking, and your wild and peculiar answers will betray the thoughts that have recently pos- sessed your sleeping moments, and convict you of being a dreamer after all. But, you will' say, the theory of those who hold that the mind can become a blank in heal thy sleep, is that dreams occupy the short period of passing to the waking state. Now I cannot see how this is to be proved. Of course it is true that just before waking sleep becomes more light and the inn ,geii which pass through the mind more vivid; but how are we to prove that this is the only period of dreams? People remember, it is true the dreams that they have dur- ing light sleep and just before waking, better than others, but that is because the lir lin is at that time in a more sen- sitive condition, resembling more nearly its waking state And, on the o, ,er hand, people in really deep sleep will not unfrequently eaow signs of inward disturbance by mutter-

div.head: THF'EXAMINER, SATURPAY, FEBRUARY 23.1884.
div.p: THF'EXAMINER, SATURPAY, FEBRUARY 23.1884.

lug, moving the limbs, and even shoaling. If you shake a person in this condition, or speak loudly to him, you will not wake him in very many cases; he is too sound asleep for that; but the shock you will cause to him will have the effect of diverting the unpleasant ideas which are harassing his mind, and he will become calm and will breathe regu- larly. Ask such a sleeper when he wakes up what it was that disturbed his sleep, and he will, as often as not, be quite ignorant that he had had any dreams at all. And really, when one comes to consider the matter, would it not be strange after all if we could remember our dreams as a general rule? First of all, the brain of a sleeper is less sensitive than that of a tvakeful person and, therefore, less able to record its own movementk In the next place a dream is in itself much more difficult to recall than any series of sensations belonging to the waking state, because in dream- ing the will is not employed to choose or reject the various ideas that crowd into the mind and array themselves before the mind's eye in all aorta of fantastic permutations and c imbinations. It is, of course, always much easier to recollect ideas which have been linked together by a definite order of asso- ciation than those which are not connected by any single underlying principle. For instance, it is compara- tively easy to remetnbcr a list of names all beginning with the same letter, while it is by no means easy to do this with another list in which some words can be connected in our minds by similarity of sound, others by similarity of mean- ing, others yet by similar initial letters, and so on. Still more difficult would it be to remember a number of words hastily put together without any recognised or conscious association either of sound or meaning. Now this is lust the case with dreams. They are connected together, for the most part, by the faintest and most casual links, and the will has not been exerted ha fasten those links; and for this reason I believe it is alr but impossible for anyone to remember every dream which has passed before his mind during sleep of several boars. Another reason why we cannot generally remember our dreams is given by Sir William Hamilton. "In our waking and our sleeping states, he says, "we are placed in two worlds of thought, not only different but contrasted, and contrasted both in the character and in the betensity of their representations. When snatched suddenly from the twilight of our sleeping imaginations, and placed its the meridian lustre of our waking perceptions, the necessary effect of the transition is at once to eclipse or olibetate the effect of our dreams. The act itself also of rousing us from sleep, by abruptly interrupting the current of our thoughts, throws us into a confusion, dis- qualifies us for a time from recollection, and before we have recovered from our consternation, what we could at first have easily discerned is flown or flying." The last reason I can adduce for our forgetfulness is the rapidity of dreams, and at the same time their confused character, which Aristotle wel: compares to the clouds on a breezy day, now like to the shape of a man, now of a monster, now to no shape at all. It has been said that a man can dream more in a minute than he could act in a day. Cases have been known of people having complete dreams between the first and last strokes of a clock striking the hour of twelve, or between the successive jogs of a horse when asleep on horseback as people have been. Sir Henry Holland tells us that he has dreamt and awaked from his dreams so often as three times in a minute when in his carriage. Such being the rapidity of dream!, surely the wonder is that we recollect them so often and 89 completely. Let me now briefly summarise the evidence on which Kant, Leibnitz, Sir IL Holland, Sir William Hamilton, Descartes, and Hip- pocrates conclude that sleep is never quite dreamless. (1) Because it is natural, for the reasons I have just given, that dreams should easily pass out of our memory. (2) Because after giving signs of dreaming, such as talking, moving the limbs, or walking in sleep, persons are equally oblivious of the dreams thus indicated. (3) Because careful attempts to recollect dreams made im- mediately on waking are rarely unsuccessful, if ever, and in particular, on being awakened suddenly out of sound sleep at various times he the night Sir William Hamilton, who was himself a very sound sleeper, always found that he was engaged in following out some train of sleeping thought. (4) The fact that the brain betrays no motion to the eye during sound sleep in cases in which it has been possible to inspect it, does not prove that it is perfectly , inert or devoid of consciousness. For, as Dr. Wilson Philip , has shown, this would be death, and not sleep. The vital and sensitive systems cannot exist independently of each other. It is at once evident that the sensitive system can- not exist without the vital; in plain words, a dead body cannot feel. It is less evident, but no less true, that the vital system cannot exist without the sensitive. The bond of union between the two systems is the function of breathing. The muscles of respiration are muscles of voluntary motion. We exert them, more or less mechanically, but still voluntarily, when the vitiated condition of the air in our lungs causes us uneasiness. Consequently, if our brains became perfectly inert in sleep We should cease to breathe. And if they do not become per- fectly inert, sensation in the brain does not cease to exist, and same sort of consciousness or sleeping thought does remain. For these reasons it is held that sleep cannot be absolutely dreamless. It remains for me now to say a few words absut one or two of the normal, and also about one or two of the abnormal phenomena of sleep. I have just been trying to show that dreams are not merely normal but invariable con- comitants of sleep. So far I have meant by " dreams " all chaies of thought that prevent the mind from becoming a blank during sleep, all forms of consciousness which occupy the mind during our so-called period of unconsciousness in slumber. lam not prepared to assert that all our dreams are, so to speak, pictorial, though I think we may safely say that the majority of dreams, and certainly all dreams which we can remember, have passed before our mental vision as a panorama, apparently objective to us at the time. Locke'a definition of dreaming is as follows—" Dreaming is the having of ideas, whilst the outward senses are stopped, not suggested by any external object or known occasion, nor under the rule and conduct of the understanding." It is a serious matter to criticise a definition given by the author of the famous essay concerning human understanding, but nevertheless this definition cannot be acc.mted. As is pointed out by Dale Owen, whose scientific acuteness cannot be doubted, though his somewhat eager credulity as regards the marvelloua makes one hesitate, as is pointed ont by . Dale Owen, Locks ignores the fact that during sleep the outward senses are only partially stopped as a rule ; and thus ideas frequently:are suggested by external objects and by physical sensations. And sometimes the understanding, instead of being dethroned, acquires a power and vivacity beyond what it possesses even in the waking state. As a proof that the senses are only partially stopped during sleep. I may instance such cases as when the rumbling of a passing cart is interpreted by the sleeper to be a thunderstorm in his dream. And one ought to notice in this connexion that sleepers can get into the habit of making inferences from familiar sensations, and, by the aid of memory, can interpret them correctly. An alarum which wakes you for a few mornings after a while loses its usefulness. Why? Because you hear its familiar burring sound in your dreams, and infer, by the help of memory, that it is nothing to be alarmed about ; it no longer suggests that the end of the world is come, or that the roof is falling in, or that the town is being bombarded by an enemy's cannon. Perhaps it may occur as a difficulty that you should infer that it is tirne to get up, and that you should rouse yourself. Qeite so ; but then loss or partial suspension of will is one of the condi- tions of sleep, a condition which immediately precedes and follows sleep, as dreaming often does. It is hard to exert will in order to rouse oneself either just before sleep, when one is beginning to doze off, and also just after sleep. Unless you drop off to sleep very suddenly your dreams also begin before you are actually asleep And I dare say some here this evening know how after vivid dreams, occasionally the sleeper on awakening, fancies for a few moments that he sees unreal objects ie the room about him. For instance, a boy who has been dreaming of hunting tigers in the jungle, on waking up, may actually think he sees a tiger disappear round the end of the bed. Let me now go on to illustrate the second objection to Locke's definition, viz., that some- times the understanding, instead of being dethroned, acquires a power and vivacity beyond what it possesses even in the waking state. Here lam able to give you two instances well known to myself. An old schoolmaster of mine once actually got up and worked out a mathematical problem in his sleep which he had in vain toiled at in his waking moments. The other instance is that of a boy, who, being asked when asleep by his brother where the matches were, his brother thinking him awake, got up silently, went to a drawer, took out a lo'ox of vestas, and handed it to him. The box of vestas was half-open, and he handed it to his brother upside down, so that all the matches fell out, but the sleeper was not disturbed by this. Nose the most remarkable part of the incident is yet to come. In the morning this boy not only remembered nothing about his sleeping adventure, but maintained that he never knew that there were any matches in the particular drawer from which he took them. My explanation is, that he must have known at some time that matches were put into the drawer, and that he had forgotten the fact. His brain, however, being clearer in sleep, he was enabled to recollect what was prac- tically unknown to him when awake. Just one mere instance of this. Abercrombie, in his "Intellectual Powers," tells us that that very unimaginative and practical person,Dr.Frank- lin, asserted that the bearings and issue of political events which had puzzled him when awake were not unfrequently unfolded to him in his dreams. Possibly it may seem hard to reconcile these cases with my previous statement that the brain was less sensitive in sleep; but though less sen- sitive in recording its movements, it is sometimes no less active and clear in operation. Why should the brain be sometimes clearer during sleep is a not unnatural question. I think we may explain the matter by pointing out that the working of the mind is then undisturbed by the external world. A man cannot concentrate his attention on his book, or his writing, or his mental problem if he is sitting at a window which looks on a busy and interesting street, or if there is a noise in the house, or if the room is full of smoke, or if he is hungry or in pain, or, in short, if the sensations of the external world distract' him. But in sleep what is to distract his thoughts? He is no longer alive to the outward world except to the very limited degree which I have already indicated. Why, then, is it not likely that he should be able to accomplish mental feats all but impossible to him in his wakeful hours, suggested to him, as they so often are, by his predominant in- terest at the 'time. The very fact that dreams are so rapid—a fact to which I have already alluded—shows the activity of the sluniberer's mental powers. And this rapidity of dreams brings us to the consideration of another curious and interesting phenomenon' namely, the idea of iime in sleep. Consider the two following cases, cases which, I think, must be familiar to everyone in this room: (Ist) You drop asleep—say in a railway train—for five minutes. and wake up with a start, thinking you must have been asleep for as many hours, and that you

must have passed your station. (2nd) Ton drop off to sleep on going to bed and sleep for seven or eight hours; but it seems ecamelv more than five Minutes from the time you go to sleep to the time when the servant knocks at your door and makes her main- final offering of " Hot water, sir?" My explanation of this apparent paradox is, that in the first case you enly drop into a light sleep for the few minutes that you are asleep, and that all sorts of dreaming ideas course through your brain with the literal and proverbial quickness of thought. Consequently, you more or less unconsciously judge that your sleep has been prolonged, just as you judge that a street at night is long by observing the number of lamps twinkling ilea row up to the point where they vanish. The rapid succession of thoughts in your mind makes five minutes seem like five hours. Again, I think we may find another parallel to this phenomenon in the fact that when a man makes a journey or takes a walk which is new to him, it seems much longer than when it becomes familiar to his eye. Why? Because the number of unfamiliar objects of interest which attract his attention become gradually dimin- ished as they become known to him, and cease to engage conscious observation; his acts of attention are fewer, and therefore be thinks the journey is shorter. Does not this consideration irresistibly remind us alsoof Kant's theory,that time is but a form of thought? Without thought could time exist ? Or, again, if perfect knowledge of the past, the pre- sent, and the future took the place of thought, limited by human conditions, can we not dimly apprehend that with such a Being one day leas a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day? And may we not under- stand in this light, as some do, the words of one greater than the great German philosopher, "And the angel which I saw stand upon the sea and upon the earth, lifted up his hand to heaven, and sware by him that liveth for ever and ever, who created heaven, and the things that therein are, and the earth and the things that therein are, and the sea and the thiegs which are therein, that there should be time no longer." Return- ing from this digression, I must hasten to conclude these remarks on the normal phenomena ef sleep. Before Ido so I should like to call your attention te the analogy which subsists between dreaming and insanity. On this matter I cannot do better than quote the astute remarks of Sir Henry Holland. He says, "if it were an object to obtain a des- cription of insanity, which might apply to the greatest number of cases of such disorder, I believe this would be found in the conditions which most associate it with dream- ing, viz, the loss, partial or complete, of power to distin- guish between unreal images created within the sensorium and the actual perceptions drawn from the external senses, thereby giving to the former the semblance and in- fluence of realities and secondly, the alteration or suspension of that faculty of mind by which we arrange and associate the perceptions and thoughts successively coming before us." I suppose we may sum this up by saying that the priniary character- istics of insanity, as of dreaming, are, (1) loss of will, (2) loss of judgment. We must again observe that Aristotle in his day almost, if not quite, reached the high-water mark of our knowledge on the subject. He surmised with his native acuteness that the same cause which, in certain diseases, produces deception of the waking senses, is the origin of dreams in sleep. Thus we may say that a dream put into action might become madness, in oqe or other of its frequent forms ; and, conversely, insanity may often be called a waking and active dream. The chief point of difference between the waking hallucination and the dream of the sleeper is the superior vivacity. of the former. It would not be difficult to wander rather far afield in illustrating this point, and to digress from the main road into interesting by-paths. I will, however, ask you to allow me to suggest to you this topic for your own consideration, and pass on at once to the inquiry " Can dreams have a prophetical character ?" Undoubtedly, as Christians, we must believe that dreams in times past have been frequent vehicles of divine messages to humanity. "In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falleth upon men in slumberings upon the bed, then God openeth the ears of men and sealeth their instruction." Job xxxiii, 14. And these words are consistently illustrated by narratives of prophetic dreams in other parts of the Bible, such as the dream of St. Peter at Joppa, and others which it is unnecessary for me to quote. I should say, before going further, that I am considering this as one of the abnormal phenomena of sleep. Is it possible that it has been, since the Apostolic age, even an abnormal phenome- non? We must answer that we cannot deny the pos- sibility of the phenomenon prima facie, as we cannot deny any proposition which does not invoke' 3 the violation of any of the primary laws of thought. All we can do is to sift and examine carefully the evidence for every occurrence of the phenomenon. If we find that ninety-nine alleged instances of dream-prophecy are untrustworthy, but that the hundredth is genuine the point is proved. And it is important to remember how tempting this subject is in its appeal to the love of the marvellous in all imaginative persons. It is most important therefore to discount all evidence of such phenomena,since unconscious exaggeration is apt to creep in and distort or over-colour the story. At the same time we must remember that all races of men at all times have had belief in the prophetical character of dreams existing amongst them. There are not a few people living now, in this incredulous nineteenth century, who even believe that every dream has a mystical meaning, and that there are certain laws by which all dreams may be ex- pounded. I have extininsd a large number of cases of prophetical dreams with a good deal of interest and as much impartiality as it is possible for me to feel. I think that a very large number may be explained away, and on the rest I reserve my opinion. It seems to me that this is the course which is most logical. It would be perfectly illogical to conclude that dreams could not be prohetical, unless it were possible to prove that a prophetical charecter was inherently inconsistent with dreaming. Such cases as the story which is told of a certain distinguished French author, ROW living, are full of interest but scareely prove the point. It is said that this Frenchman dreamed that his daughter and her husband would be drowned on an ex- pedition up the Seine, which was to come off on the day following the dream. He was full of alarm and begged them not to go; they laughed at his fears, and went, and met with the sad fate of which he had drearht, but too truly. Now, let us consider the evidence; a fond and and anxious father, who probably apprehends dan- ger every time his child goes out of his sight, finds once that his sleeping terrors and his waking sorrows c )incide ; but what of the many times they do not coincide? They are forgotten, but the one coincidence is graven in memory as in steel. Again, there was a remarkable case told in the newspapers a short time ago of the dream of a young man living near Durhani. A child—not related to, or connected with the dreamer—had been lost and there was fear that the little unfortunate had been drowned. Every likely piece of water was dragged, but to no purpose. At last this young man dreams that the child's body is seen by him in a cer- tain pool quite eat of the way, and of which no one had yet thought. Acting on this suggestion, they search the pool, and the poor little body is found there. What are we to make of this? I think we are justified in referring this cm to the clearness of thought which frequently is known in a dreaming brain. The sleeper thought the case out; all the likely places, he remembered, had been searched ; he then thought of the less likely places, and most likely ar- rived at the truth by sifting the probabilities of the cases, in just the came way as the mathematician thinks out the pro- blem asleep which was too much for him awake. Now if be had dreamt accurately about minute details, say, of the child's dress, or position in the pool, or so forth, we should be bound, I think, to accept his dream as a proof. But I have been unable to get any evidence of this kind at first hand. I do not say that It cannot be got, but only that I have not got it. And, speaking generally, since extraordinary matters need ex- traordinary proof, I think we must conclude that belief in dreams of this sort as facts must be based entirely on per- sonal experience; as possibilities I see no reason for oppos- ing them. We now come to the less abnormal phenomenon of somnambulism, in which the sleeper acts his dreams; that is if his dreams call forth muscular movements correspond- ing to them, we call this phenomenon somnambulism, or sleep-walking. Probably everybody here has heard of some cases of this peculiar phase of sleeping action. It will be su- fficient, therefore, if I note briefly someot the more noticeable characteristics of it. Sometimes the somnambulist's atten- tion is so cornpletely fixed upon his own trains of thought that he is only conscious of external impressions which are in harmony with them. No ordinary sounds, odours, pricks, pinches, or blows make themselves felt; and yet if anything be addressed to the sleeper which is harmonious with the notion that is occupying his mind he may take cognizance of it and interweave it with his thought. Carpenter gives an instance of a young lady formerly known to him who, when at school, frequently began to talk afier being asleep for an hour or two, 'her ideas," he says. "almost always ran upon the events of the previous day; and, if encouraged by leading questions addressed to her, she would give a very distinct and coherent account of them. To all ordinary sounds, however, she seemed perfectly insensible. A loud noise would awake her, but was never perceived in her sleep-talking state. And if the interlocutor addressed to her any questions that did not fall in with her train of thought they were completely disregarded. By a little adroitness, however, she might be led to talk upon almost any subject ;—a transition being gradually made from one to another by leading questions." It is an important and distinctive feature of the somnambu- listic state that there appears to be in it a dual consciousness. For while neither the trains of thought nor the actions of that state can be recollected in the waking state, they are frequently remembered on the recurrence of the somnambu- listic state, even after a very long interval, and of this in- terval there appears to be no consciousness whatever. The same thing happens, but more rarely, in ordinary dreaming —the dreamer sometimes recollecting a previous dream, and even taking it up and •continning its thread. Carpenter again gives us the illustration we require : "A servant maid," he says, "rather given to sleep-walking, missed one of her combs, and, being unable to discover it on makin.; the most diligent search, charged the fellowmervant who slept in her room with having taken it. One morning, however, she awoke with the cord) in her band, therhei,, remembrance of the occur- without preserviee any waking rem emembrance be no doubt that she had put it away on a previous night occur- rence, and that sris had recovered it when the remembrance of only wl'ttl eitsst,hareiningtaiceehwitahsabdroubogenht steOcrheeterd.b"y the recourrdremncoereof. it has beta said that if our dreams were onay a e thmerev self-consistent and had a little more order an sequence e. tenafiliutyenoctedurjoe some degree those would be another life. judgment and loss of will in external world. &SANFORD PLOUGHING IVILTCFL—The Rainford annual ploughing match was held on Weclnet.day on a fled in Moe- borough-lane, Rainford, in the occupation of Messrs. Ciare and Fazikerley. The first-class prizes, open to all England, ranged from £5 down to 10s, while the second-case prizes. set apart for non-prize winners since 1878 varied from £4 to 10s. Altogether there were 22 covvetitors. The follow- ing is a list of the prize winners :-4 John Banks, plough- man, Burscough ; 2, Thomas Blackburne, farmer, Skelmers- dale ; 3, John Wilkinson, ploughman, Ditton ;- 4, William Wiswall, ploughman, Rlinford ; 5, Chas. Sephton„ Plough- man, Rainferd. Second-class: 1, Saml. Reshot- ham, ploughman, Rainford ; 2, James Web- ster, ploughman, Penketh ; 3, Henry Caldwell, ploughman, Rainford; 4, George Fishwic'a. ploughman, Upholland ; 5, Henry Hooltan, ploughman. Skelmersdale ; 6, John Walsh, ploughman, Rainford.—Third clase: 1. Richard Birchal I, ploughman, Rainford ; 2, Stephen Greve.. ploughman, Bickerstaffe ; 3, John Mills, ploughman, Rain- ford. Mrs Berry, Lathom, won the first prize for the beet turnout, and Mr Peter Beardman the second prize. The judges for ploughing were Messrs John Halehall, Hale Bank, and John Bulberry, Haydock; and Messrs D Ledson, Fazakerley, J Barnes, Liverpool, and J Jarvis, Liverpool, for turnouts. It may be mentiened that the work on the whole was considered to be very good. RAINHILL. ' We understand that the Rev. William Danks, MA., of Queen's College, Oxford, formerly curate-in-charge of Rain- hill, has been presented to the vicarage of St. Margaret's, Ilkley, near Leeds, in succession to the Rev. Henry B. Ottly, MA. CHURCH Scaoot SERMONS.—On Sunday, the 17th inst., special sermons on behalf of the Church Schools were preached by the Vicar. Large congregations attended both services. The collections amounted to £l2 13s 84, a sum slightly in excess of the amount collected at the last school sermons. A Row AT RAINHILL.—At the Prescot Police Con en Tuesday, three women named Elizabeth Cooper, Elizabeth Ball, and Margaret Houghton were each bound over to keep the peace for having committed a breach of the peace at Rainhill.—John Houghton, the husband of one of the above- named defendants, was else charged with having threa- tened Elizabeth Cooper on the same day as the breach of the peace occurred, but the case was dismissed. Rano= REFORM CLUB COMPANY, LitgmEn.— Regis- tered on the Bth instant, with a capital of £l5OO, in £1 shares, with the following as first subscribers :—S. W. Raw- lins, Rainhill, Prescot, manufacturer, I share; A. Cross, Rainhill, Prescot, 1; T. Hanmer, Prescot. manager, 1; W. Evans, Whiston, average adjuster, 1; G. Tomkinson, Rainhill, accountant, 1; J. Shackled, Rainhill, broochmaker, 1; S. Mercer Rainhill, toolmaker, 1; J. B. Thomson, Rainhill, accountint, 1. Registered without special articles.

MAGIC LANTEIIN ENTERTAINMENT.—A, magic lantern entertainment was given in the Boys' School on TueAday evening last. The apparatus and slides were kindly lent by Mr. B.G. New, of Kirkdale, Liverpool, who had arranged to be present to show and describe the pictures, but was pre- vented by illness. Two exhibitions were given ; the first at six o'clock, for school chitdren and members of the Band of Hope, was well atterded ; but at the second, at eight o'clock, for adults, the attendance was but moderate. The views were illustrative of 'The Pied Piper of Hamelin ;" "Jane Conquest," "Meg and her brother Ben ;" and the humourous story of "The Tiger and the Tub." The pic- tures were shown by Mr. J. Robinson, of Liverpool, assisted by Mr. D. Seddon, while the descriptive narratives were read by the Rev. J. Barton, Mr. J. Iligbam, and Mr. J. Rudge, ma m inner that added materially to the interest of the entertainment. The proceeds were on behalf of the Band of of Hope held at the Church Schools, under the presidency of the Vicar.

BENEFIT CONCERT —The enlargement of the Rainhill Asylum has been the means of introducing into the neigh- bourhood a large number of hi;hly-respectable artisans from Yorkshire and other parts, who have readily placed their varied and artistic musical abilities at the disposal of friends for charitable and social purposes. Oa Wednesday evenine last this excellent spirit of cordiality was shown in a most exemplary manner in the way in which they willingly came forward and, with the assistance of the Misses Keefe (Rainhill), Mr and. Mrs Webster (Huyton), and Miss H. Wood as accompanist, gave an interesting concert on behalf of two of their fellow- workmen, Messrs Phythian and Barstow, who for three months, through sickness, have been incapacitated from fol- lowing their usual employment. The programme, consist- ing of songs, duets, and pianoforte selections, was an ex- ceptionally long and varied one. The respective performers acquitted themselves remarkably well, but special mention should be made of the humorous songs of Mr. G. Hurst, the popular humourist aud mimic. This gentleman:was a host in "himself, and in his songs, "Baby's got a tooth" and "The Showman," especially the latter, kept the audience in roars of laughter, and was vociferously encored. The Misses It. and K. Keefe were in excellent voice, and ren- dered their songs and duets in a manner that gained for them the hearty plaudits of the audience. Mr and Mrs Webster, of Huytou, who on this occasion made their first public appearance in Rainhill, sang the "A B C duet," and the songs, "The British Lion" and "The Blind Girl's Dream" in a most artistic manner. Mr Morgan in all his songs, especially "The Death of Nelson," displayed a capltal tenor voice, and sang in a most finished and refined style. As accompanist Miss H. Wood rendered valuable assistance, and in her selections played with energy and great taste, her performance of " Com-e-Gentil," by Don Pasqual. played with the left hand only, was decidedly a musical novelty, which showed to great advantage all the abilities of the performer. There was a crowded audience, which represented only a portion of the tickets sold, so th 4 in ill probability a good surplus will be left for the needy recipients.
