ASHTON. ST. THOMAS'S SCHOOLS, ASHTON.—The annual congrega- tional tea meeting in connection with St. Thomas's Schools, Ashton, was held on Monday evening, when a large number of persons sat down to a most excellent and enjoyable tea. After all had partaken of the good things provided, a mis- cellaneous concert was held, when there was an increased attendance. The programme was an excellent one, and consisted of both comic and sentimental selections, several of the pieces being given by the singers attired in appropriate costume.

CADISELEAD. WATER Surky.—A public meeting was held in the Con- gregational School-room, on Tuesday evening, to determine the question of water supply for Cadishead and Irlam. There was a full attendance. Tne subject was thoroughly debated with spirit and harmony. It was resolved to have the water brought in pipes on the conditions laid down by the Barton Rural Authority, viz , to pay £5O a year pro-rata to spread over the entire district of South Barton for five years. There is a lamentable lack of good water, generally speaking, in the district, especially in Irlam. In some in- stances people have been obliged to make use of water hardly fit for cattle. In some of the houses of Cadishead the supply is good and ample. The pipes will be laid forthwith, with the understanding that it is a matter of choice as to whether the people receive it into their houses or no.

. . SERVICE OF SONG.—A service of sacred song entitled " Moses " was generously given on Wednesday night, in the Wesleyan schoolroom, on behalf of objects in connection with the Cadishead circuit—Wesleyan. It commenced at eight o'clock. The weather was wild and stormy, which to soma extent interfered with the attendance. 'l'. Hacking, Esq , circuit steward, read the connecting parts, which gave the history of Moses in full outline, The names of the songs were, The ark of rushes," A joyful mother," The escape," Holy Lord," The promised land," Be of good courage,' A father's hand," Waters turned to blood," The Egyptians' cry,' The Passover," I' he deliverance," Hosanna,' The pursuit," Fear net," Onward," Pharoah baffi ad, 'The overthrow,' Praise to the conqueror.' The parts were well rendered, sung with precision, taste, and tune. The harmony was thoroughly sustained throu..,,hoet. Conductor Mr. T. L. Browne. Mr. N.Whitfield ably presided at the organ. The best thanks of the meeting were presented to Messrs. Brown, Browne, and Whitfield, and to the members of the tonic:sol-fa class for the generous kindness to the funds of , the circuit.

GOLBORNE. TEE APPLICATION FOR ADDITIONAL POLICE FOE GOLEORNE.—At the last meeting of the Golborne Parochial Committee, the Surveyor (Mr. C. S. Bennie) reported that he had obtained 80 signatures of the principal ratepayers to the memorial asking the county justices to provide the township with two additional police constables, and it had bten forwarded to Colonel Moorsom (chref constable.) On the 4th instant he (the surveyor) received a letter from Mr. Superintendent Weir, stating that Colonel Moorsom had directed him to acquaint them that he would lay the memo- rial before the justices at the proper time, but that increases of the strength of the police force were not resolved upon until the autumn, except under the most urgent circum- stances.

MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—The meetings of this society were resumed on Monday evening last, when a paper on the "Methodist Rules" was read by Mr. J. D. Janes, of Runcorn. The essayist, in a lengthy paper, showed the adviaability, and also the practicability, of keeping those rules. The following gentlemen spoke—viz., Messrs J. H. Gamon, R. Hughes, S. Barrow, and J. Looker. Rev. S. Mees presided. _

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

DRAMATIC ENTERTAINMENT AT HAYDOCE —A dramatic entertainment, entitled "The Sleeping Beauty," was given in the English Martyrs' Catholic School, liaydock. on Mon- day evening last. The proceeds were in aid of the school funds, and we are glad to hear that a good sum was realised —the schoolroom being filled with an appreciative audi- ence. The various characters in the piece were taken by the scholars, and, as on a former occasion when the same piece was performed, t hey were creditably sustained through- out. _ _ _

HOLLINS GREEN. SLANDER. CASE: THE EFFECTS OF IDLE GOSSIP.—At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, a case of slander, which had been repeatedly adjourned, cams or. for hearing before the Judge(W. Wynne Fioulkee, Esq.), and in which Mrs. Charlotte Petford, innkeeper at Hollins Green, sued the defendant, Joseph Shaw, a publican residing in the same township, for £lOO, as damages for slanderous statements to various people in Hollins Green, respecting her.—The plaintiff was represented by Mr. J. T. Moore, and the defendant by Mr. W. H. Jenkins.—lt transpired that the case had been remitted from the High Court of Justice, and Mr. Moore intimated that the parties had agreed to a ver- dict for the plaintiff subject to the question of damages being referred to the Registrar.—Mr, Jenkins said he agreed to the course Mr. Moore had mentioned. He would take this, the earliest opportunity be had had, to express on be- half of the defendant the regret on his part that cause for this action should ever have arisen, that the repetition of idle village gossip should have been made by him, and re- sulted as it had done in that serious action. It was only due to the plaintiff to.make that public apology on behalf of the defendant, who now expressed his deep regret that cause for the action should have arisen. His Honour remarked that it was the proper course to take, and the case dropped.— We hear that considerable interest had been excited in the minds of the good people of Hollins Green concerning the action, as many thought Some spicy details connected with the alleged slander would be forthcoming. It looked like this at one time, counsel having been communicated with by both sides to appear in the case, but on second thoughts. which are always said to be the best, it was deemed expedient to come to an amicable Settlement. SHOOTING GAME WITHOUT A LICENSE: WHERE WAS THE Przteaseerr ?—At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday, a young man named James Arstall, of Hollins Green, was summoned that he did on the 30th November use a certain gun for the Purpose of killing and pursuing certain game, to wit, a pheasant, not having a certificate for the same.—Mr. Ray, supervisor of exise, appeared to prose- cute on behalf of the Inland Revenue, and Mr. Garthwaite, of Manchester, appeared for defendant—lt appeared from the statement of Mr. Ray that Messrs. Hargreave and Taylor. the owners of certain land at Hollins Green, had been to considerable expense in rearing game, but having lost numerous birds from time to time, it induced the game- keeper on Friday, the 30th November last, to secrete himself in the willows by the side of the bank to detect anyone in t pursuit of game on the opposite side. The pheasants, it seemed, were in the habit of crossing thewatreppaend te three ee willows in the early part of the day. of or four others were seen coming fromth c Defendant villagelot walking towards the canal bank. The gamekeeper eight them for a few minutes, but shortly afterwards he heard one or two shots fired. Arstall was neat observed walking along the river bank with a gun over his shoulder and looking at the top of the willows, and after going a few yards be saw a hen pheasant rise. Defendant took adeliberate aim at it and the bird fell apparently dead. The gamekeeper then made himself, known to defendant, and challenged him with the act, upon which the latter jumped over the fence and ran away,— This statement was corroborated by the gamekeeper, Daniel , Greave, but was denied in toto by Mr. Garthwaite, who said ' that his client had a perfect right to be on the land in ques- tion, but he was not in pursuit of game. Defendant was in the field about nine o'clock, and he tried to shoot a rabbit, but he was so skilful that he could not hit it, although be had two or three shots at it. The pheasant only existed in the imagination of the gamekeeper, He called witnesses, whose evidence was to the effect that on the Lancashire side of the water, where defendant and the other men were observed, no pheasants were ever seen.—The magistrates considered that nothing could rebutt the evidence of the g timekeeper, who Saw the pheasant fall, and inflicted a fine of 40s. but without costs. SCHOOL BoArtm.—The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Board School on Tuesday evening. Pre- sent—the Rev. T. P. Kirkman (chairman and clerk), and Messrs. asmes Hatton. Lewis Birchall. Richard Turner, and Alfred Dixon (attendance officer). Time attendance officer presented his report, which stated that he had visite4 the various schools in the district during the past month, when be found that 44 children bad been away sick during the month from various causes, but most of them had recovered, and were now attending school. He also st.ted that he had served two notices for children to attend school in pursuance of bye-laws, and one notice of warning to parent under sec- tion 11: also that he had warned five parents that unless their children attend school more regularly they will be summoned to appear before the Board to show a reasonable excuse for such absence. The report having been adopted and several accounts passed, the proceedings terminated. WINSPORD.

A FAITHLESS HUSBAND—The utmost excitement pre- vailed at the Wahanton end of Winsford on Saturday morn- ing. An ex-guard of the London and North-Western II iil- way Company, who had left his wife and four children to get on as best they could, and had turned them out on Fri- day night into the bitter cold, was himself the subject of popular fury such as no one ever saw at Winsford before. Re had been obliged to flee from home on the facts becom- ing known that he had left his own wife for a neighbmr- idg lady, in addition to his bad and unkind treatment of them. He tiad for refuge to the railway station, and had to be locked up from the wrathful populace—who secured as 14 they would tare him to pieces. Again at night the same was once more enacted, so that ths police locked the man up into the police station. Even that was a God-send to the ntan. Trio lesson will not soon be forgotten by him. div.head: sttion.
div.p: sttion.
By Mr. JOHN ILAKINSON.
By Mr. THOMAS TUNSTALL.

BY a majority of 49—the numbers being z6z votes for, and 311 against—the House of Coin' mons has very properly rejected Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE'S motion,which proposed to cell' sure the Government for their policy with regard to Egypt and the Soudan. Though amply sufficient for all practical purposes, the majority does not at the first blush appear, very decisive; but let it be remembered thal- -18 Liberals were absent from the division: that five others deserted their party aria threw themselves into the arms of the Oppo' sition, and that the bulk of the Parnelllte9 voted with the Conservatives, and it will at once be clear that the victory is much more' complete than the numbers seem to indicate' Then, again, there was much to favour the Opposition assault. We know of no occa- sion dulin7 the present Parliament when the Government have been attacked that the current of events have contributed so ,'°' to the support of their opponents as in U'et present instance. There was in the firs. place the disaster to Mc:Ks PACHA and ins army, next the defeat of BAKER PACjlti subsequently the fall of Sinkat—and of eac.,."5 of these unhappy accidents the most ht been made -and lastly, the adverse vote

The House of Peers, which could not fail to have had its influence; yet the Government in the face of these adverse circumstances have been able to administer a severe rebukel to the front Opposition bench and their 1 followers. This is the third critical division which has taken place during the present Parliament. The two previous divisions were taken—one on the 3oth March, 1882, When the closure resolution was carried by a, Majority of 318 to 279, giving the Govern- ment a majority of 39; and the other on May 3, 1883, when the forces of bigotry, preju- dice, and intolerance combined to throw out the Affirmation Bill, which was rejected by. 292 against 289—thus placing the Govern- • bent in a minority of three. If, then, we 'exclude the defeats which the Administration •Itave sustained on the BRADLAUGH incident, it would appear that the Government have a, More firm hold upon the constituencies now than they have had at any previous period of their existence. The reason of this is not, we think, far to seek. Their policy, alike home, foreign, and colonial, has about it,none of that brag and bluster which characterised the conduct of their predecessors, and there is no desire to go behind Parliament and negociate secret treaties and conventions; on the other hand, their actions are open and transparent, they state their views candidly on every ques- tion which arises, and when they propound a Policy they are prepared to stand or fall by it. The House of Commons can see this, and seeing it the majority of the members wisely give the Government their vote and con- fidence. The supporters of the vote of cen- sure could, of course, have but one object in view, that being to inflict upon the Go- vernment a defeat, and, if possible, to hurl them from power; but even assuming that the members of the Administration are as bad and ! wicked as they have been recently painted, and that they had been supplanted by the Conservatives, we fail to see that any good to the country could have resulted. The Con servatives are, if not without a leader, at any zate without a policy; and to have given them a lease of office at the present time, 'When England is pledged to Europe to a 'course of action in Egypt of which Conserva- tives disapprove would have been the height of madness. Let any intelligent individual read the lengthy debate on the Egyptian ques- tion in the hope of finding an enunciation of What the Conservative policy would have been, and he will read in vain. Of con- tlenmation of the Government there is enough, of fault-finding there is plenty, but the greatest 'care has evidently been taken not to submit 'an alternative policy. We only gather what that would have been by inference or from 'hints dropped here and there. If the argu- ments of the Opposition mean anything at all, it must mean this, that they would annex Egypt, yet they are afraid to say so. One gentleman. indeed, Mr.AsHMEAD-BARTLETT, 'was bold enough to suggest the annexation of Egypt and the Soudant for a definite term of years, but `corning from such .a quarter we suppose we must accept this suggestion, as, to use a phrase of Lord BEACONSFIELD, "the hair- brained chatter of irresponsible frivolity ;" yet we are not quite sure that the member for 'Eye did not accurately represent the views of the front Opposition bench, though the occu- pants thereof fear to avow it. Lord HARTING- -PON has put the attitude of the Opposition very clearly in the concluding words of his able speech, in which, in winding up the de- bate, he says Before you seek to displace US I think it would be better, or at all events it would inspire the country with more confi- dence, if you, could produce a policy con- ceived by .your leaders which your party could adopt and carry out. But in my opinion you have none. You have no definite aims. You have no definite zconception of the means .by which such aims as you have are to be carried out, and very few of you even agree on the Objects for which you are to act. Yet it is Clear that although you have no definite con- ception of a -Soudan or even of an Egyptian Policy, you are as willing as you have ever been to pledge the country to vague, unde- fined, and.vast engagements, and to risk the resources of the country in unnecessary enter- prises. You are to all appearance as ready 'ooW as ever you were to undertake engage- 'Meats of the , nature and character of the Anglo-Turldsh Convention, and you are as ready as ever, to involve the resources of the 'country in the prosecution of a war as un- necessary,,if not as unjust, as the Afghan war " To these strictures of the noble Mar- the.leader of the Opposition offered but a feeble response, because, no doubt, he4.elt ,the 'words of Lord HARTINGTON were only 130 true. Having been ignominously beaten 111 the recent debate, the Opposition have Ilow turned their attention to other questions On which to harrass and worry the Govern- '.,T,!ot. The proclamation of General GORDON, 0 has always discountenanced slavery, is PPosed to encourage a traffic in human be- 4gs, hence ev,.,ry word and line of this docu- Inent must be criticised with the object of 'Catching the Government tripping; and the Annexation of Mery by. Russia is another bject which the Conservatives appear to be 'Making the most of in the hope no doubt of 'arousing the old feeling of hatred against Russia so prevalent before the Berlin Con- ference. We venture to think, however, that the Government are too firmly rooted in the ,confidence of the country for the Opposition to succeed at present in dis- placing them.

W. A. Coleridge, from St. Chad's College, Densteme, has gained an exhibition of the value of £95 a year at All Souls College,,Osdord. In the House of Commons, on Monday, Colonel Ireland Blackinarne presented a petition in favour of the Repeal of the contagious Diseases Act from Wesleyans at Whiston, Present, Earlestown, and St. Helens. Harry °gbill, of Newcastle, Staffordshire, was added to the board raf dircctors. ..i•ATTLMPTED OnTALGE ON A WOMAN AT WkDNES.— Xerterdav, at Widoes Police Court, before Mr. John. Brock, tin Murray, a labourer, was charged with attempting to i'.'433tnit a rape upon Eliztheth •Flyna, a married woman :ving at Moss Bank. About seven o'clock on Monday venitig Mrs Flynn'and another woman were visiting vari 0-- us places in the town in search of the latter's husband. A length they found him in a public-house in Lugsdale, Tai with him was the prisoner, who paid for Mrs Flynn a E" of gin. They left the house together, and after walk- a considerabie distance towards home the prisoner, 4gainot the woman's will, separated her from her corn- . div.p: UNJUST SCALES AT RuNeoax. John Lightfoot, of BraAlty•street, was summoned before the Runcorn magis- ' tiaras, on Monday, for having in his possession for use in trade a pair of scales which were unjust. The defendant's wife appeared and pleaded guilty.—P.C. Bossons having proved that on the 9th January he found the defendant's scales 1.1 drachms out of balance, the defendant was fined 5s and costs, 9s 6d. LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE BIND OF 110Pli UNION.— This Union has now attained its 21st year, and it is pro- posed to mark the event by a gathering of workers in the cause from all parts of the kingdom. The Mayor of Man- chester has consented to preside at a conference to be held 'in the Mayor's Parlour on the 13th of March. The open- ing paper will be contributed by the Rev. S. A. Steinthal. On the evening of the same day the Bishop of Manchester I will open the proceedings, at a grand soiree to be held in the Great Hall. RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. James Reynolds and Mr. James Handley, the Runcorn School Board, represented by Mr. Bowyer, prosecuted the following persons for commit- ting a breach of the Education Act :—John Critchley, John O'Neil, James Sharkey, Kate Morris, E. Lightfoot, Henry Skelding, John Antrobus, Elizabeth Maddock, Edward Hughes, John Whitefield, John Darbyshire' Martha Alice Jackson, and George Buckley. The usual penalty of 5s including costs was imposed in each. INQUESTS AT RUNCORN.—lnquests on the bodies of two infant children were held by Mr. Ridgway in Runcorn Police Court, on Monday afternoon. The fatherslof the children were George Dutton, Mason-street, and John Mason, 55, Wellington-street. It appeared that both children a few hours after birth were seized with convulsive fits, and before medical aid could be obtained they died. Everything pos- sible seemed to have been done by the parents and neigh- bours. Verdicts to the effect that death in each case resulted from convulsions were returned, and no blame was attached to any person. BRUNSWICK WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN.— The annual meeting of the teachers of this school Was held on Monday weA, and was presided over by the Rev. E. J. Robinson. The business of the meeting was to receive vari- ous reports for the past year and to appoint officers for the current year. It appears from the secretary's report that there are on the school books 63 officers and teachers, and 626 scholars, the average afternoon attendance for 1883 be- ing 46 and 406 respectively. On Monday last the teachers' yearly tea meeting was held. After tea the meeting was' adjouraed to one of the vestries, where a harmonious and I enjoyable evening was spent. SERIOUS SCAFFOLD ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—About half- , past nine, on Wednesday morning, a serious accident oc- cured at the Vineyard Level Crossing, Lugsdale, where the London and North-Western Railway Company are con- structing a massive brick bridge. Five men engaged in the work were standing on a scaffold, consisting of planks, when .the structure gave way without warning, and the men were precipitated a distance of 20 feet to the ground, which was strewn with materials. One of the men named Thomas Mahoney had his leg broken at the ankle, and just below the knee, and he was removed on a stretcher to the Aocident Hospital. It was thought the injured limb would have to be amputated, but an effort is being made to avert such a • calamity. Two other men were badly shaken, but were able to resume work on Thursday morning. A few minutes after the accident Mr. Coroner Brighouse passed the spot, and closely examined the fallen structure. SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.—At the Adelphi Hotel, Lugsdale, Widnes, on Wednesday morning, Mr. Brighouse, the county coroner, held an inquest touching the death of Margaret Sullivan, a widow, 44 years of age, who lived at 26, Grove-street, Widnes. It seemed that the deceased retired to rest at a quarter to twelve on Saturday night, and her daughter Mary, who slept with her, went to bed shortly after midnight. At that time the deceased was sleeping soundly, but about five o'clock in the morning the daughter I awoke and missed her mother. Hearing a noise downstairs she descended, and found her mother lying on the floor:of the kitchen in a dying condition. Mrs. Fitzpatrick, who lived in the same house, was attending to her, but she died in' a few minutes. It was stated by a juryman that thel deceased suffered from heart disease, and an Insurance Society had recently declined to insure her. A verdict to the effect that dust resulted from natural causes was re- turned.

SHOCKING WIFE DESERTION AT WIDNES. —At the Prescot Police Court on Tuesday, Mr. S. H. Hartley, on be- half of the Prescot Guardians, asked the Bench to commit Richard Holden, lately of Widnes, to prison for the full term for wife desertion. From the statement of Mr. Hart- ley, it seemed that a few months ago the prisoner and his wife left Widnes for Yorkshire owing to his having been ,fined at the Police Court there. After getting to Tadcaster, be deserted his wife, who then made her way back to Wid- mee. She was in a state of pregnancy at the time and ap- plied for relief. An order for the Workhouse was given, and she went there for a short time, but having applied for a discharge, she left the workhouse and went to Widnes again. It afterwards came to the knowledge of Mr. Scan- nell, relieving officer, that she had obtained. a bundle of straw, taken it into an empty house, and was there confined. The mother and infant were then again removed to the workhouse.—lt appeared however, that the prisoner had taken his wife to her father's at Tadcaster, and that when he left her her father put her out. It also appeared that Hot- den had made attempts to enter into communication with his wife. The Bench taking this into consideration only sent the prisoner to gaol for seven days. NMI BEGGAR AND lies TEXT.—At the Widnes Police Court, on Tueaday, before Mr. G. rilkington, John Smith, who said he came from Runcorn, was charged with beg- ging.—P.C. McMasters said about seven o'clock on Mon- day night he was on duty in Ann-street West, and saw the prisoner go into several shops. Witness followed him in- side one place, and the proprietor 'told him that he had given the man a copper because he said he was hard-up. He found on prisoner a quantity ,of bread. 2s in money, a quantity of sugar in pound and half-pound packets, tea, soap, pieces of bacon, the whole being concealed round his body and in the pockets of his coat. The prisoner had a shade over his eye and a stick in his hand, and pretended to be blind.—lnspector Wood rercarked that men like the prisoner sold the bread they got to people who kept pigs. The stuff found upon the prisoner weighed about 121b5., and filled a small hamper when in the court. It consisted of tea, sugar, lard, bacon, and soap; also a copy of San- key's "Sacred Songs and Solos," and on a piece of paper was written, "Be thankful with thy calling, and shun the, paths of beggary." On another piece of paper were found memoranda of the following names, with hieroglyphics op- posite to them:—Mr. Zith, Baptist minister, Southport; Mr. Ward, Congregational minister, St. Helens; Dr. Carr; Mr. Piggett, minister, St. Helena; Lady Carr. The pri- soner said he came from Runcorn, and was looking for work.—The Bench sent him to gaol for 14 days' hard labour. FUNDSAL OF THE DATE MRS. Jaw". ow FARNWORTIT.— The mortal remaies of Mrs. Jeff, widow of a former vicar of Farnwortli. were interred at St. Luke's Church, on Monday. The deceased for some years previous to her death resided at Southport, whither she retired on the death of her hns- band. The body was conveyed from Southport to Warring- ton by rail on Monday, and was thence borne to Farnworth, and was met at the church gates by Mr. Llewellyn Evans (South- port), Mr. John Watson (Torteth), Mr. Hodgett "(Little Sutton), cephews ; Mr. Kidd and Mr. L. Kidd (Farnworth). Mrs Jeff was well known by many of the older parishioners, and by a large number of persons gathered near the Church on the arrival of the body. Amongst these present at the grave side were Dr. Hunter, Mr. T. Knowles, Mr.. Doward, Mr. Jackson, Miss Bond, Mrs. and Miss Langton. The funeral service was read by the Rev. George Bond, vicar, who delivered a short address. He said that was no ordin- ary grave, co common funeral; for lying there was one who bad for many years made herself beloved by the people of the parish; one from whom many families beyond her own had derived the highest benefit; one whose husband, after spending 40 years amongst them, at last retired from his office full cf years and honour. Re-ehortiv afterwards (Led, and his widow lived on still fell of good- works, and cot until the close of last week did she pass away. She had come to the grave in a full age like a shock Of corn cometh to his season.

I.FARNWORTII IPARISEt Cauncri.—The annual congrega- tional tea party took place on Friday evening week, and there was a large attendance. .At the subsequent entertain- ment the room was crowded. Mr. U. W. Beinun presided, and he was supported by the Revs G. Bond, M.A , S. A. Spooner, M.A., andJ. Holden. In a short address, the Chairman suggested the formation of a debating -society in connection with the school. The subjects discusted might be political or social, literary or scientific, just as might be suited to the members; and he was sure if the matter was taken up with interest the amount of self-tonfidenee which would.be gained wEs difficult to obtain in other ways, and the habits of criticism .which were formed would .te most useful in every day life, and especially in any sort of public life. He urged the young men present to study natural history and other scientific subjects.—The BAW. Geo. Bond also spoke, and referred to the projected restoration of the new church, towards which King's College had promised 1.50. Operations could not be commenced until they had a good sum,in hand, but he bad abundant reason to think they woule raise the £1,500 required to remove the gal- ' leries, restore the edifice, and to make the church one of the finest old churches in the country. An excellent pro- gramme %vas gone through during the evening.—On Satur- day evening the annual distribution of prizes to the chil- dren who had attended Sunday schizo' regularly took place, the Rev. G. Bond presiding There was a large attendance. Mr. A. Davies read the aanual report, which stated that the number of scholars on the books was 275, maids up as follows i—Senior boys, 106; senior girls, 60.; juniors and infants, 109. These it were slightly below those of last year, but t was satisfactory to know that the attendance of individual classes had increased. In the senior boys department the attendance was—caorning 69, afternoon 74; girls— morning 37, afternoon 50; juniors' and ikfants—morning 63, afternoon 64. The number of scholars who received prizes was 94—the senior boys claiming 42, senior girls 28, juniors and infants 24. This was a large increase on last year, the total then only being 55. Twentyrtwo scholars. aye boys, and 17 girls had qualified themselves for the prizes of Bibles and Prayer-books, given by the trustees of the late Lord Wartqn, who ,Jell certain estates in York- shire, part of the proceeds of which were to be distributed as prizes in certain parishes to those children who learned seven psalms during the veer. The prizes to the boys were then disrributed by Mice Bond, and those to the girls by *vs Uibhsfl Vntep of thanks were accorded to various i the tr,bn2l, and the meeting I tertnia........

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 23, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 23, 1884.

WIDNES LOCAL Boma, ELECTION.—The annual election of five members of Whines Local Board is fixed to take place at the latter end of March. The retiring members are—Messrs. F. H Gossage, E. Carey, Samuel Sadler, W. H. Kershaw, and Thomas Handley. Nominations will bs received up to and including the 22nd March. BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVMENT CLASS, RUNCORN.— An intereating meeting of this class was held on Wednes- day. The evening was devoted to music and readings. Mr. T. Simister preeiSed, and Miss Jones, Miss Jame% and Miss , Horton, Messrs. Craig, Shore, J. W. Moulson, T. S:mkin, and W. Hazlehurst took part in the proceedings. Miss Wright presided at the plane. A THROUGH LINE FROM WIDNES TO SOUTEIPORT::—By the beginning of April the new line of the Cheshire Lines Company, which branches from the north extension at Fazickerley, will be opened to Southport. It may afford the people of Widnes some satisfaction to know that on the opening of this line they may travel direct to the popular seaside resort. AN IDLE VAGABOND AT WlDNES.—Yesterday, before Messrs. J. Brock and F. H. Gossage, at Widnes Police Court, Michael Henry, a big, strong-looking fellow, was charged with sleeping in a chemical works that morning.—P.C. Thompson proved finding the prisoner asleep on Messrs. Hutchinson's chemical works. Inspector Wood read a long list of offences committed by the prisoner, and said he was utterly incorrigible. He would not work.—air. Brock said there was no doubt the prisoner was an idle vagabond, and the Bench sentenced him to three months' hard labour. Rtneemeat Y.M.C.A. HISTORICAL SOCIETY.—At the fort- nightly meeting of this society, en Thursday, Mr. E. Rhodes lectured on the subject of international arbitration. Mr. Rhodes held that war , was an embodiment of the questionable principle "Might is Right," as it appealed to brute force independent of reason. International arbitra- tion; he coatended, was founded on principles of justice to all, both to the weak and to the strong, as it 'appealed to . the decision of an impartial and unprejudiced authority, and he urged that the time had arrived when European inteinational differences ought to be settled by arbitration. A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer. Mr. J. Craig occupied the chair. 'IRE RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD AND ELEMENTARY TEACHERS.—Much indignation has been caused amongst the j head teachers of the public elementary schools in Runcora in consequence of a communication addressed to them by Mr. F. Rigby, clerk to the Runcorn School Board. This I communication stated that in future the Board will not take cognizance of children who make six attendances out of 10 each 1 week, and as such a decision is frought with important re- sults the teachers have held a meeting to consider the ques- tion, and appointed a deputation to wait upon the chairman!, of the Board with reference thereto. Several of the teachers exptessed a desire to forward a copy of the letter to the ' Education Department for their consideration. THE INFLUENCE OF SURROUNDINGS: A Yonero WIDNES THIEF—At the Petty Sessions on Wednesday, before Mews. , J. Brock, J. C. Gamble, and F. H. Gossage, Mary Worthing- ton, 11 years of age, was brought up on remand charged I with stealing half a crown from the till of the Qmeen's ' Arms public-house, Lugsdale, occupied by Charles Davies. —Particulars of the robbery, which took place on Friday week, have appeared in The Examiner. The prisoner was convicted of felony at Widnes Police Court a few weeks j ago, and Mr. Brock said it we quite evident was going I to the bad, and unless she was removed from the custody of the persons who had her at present under their control, she would go worse and worse.—The Bench had therefore de- cided to sentence the prisoner to 14 days' imprisonment, afterwards to be detained four years in a reformatory school. ROBBERY FROM A WIDNES WORES.—Yesterclay, at Widnes , Police Court, George Washington. a coloured man, and I Edward Carroll, a youth, were charged with stealing a hare- mer, of the value of 15.2 d., the property of Richard Woods, I living at 59, Pitt-street, Widnes. Woods is a stone breaker at Messrs. Hall and Shaw's chemical works, and on the I evening of the 7th inst. he placed the hammer is a hut. Next j morning he found that it had been taken. On Thursday, the 21st inst., Francis Maguire, a stone breaker, who lives in I Albert-street, went into Snape's works, and there saw the prisoner Washington using the stolen hammer. He told hint it belonged to Woods, and the prisoner at once gave him I possession of it, saying he had received it from Carrol.— P.C. Hargreaves deposed to apprehending the prisoners. In reply to the charge, the prisoners made statements involv- ing each other. Carroll stated he saw the hammer on a stone heap in Hall and Shaw's works, and that Washington I told him to fetch it.—Carroll pleaded guilty, but Washing- ton denied any knowledge of the theft.—Carroll was sen- tenced to 14 days' imprisonment, and Washington, who had been previously convicted, was committed to gaol for a.l month with hard labour. ' ASSAULT ex 'TII6 POLICE AT WIDNES.—At WlOllOB Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, John Moran and Francis j McHugh, labourers, were charged with 'being drunk and I disorderly, and also with assaulting P.C. Collier whilst in I the execution of his duty.—About helf-past four, on Mon- day afternoon, McHugh, wheiwas drunk, was fighting with j another man in Marsh-street. The constable, therefore, ar- rested McHugh. On arriving at Waterloo-road, on the way J to the police station, Moran came upon the scene. , and violently attacked the constable, striking , him about the head and body with his fists , and kicking him severely about the legs. j McHugh also attacked him, and between the two the con- ' J stable was thrown to the ground. He managed, however, I I to regain his feet, and in the struggle two large windows I were broken in the shop of Mr. J. Betney. Collier having I received the aid of several other officers the prisoners were secured and conveyed to the Police-station.—Sergt. Beaker said the assault was a most unprovoked one, and he hoped 1 the Bench would mark their opinion of it.—Mcliugll said he "disrentemkered nothing" about it. He had been in Widnes I 20 yoirs, and this was his first appearance before their wor- ships.--. Moran also denied any recollection of the ocour- rence.—Mcilugh was fined 5s and costs for being drunk, and lOs and costs for the assault, in default 21 days' hard labour; Moran was sentenced to a month's bard labour without the option of a fine. UNLAWFMLY WOUNDED ,BY A BOY AT WlDNES.—Yes- terday, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. John Brock, Richard Tonkies, 14 years of age, was brought up, on re- mand, charged with assaulting a youth, named William Mullen, who lives at 81, Mersey-road, Widnee.—From a statement by Inspector Wood, it appeared that on Monday night, about eight o'clock, the lads were standing in West- street, near the Salvation Army. The prisoners were using very offensive language, and when the prosecutor told him to be quiet he threatened to "run a knife into him." As he still continued to use bad language, the prosecutor gave.j him a push, calling the prosecutor an "Orange bastard." The prisoner pulled a knife out of his pocket, and struck him in the face, inflicting a wowed two inches long on the upper lip. He then fell to the ground, and whilst lying there attempted to strike the.prosecutor on the legs. The wound, which bled profusely, was stitched up by Dr. McDonnell.—This statement was corroborated by the pro- secutor, and Wm. Holland, 15 years of age, of 58, Beamont- street, and Matthew Lyons, lodging in Irwell-streee—The prisoner cress-enamined the witnesses, to show that Mullen had knocked him to the ground and kicked him. He alleged that he had the knife in his hand cutting a stick. FLOUR FOR PANCAKES.
OUR LONDON LETTER.

BALAAM IN POLITICAL LIFE-THE EFFECT OF THE VOTE OF CENZAIRE-THE PROSPECT, THE SESSION, THE DISSOLUTION-RUMOURS AND FACTS - CLEMENCEAU IN LONDON - THE PRINCE OF WALES AND HIS COLLEAGUES- PICTURES FROM DICKENS-MR. TENNIEL'S CAMEL-THE THEATRES.
. LONDON, Thursday.

Sir Stafford Northcote has been playing the part of Balsam again. Called upon by the hot-headed partisans in his following to curse the Government altogether, he has altogether blessed them. There is, of course, this differ- ence between his conduct and thatof the prophet. Sir Stafford really meant to carry out his mission, and did his pest to aecemplish it. But circumstances were against him, an his effort has proved to the Government an unmixed bless- ing. The debate was wearisome even beyond precedent. Sir Arthur Otway's good fortune in getting a couple of hours sleep whilst it was going forward is greatly envied, though it is admitted he was a little unfortunate in the choice of time. For others who could not sleep and evea had to listen, this debate has added twelve months to their years. But the words were not all waste. They cleared away much that was obscure. They brought to light forgotten facts, and by an infinitude of detail they established the truth that so far from having been "vacillating and inconsistent" the Government have from the first steadily pursued a clearly defined policy. The debate has also bronght into prominence the fact that the Opposition, tore =ander by internal dissension, have nothing to offer in bidding for Mr. Gladstone's place. "We have a policy and you have none," Lord Hartington said across the table at one o'clock yesterday morning, a sentence which exactly describes the position of the two parties.

It might reasonably be expected that having bad their innings, seriously and deliberately attempted to turn the Government out on the question of policy, and having failed, the Conservatives would now be inclined to retire within their camp and really set to work about the busi- ness of the Session. That, however, is an expectation which no one in the House cherishes. In asserting that the Government greatly benefited by the attack on their , foreign policy, an advantage that remains with the Opposi- tion must not be lost sight of. It is now more than a fortnight since the Rouse met, and the debate on the Address is not yet concluded. One- I thirteenth of the average duration of a session has passed, and not a stroke of work has been done. That is some- thing gained for the Opposition, and it is an advantage they are inclined to extend. If they cannot beat the Govern- ment in the division lobby, they can baffle them on the 'Orders of the Day. They cannot turn them out; but they can, with the assistance of their Land League allies, prevent them doing more than the minimum of good whilst they remain in. It is in this direction that their efforts Will now be turned, and they congratulate themselves upon the success I that has hitherto attended them.

There is in the air a conviction that the General Election is near at hand. On this ground great difficulty- has been met with in seeking fora suitable candidate to stand ao.ainst the renegade member for Brighton. The answer of several good men who have been applied to has been to the effect "what is the use of my going to the expense and trouble of contesting the borough when we may have a general elec- tion within three or foal' months ?" I have good reason to know that this apprehension of the immediate proximity of a general election is not entertained by Ministers. Of course, everything is not in their hands. Events may arise which would force a dissolution upon them; bat I can state with certainty that in view of the prospect as it now stretches forth, including the contingen- cies attending the new Reform Bill, a dissolution is not ex- pected till the autumn of next year. This was the case before the division of yesterday morning, and is naturally strengthened by that event A moment's consideration will show that there Ii no reason why Ministers should hasten the natural course of events. They have a strong and united majority in the House of Commons. They enjoy undisturbed and perhaps lin increased degree the support of the country. They have much work to do. Their condition cannot by any chance be improved after the next general election, which will, moreover, bring in additions to Mr. Parnell's following, and make Parliamentary life more unendurable and public work still harder of accomplishment. The hero of the week in London society has been M. Clemencean, who has come over here avowedly on the mis- sion cf enquiring into the condition of lbe working classes. Clemenceau is a man who came to the front in France about the troubled time of the Commune. He made his way in political life by going a pace a head of Gambetta. He played towards tkat great man much the same part that Mr. Healy threatens to play towards Mr. Parnell. When, Gambetta, waxing fat with the sweets of power, took to . I taking his morning tub out of silver bath, Clemenceau went into Opposition, and to some extent superseded Gambetta as the idol of the people. Since then he has himself assumed responsible position, and responsibility has had its usual effect of toning down. Instead of the fiery sates culotte which those who vaguely know his history expected to see there is presented in many drawing-rooms a quietly-dressed gentleman with pale face, closely shaven except for his moustache, who ap- pears in faultless evening dress, and chatters on all eubjects save the condition of the poor. M. Clemeneeau's programme of engagements is growing tc be a joke. It was arrangeei before he came that the first persons he should see were Mr. Burt and Mr. Broadhurst, who may be supposed to know something of the working classes. The very first engagement he kept was at one of the pleasant Saturclal dinners given by Sir Arthur Hayter. On Monday he dined with the French Ambassador, attending two receptions after- wards, and every night since he has been in the world of fashion. As he is bound to return in a week he has arranged to see the two working men's members to-morrow. The interview will, I am afraid, be rather a bore after those more agreeable investigations of the condition of the work- ing classes which can be made at costly dinner tables and in brilliant drawing-rooms.

The appointment of the Prince of Wales on the Royal Commission to enquire into the housing of the poor is a ' very remarkable fact. It is the first time in English history that the heir-apparent has undertaken similar duties. But I what makes it more remarkable is the company in which the Prince will find himself at the Board. Mr. Jesse Col- lings is not, politically I mean, cut out as a companion for princes, nor did Mr. Broadhure, when he weileed the stone- mason's mallet, dream that some day he would sit shoulder to shoulder with the Prince of Wales. But the oddest con- junction is that of the chairmanship. How many years is it since Sir Charles Dilke went about the country proclaim- ing himself a Republican and delivering lectures to show that Republicanism was the best form of Government ? It seems but yesterday—though it is, alas ! eleven years since. I heard him in the House of Commons move for an enquiry into the €xpenditure of the Civil List. And now the Princ of Wales is a member of the Commis- sion which Sir Charles bag been instrumental in forming, and over which he will preside.

The incident is creditable both to the Prince and the baronet. I have long formed the opinion that though apparently like John Gilpin, on pleasure bent, the Prince of Wales is one of the shrewdest contemporary men of the world. From the very first he has made friends both with Mr. Chamberlain and Sir Ghana Dilke, and it is a re- markable thing for good Constitutionalists to dwell upon, that among politicaLipersonages these two are the most in- timate and the best received at Diarlburough House. I epect the Prince will take an opportunity of seeing IVI, Clemtuccau before that distinguished Republican leaves town. He was in the galley of the House cf Commons yesterday morning when the Prince entered. His Royal Highness immediately " spotted " him, and asked his equerry if it was he. The equerry did not know, but Lord Barring- ton did, and having identifiei him it was curious to note how from time to time the Prince of Wales turned aside from Lord Hartington to stare at the Frenchman.

It is strange that artists so seldom turn their attention to Dickens's works, though in nearly every page there is some episode or sketch of character suggesting a subjcet for the painter's brush. Certainly the original illustrations have already .done much, but great as are our obligations to 1" Phiz " and Cruikshank it is through the element of caricature that we appreciate them most. An admirable picture of old Ralph Nickleby is just finished for one of the Spring Exhibitions, by Mr. William G. Sprunt, a talented young artist whose works should soon be more widely known. Everyone is familiar with the tragic his. tory of Ralph, the relentless miser, who, failing to compass his schemes, put his own dark end to them. He stands, with clenched hands, in the garret where the beam and rope await the perpetration of the final act. The window lets in sufficient light to show the strong character of his features, in which the artist has delineated the workings of a maa full of the determined purpose. Mr. Sprunt is one of those gifted members of his profession who combine strength in the conception of their subject with an apprecia- tion of rich colours and their trUe value. He has now in progress a companion picture, in which Barnaby Rudge winds his way home at eve with Grip, the raven, on his back, and with a heart as fight as though the sun had never set. The yellow glpw in the sky and shade on the hills suggest the contrast between poor Barnaby's strangely mirthful life and the mysterious gloom in his home. He wears his frills and furbelows, the broken feathers in his hat, and the many motley scraps" that form his fantastic adornment. Following him corns the befriended dogs, who probably find more method in Barnaby's madness than is visible to the rest of the world.

There is a very curious mistake in the wonderful sketch of a camel which appears in this week's cartoon in Punch. Mr. Tenniel, though he never saw a camel outside the Zoo- logical Gardens, has caught with wonderful skill the pose of the head and the carriage of the body. But he has made the camel move forward at a walking pace on three legs. It is one of the peculiarities of the camel that if it performs the apparently impossible feat of moving forward on two legs. That is to say, it alternately raiees at the same time the front and hind leg on its left side, and the front and hind leg the right side, a method of pro- gression which has mach to do with the discomfort of camel riding, and makes peculiarly appropriate its title "the ship of the desert." The marvel is not that Mr. Tenniel should make a slight mistake of this kind, but that be should make so few. Drawing all kinds of thingsare- queutly going to foreign lands for his subject or his costume, it is astonishing how he gets the atmosphere of places he has never seen. He is, perhaps, the most abso- lutely untravelled man of his years and position. He once made a journey on the Continent, and was away as much as five weeks. But that is the only holiday he has taken for 20 years, and he speaks of it as a remote and excep- tional event, akin in some respects to his christening or his teething. He doesn't even journey as far as the House of Commons. lam not sure that he has ever been there in his life; and yet his portraits of its principal characters are unique in their life-like fidelity. The record of the dramatic events of the week includes a three•quarters success and a half-failure. At the Hay- market Sardou's "Peril" has been restored. Its first appearance belonged to the old days when the Kendals were part of the Bancroft troupe. Now we have Mrs. Beere instead. She's very lovely, very languishing, and very intense, hut she's heavy. She's a wonderful dresser, but her variety is confined to her wardrobe. In her acting she's monotonous. The play is, from an English point of view, absurd, and to make it pass it was needed to have a little espieglerie. Madame Fargeuil, who took the original character, had much; Madge Robertson had plenty. Mrs. Beers had none. So she falls back upon intensity and petticoats, and the fall is great. The whole play jars. Forbes Robertson tries to act a bluff English .country squire. He can no more do it than Major O'Gorman can dance on a tight rope. Bancroft as thq doctor is excellent. It is the one bit of nature in the piece. At the Avenue there's a very bright little opera called Nell Gwynne. I don't think I ever saw such lovely dresses. Miss St. John—who is, I believe, Mrs. Marius—has come back to the boards looking superbly. Her dresses of the Restoration period are perfectly beautiful. The Princess of Wales very, evidently thought so, the night she was there. Planquette has written the music. It is very tuneful and contagious. Already the street boys have taken. One does not criticise their kind of performance too severely. One goes to be amused, and Nell Gwynne is amusing. The manager evidently believes In it, for he has mounted it with what almost seems a ruinous splendour.
METHODIST FREE CHURCH MISSIONS, RUNCORN. ..

The annual sermons in behalf of the home and foreign missions of the United Methodist Free Church were preached in Ellesmere-street Chapel, Runcorn, on Sunday, by the Rev. W. Valise, the circuit minister. There were good audiences at each service. On Monday evening the annual meeting in aid of the same object was held under the presi- dency of Mr. John Humphreys, who was supported by the Revs. W. Vaase, J. D. Thomas, E. Williams, and N. Wvsh, of Northwich, who was the deputation. There WAS a fair audience. The Rev. W. Vallee having offered prayer, the CIUIRSIAN delivered an address. He said the cause of missions ought to enlist the sympathies of every Christian man, woman, and child. Perhaps one of the most pleasing features in connection with this great work:was the interest taken in it by the children of their Sabbath schools. He did not think it was possible to find any better illue4ration of how little hands and willing hearts could help forward the Redeemer's Kingdom. If it were possible to trace the pro- gress of Christian Missions from the time of the Apostles 'down to the present day it would furnish us with one of the most interesting and instructive books which had ever been given—second only in point of interest and instruction to the Bible itself. ( Hear, hear.) But even if such a book were undertaken it woald. fail to show the progress which had been made, the difficulties which had been overcome, the wonders which had been wrought, and the immense cost at which such great success had been achieved. Who could describe the perils, the dangers, the difficulties, and trials to which the missionaries had ever been subjected P (Hear, hear.) It had been the same in all ages; it was the same to-day. They had to bid farewell to friends, in very many instances for ever; how frequently we heard of them leav- ing their loved ones in the cold silent grave in far off lands; and how many fell a victim to disease and death. What an awful amount of self-sacritice this represented; and yet it was not the total, for to it must be added the vast same of money raised in this and other lands for the put pose of carrying 041 this great work. Looking at this y point of view, it yielded a good re- question from a world turn. The missionaries went to labour amongst uncivilised savages. By-and-bye these savages were led to embrace the ;towel of Jesus Christ; and almost invariably the result was the introduction of trade and commerce into the coon- try—merchants and manufacturers immediately followed in the footprints of the miksionary—and to-day Runcorn and Widnes profited to a large extent by the commerce which was thus es.ablished in foreign lands. This, he thought was conclusive proof that, even viewed from a worldly standpoint, missionary work paid, and to-day England was reaping splendid advantages from the intercourse that had been established in all parts of the world. (Applause.) But this was a narrow and confined view to the Christian man. They looked upon the poor, dark benighted heathen, and re- I membered that Jesus Christ said to His disciples, "Go ye forth into the world and preach the Gospel to the people baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost," anti they that believed the Gospel endeavoured to extend it to every land upon which the sun shone. (Applause.)—The Rev. W. VAusx read the report, observing that the missions were divided into home and foreign. At home there were a number of mission stations founded for the purpose of extending the Gospel in parts where Methodists wonld not at all events be, and these churches were supported, out of the mission fund. The Runcorn circuit received the sum of £35 a year to assist in the various expenses. ' In Australia the Society had 27 mission stations, in India 3, East Africa 3, West Africa 3, Jamaica 9, New Zealand 11; total. O. The income of t of 2 the ,250 . The Society for the past year was over L 17.000. and the expendi- ture upwards of .£19,000. leaving a deficit Runcorn circuit raised 13 Is Bd.—The Rev. E. WILLIAMSthen delivered a short address, and he WAS followed by the Rev. N. WYSE'. who spoke on the different aspects of mis- ion try labour.—The usual votes of thanks closed the pro- ceedings.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon, the members present being Mr J Ashton (in the chair), the Rev J W N Tanner, the Rev J Lockwood, Messrs J Highfield, J Smith, J Mclntyre. J G Hamilton, W Jackson, James Derbyshire, E A Wallington George Whitlow, J Weir, T Massey, T Norman, W Handley, F Fairhurst. and 3 Campkin. Mr R I Daneey, Poor Law Inspector, was also present.

div.head: LIVELY PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: LIVELY PROCEEDINGS.

IMr. WHITLOW referred to the surcharges whith had been made by the Local Government Board on the townships of Halton, Walton Inferior, and Walton Superior. If the deputy-clerk had been present he should liked to have asked him who sat him to work to get those surcharges made.—The CLERK: The auditor did. Those were sur- charges incurred by the auditor against the assistant over- seer, and the Local Government Board had ordered the items to be charged.—Mr, WHITLOw said that ought not to fall on the townships, and the man who Pet the clerk's son to work ought to pay.—The CLERK: That was the auditor; I know nothing more about it. —Mr. Winnow: Oh, that won't do.—The CLERK: I beg your pardon; I appeal to the chairman.—Mr. NORMAN: I think • this is too bad. What ia the world has the clerk to do with It ?—.3lr, WHITLOW: Don't you make any mistake; they have no right to gO. on the townships The CLERK: Well, I have nothiag to do with it.— Mr. WHITLOW asked who did not, if the Clerk did not ? Mr. NORMAN (to Mr. Whitlow): You have the auditor to fly at; why don't you fire at him ?—The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Whitlow was entirelY wrong, and rather out of order.— Mr. WHITLOW: Ws know who has planned it all.—Mr. NORMAN thought that was a downright insult to the Clerk and to the Board, and he should not sit there and hear such reflections cast upon the Clerk.—Mr. WHITLOW: It is the Clerk's fault, and no one else's.—Mr. NORMAN: Why don't you fly at the auditor ?—Mr. Wnirt.ow said everyone was against him. The affairs of that Board were managed by a very few Guardians, and it was no use going there to try and do anything.—The Rev. J. Lockwoon said these complaints came (roes a man who seldom attended the meetings of the Board, and he thought it was abominable.— The Board proceeded with the next business.

div.head: FATHER NUGENT AT WIDNES.
div.p: FATHER NUGENT AT WIDNES.

_ Under the auspices of the St. Bede's Young Men's So- ciety, Father Nugent on Tuesday evening delivered his popular lecture on "Buy your own cherries,' in the Widnes ' Volunteer Hall. There was a large attendance, the building being well filled. Father Finegan presided, and on the plat- form were—Messrs. R H. Davies, J. Morrison (president of the society), R. Bradshaw, C. McCarthy, D. Forster, Peers, Tallon, and John Teflon. Amongst the audience were the Rev. J. Morton (Primi.ive Methodist), Dr. McDoaald, Mr. H. B. and Mrs. Shores, Messrs. Richards, Austin Cowley, R. Hirst, Alcum Cowley, Oakden, Joseph Hunt, Melville, Peter Glover, and T. Sadler.--In introducing the lecturer, the CHAMMLN said some time ago the Young Men's Society asked him to invite Father Nugent to deliver a lecture, and as chaplain of the society he always endeavoured to accede to the wishes of the members when they were in the right direction. He thought their wishes on that occasion were in the right direction, and there could be no one to come and speak to them whose presence would be more welcome, and whose words wouid be more acceptable than the Rev. Father Nugent. (Applause.) The temperance question was absorbing not only the minds of individuale, but the minds of nations. It was a question that had thrust itself not only into the pulpit but into the Legislature, and it was a question upon which he hoped the Legislature would soon act with vigoar. (Applause.) A great deal was said about making people temperate bylaw, but he believed that much could be accomplished by Legislature as well -as by those who gave moral advice. If England was to hold the place amongst the nations of the future, which she had held in the p Ist, she must in the future be more temperate. She must have of the money which she earned, and she must resolve to have more money at her disposal for the purchase of those things which were neces- sary to existence. She must have less drink, and more food and snore clothes; less riot and less disturbance, and more peace and happiness. (Applause.) There was not another persm who was more capable of speaking on the temperance question than was Father Nugent, who had spent a useful life in endeavouring to do battle against the great enemy— drink. His usefulness was acknowledged not only by his own people, but by everyone with whom he came in con- tact. In conclusion, the speaker referred to Father Nugent's recent tour in Canada and said be honed tba people of Widnes would acknowledge his efforts on behalf of the people of England in the same enthusiastic manner as they had in Canada. (Loud applause.)—The Rev. Father NUGENT, who was received with applause, then proceeded to deliver his lecture, which was founded on the Ry. J. W. Kirton's story. It was delivered in a very graphic manner, and illustrated by dissolving views thrown noon a screen from a bi-unial lantern manipulated by Mr. B. Conlon, of Liverpool.—At the close, Mr. McCarthy, secretary to the League of the Cross, sang several temperance pieces, and gave a recitation in a very effective manner.—Mr. J. MOR- RISON moved a vote of thanks to Father Nugent, Mr. McCarthy, and Mr. Conlon.—Mr. R. H. Hems, in seconding the motion, observed that Father Nugent was the champion of the cause which he had at heart. He thought there was as much money spent in drink in Widnes as would provide every family with a comfortable home and good food —The motion was carried with loud cheers, and the LECTURER. in replying, delivered an excellent temperance address. He adverted to the satisfaction he had experienced in visiting Widnes that evening. For twenty years he had been chaplain in a Liverpool prison, and he had not only seen the sad effects of this terrible enemy drink, but he had received from the victims histories of their lives, and they had described the misery and degredation drink had brought them to. It was a moral leprosy sweeping over the face of the country, and every man that held any position in society was bound, if he loved his country and was prepared to do his duty, to make an effort to check the evil. (Applause.) Let them not wait for legislation, for by taking action toemselves they would throw weight into the scales of any Government that held the balance of power in the country. (Applause.) Prink was not only the cause of social misery, , but it was the source of nine-tenths of the crime committed. During , the 20 years he was in the Liverpool prison over 160,000 persons had passed under his care, and strange to say, there were more women than men. That was the only prison in the world where the women exceeded the men. Ha un- hesitatingly told them that they were their people—Catho- lics—and he appealed to them to enroll themselves under the standard of the cross, and to make a sacrifice for the God that died for them. (Applause.) He was not a fanatic —he was not an extreme man; and during the 38 years he had been a priest he bad identified himself with the working classes. (Applause.) He had sympathy for the working classes. (Applause.) He knew what the men in chemical yards had to undergo, and he knew that the men who ab- stained from drink did their work better than a man who took drink. (Applause )—After a few remarks from Father Finegan, the meeting terminated.

_ AUTHORITY _. On Tuesday afternoon, an ordinary fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held in the Dutton Workhouse, the members present being Mr J Ashton (in the chair), the Rev J W N Tanner, the Rev J Lockwood, Messrs J Highfield, J Smith. J M'lntyre, J G Hamilton, W Jackson, James Darby- shire. E A Wallington, George Whitlow, J Weir, T Massey. and J Campkin.—The Clerk (Mr. Linaker) read a letter from the Local Government Board, dated 11th February, sanctioning the borrowing of £BOO for works of sewerage and sewage disposal in the township of Frodsham, respecting which an inquiry had been held by Major Tulloch. With reference to the contemplated works of water supply for Frodshant, the Board were informed that it was proposed to intercept certain snrings above the village which now flow into the river Weaver. The Board were not aware that any objection had been made to such a course, but per- sons whose interests might be injuriously affected by the diversion of the water would not be debarred from taking steps in the future which might seriously interfere with the operation of the scheme; and therefore the Board recom- mended the Rural Sanitary Authority to obtain the consent Ire writing of all the riparian owners to the works now in contemplation. After some discussion it was agreed to adopt the recommendation of the Local Government Board. I —Mr. Henry Bancroft, of Manchester, the consulting en- gineer of the Board, forwarded a report to the Board showing that the construction of the Manchester Shin Canal would entirely de- stroy the Stockton Heath and Wilderspool drainage, and he would suggest that the authority see to the protec- tion of their interests by the insertion of a clause in the Manchester Ship Canal Bill_Mr. Hamilton proposed that the clerk take the necessary steps to have a petition prepared for the insertion of a clause in the bill for the due protec- tion of their interests, and that the chairman be empowered to sign the petition j .—This was seconded by the Rav J. N. Tanner, and carried.—Mr. Adams. deputy medical officer f of health, presented a special report as to the existence of typhoid typhoid fever at Frodsharn. A youth named Farrell been attacked by the disease, the spreading of had which he attributed to the use of impure drinking ter. been an outbreak of scarlet fever, but he There had h s unahle to trace i its origin. The patients were strictly solated, and every precaution was being taken to prevent the extension of the disease.

div.head: WIDNES TRADERS' ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WIDNES TRADERS' ASSOCIATION.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of this association was held in the offcer's room of the Volunteer Hall on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. E. K. Muspratt, the president, occupied the cbair„ and theta were present Messrs. T. S. Timmis, John Bronle, Henry Brunner, H. L, Jones, George Pilkington .P., H. Wade Deacon (hon. secretary). The mlnutes O.Y f the last meeting having been read and confirmed, . The How. SECRETARY read the report as follows :—" The committe begs to make its anneal report. After the lest ' annual meeting the promoters of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, which had failed to pass the standing orders of the House of Commons, were allowed by special resolution to carry this Bill before a committee. As there was no guarantee in the Bill that the access to the Widnes Canal and Dockwonld not he impaired or obstructed by the constructien of the canal your committee, acting in concert with the Widnes Local Board, urged the promoters of the Bill to insert a special clause protecting the interests of the traders, and the promoters agreed to do so. The Bill, however, was thrown out by the Committee of the House of Lords. This session the Bill has been again introduced and the claim agreed upon last year is printed in it. Owing, however' to Alterations in the Bill the clause of last year is now hot sufficient, and the Local Board and your committee are negotiating with every prospect of success for the inser- tion of the necessary additional clauses. An important clause is introduced in the London and North-Western I3ill. Under the Consolidation Act of 1846 there is a provision that the railway company shall net be compellable to find waggons for coal traffic, but where the company does not find them then an allowance is to be made of one-eighth penny per ton per mile. In the clause in the Bill it is pro- posed that where the railway company provides waggons for coal traffic a charge of 04 per ton may be made on all traffic conveyed for a less distance than 30 miles, and other clearest for longer distances. Hitherto the railway company has not provided waggons for coal traffic, but it appears that it proposes to do so in future, and if the company decides to run its own coal waggons private traders will soon find it impossible to rim theirs. Under these circumstances if is most important for traders, and especial), for those traders whose fuel traffic is short distance traffic, to see that the charge which they may have to pay for waggon hire under the new clause is not more than they now pay to colliery owners. In this district the usual charge for use of waggons is 31 or 44 per ton and under the proposed delis° the Railway Company would be en- titled to charge, and most probably would charge, tli per ton. The clause, therefore, obviously _requires amendment,. and your committee is trying to get the desired alteration made. Should the negotietiens fail the committee recom- mends the Association to petition Parliament against the Bill, and though the cost may be considerable, yet the effects of the clause as it now stands would be so injurious te the interests of the traders in Widhes that your committee hes no hesitation in advising a stormy opposition. In order to carry eut this action it will be necessary to provide funds, and the committee recommends that it be authorised to make a levy of not exceeding 3d in the £ oaths gross an- nual value of each member's works as it now stands in the books of the township. The committee has communicated with Mr. Sinclair as representing the St. Helens traders with the view of netting them to join in the opposition and also in the expense, as the matter appears to be as important for them as far as your committee will watch with close atten- tion the Railway Bill 14 hich the President of the Board of Trade promises to bring before Parliament this Session, and will take action if any appear necessary in the interests of the traders as soon as the provisions of the Bill are knoWn. The statement of accounts showed that there was a balance in haocl of £99 6s lid,

Mr. T. S. Tttf:,tts, at chairlaan i t.:10 cominittee, moved the adoption of the report. He sail the committee had reason to believe that the promoters of the Manchester Ship Canal would do all the association and the Widnes Local Board combined could reasonably ask them to do. They were anxious to meet them in every way, and be thought they might consider the matter settled. Referring to the action of the associtation in reference to the proposed rail- way rates mentioned in the repoct, Mr. Timmis said the president of the Board of Trade had been asked to inteefere in the matter. A very courteous triply Ind been received from the Board of Trade saying they would give attention to it, and pointing out what the committee expected, that if the matter was of such vital importance to Widnes,they had better appear against the bill in the House of Commons. Tbe proposed new rate would practically be an advance of threepence per ton, but there was a further threepence which the railway company had allowed in 24 miles which the coal owners got in their own pockets. The coal owners would not now receive that 3d., and to recoup themselves the coal owners would probably charge the consumers that amount extra per ton. The railway company when they were asked to give an amended clause, said they had no in- tention of applying the clause to Widnes district. This reply, however, was not satisfactory, for if they got . the power what was to prevent them using it.

The HON. SECRETARY stated that he had written to the solicitor to the company asking if they would give the manufacturers a proviso in the bill that the clause should not apply to Widnes, but they would not do so. Mr. Thous said it was no use protesting and petitioning unless they were prepared to spend the money necessary. A levy of 31 in the £ upon the rateable value of each works, would cover the expense, which would not be very large if the St. Helens manufacturers decided to co-operate in the opposition.

The CHAIRMAN seconded the resolution. Referring to the statement by the company, that the clause should not apply to Widnes. and the Widnes manufacturers would be able to run their own wagons as heretofore, he said when railways were first started it was expected that manfacturers would be able to run their own locomotives, but they soon found that this was impossible. The traders bad asked if with the short distance traffic in Widnes they could not use their own locomotives in dealing with waste traffic, but the company had refused. They practically said it was impossible for them to allow this because they could not work the private' traf- fic with their own. Judging from the cause the company had adopted in the past they might very fairly conclude that when they bad got the power to run their own wagons they would give all despatch to their own wagcns, and those of the manufacturers would be run off the road. He was certainly prepared to say that threepence per ton for short , distances in the case where a colliery was conveniently situ- ated, paid for the wagon hire. It was a question which affected colliery owners as well as manufacturers. They ought, if possible, to obtain united action upon the matter, for unity was strength, and of great advantage when oppos- ing a railway company, which was always united., while in- dividual traders as a rule were not united. The same idea would apply to the railway bill which would be broUght in by the Government. Mr. Chamberlain, the President of the Board of Trade, was understood to have c,nne down to the opinion of the permanent officere of the Board of Trade, that terminal charges should be made, when it had already been decided is tiae courts of law that these terminals can- not be charged. That was a very important point. The whole difference of opinion was as to whether these rates were legal or not legal. In the new government Bill the powers of railway companies would undoubtedly be ex- tended, they would be granted power to make terminal charges upon goods, and the manufacturers would find themselves practically worse off than before. This could only be met by the union of all the traders of the kingdom. Mr. H. W. DEACON agreed with the previous speakers with regard to the London and North-Western Railway Bill. He had got a semi-official opinion from Mr. Henry, the counsel. That gentleman said if they could get an'acknow- ledgment that this rate would not apply to Widnes it 'would be sufficient, otherwise he would strongly urge opposition. The matter was also under the consideration of the South Lancashire and Cheshire coal owners, and they promised to, let him know the result of their deliberations. He thought they ought to oppose any increase of the rates until there was a re-classification of goods and tolls together. (Hear, hear.) He thought this was really the strongest ground they had for opposing Clio 6,1 rate. With reference to the Ship Canal, he was of opinion matters would be arranged without having to oppose them. The report was adopted. Mr. R. L. JONES moved that the Executive Committee be- authorised to oppose the London and North-Westery Rail- way Bill in Parliament if it be found necessary to do so, and to make a levy of 3cl in the £on the gross annual value of each member's works as it now stood in the poor rate books of the township for the purpose of meeting the expense of the opposition. Mr. G. PILEINGTON seconded the motion, which ran carried. Mr. H. BRUNNER moved that as the interests of all the traders of Widnes were affected by the London and North- Western Railway Bill, those traders who were not members. of tate association be asked to join the aesociatlOn, and hear part of J f. the i3ocic, jp, seconded eeßzuense in opposingsecondthe ur. • and it was carried. The meeting shortly afterwards -terminat.ed.
