div.head: Xettero to the gaitur.
div.p: Xettero to the gaitur.

MR. WHITHAM ON TEETOTALLERS. Sir,—ln his letter last week, Mr. Whitham says "I have very rarely met with teetotallers who understood temper. sties. It seems to be a fatality that these men should be a narrow-minded lot of abusive ,lespots, who think to reform the world by pushing the teapot down everyone's throat." The wonder to me would be to learn that he ever—to say nothing of "rarely "—met with a teetotaller who understood temperance as he appears to understand it. If temperance means frequenting a "pot-house" for the purpose of drink- ing even to the accompaniment of political discussion; then the teetotallers willeoever understand it in the sense of ap- proval. Neither will they be beguiled into forsaking their temperance in order that by taking up Mr. Whitham's spuri- ous temperance they may have an opportunity of delivering a dozen or so lectures to publicans on their bad ways. That publicans are pachydermatous is notorious; and I can easily imagine Boniface grimly smiling as he "pockets his pride" along with Mr. Witham's money, unhurt by his homily. I , make no apology for "shoving an oar in" this discuss:on ; keeping, ef course, to the main question and leaving "A Ratepayer," whoever he may be, to take the personal mat, ters in his own hand. Such an outrageous misrepresentation of teetotallers and their aims wat never made outside the -organs of the liquor traffic. Is it a decree of fate that tee- ' totallers should be a narrow-minded lot of abusive despots? I was always under the impression that they were among those who wished to liberate their fellows from the despot- ism of the beer-pump and the tyranny of liquordom. As to their narrow-mindedness, that is a matter of opinion. I have yet to find that the teetotaller has been behind hand in any of the great reforms which have been carried out in the country, whether religious, social, or political; and the rot about his getting astride his hobby and tilting at every- thing that does not proceed from the pop bottle is—well, is rot. That is just what troubles the publican; he cannot get the teetotaller to leave him alone. He is so persistent in his work that one of the publican spokesmen, referring to the body of temperance workers, said These people will never be beaten. Nothing would please the drink sellers better than to see teetotallers "tilting at windmills," so that they might have a little breathing time. Mr. Whitham is sure— his degmatism on all matters is proverbial—that men of his class who control their appetite for speaking and drink- ing (it may be news to some to learn that he is in the habit of bridling his tongue) are much superior to men who have to take the pledge because of their want of self-control. I fail to see the superiority. Besides, it is not every one who pledges to abstain from alcoholic beverages who does so be- cause of a failing in the direction of excessive drink. In com- ,mon_vrith the rest of my unfortunate fellow creatures. I was born a teetotaller, and, my education having been neglected, I have had the Misfortune to remain one ever since. Mr. Whitham is welcome to his cheap sneer at the temperance pledge, considering that there are seven millions of peoPle in these islands who are total abstainers. He. is also sorry that there is drinking at a political club in Warrington. If he means the one in Rewsey-street, why did he not oppose the introduction of the system of drinking when the matter was discussed in the billiard room some years ago? I was present, and did not hear him raise his voice against the de- grading proposal to turn the club into a drinking place. Mr. Whitham seeing the growing power of the teetotal party in the Liberal ranks, fears a split, because it fa likely that a teetotal plank will be introduced into the platform. The "watery nostrum," as he calls Local Option, is already at the front, and if Mr. Whitham will not support a Local Option candidate, then the candidate must manage to do without him. Does Mr. Whitham wish to pose as the roe- buck of Warrington Liberalism? If not, I would urge him to rub off some of the angularities that mar his political usefulness, and devote his undoubted abilities in the good cause. Li conclusion, Mr. Waltham, of all men, quotes Scripture, and bids teetotallers study the passage, "Not that which goeth into the mouth defiieth the men." When -that something which amen takes into his mouth is alcohol, B does defile a man, nothing more so. I suggest in return, the study of the same passage in the light of Shakespeare's "Oh ! that man should take an enemy into his mouth to steal away his brains."—Yours, /cc., J. D. JONES. Runcorn, Feb. 18, 1884.

div.head: DISESTAMASHMENT.
div.p: DISESTAMASHMENT.

Sir.—Your correspondent, the inquisitive dipthong, in last issue asks of me three questions which I class as frivo- lous, quibblin.4, and impudent. I. "By what Act or Acts was the Church of England established ? " Now as I am not a legal authority I cannot gi-re him specific information on this point; but being in possession of a little common sense, and seeing men who I think are probably wiser than the twin vowel and myself in this matter who are striving to disestablish the English Church by Act of Parliament, I concluded that Parliament was a faction in the establish- ment thereof. But if " CE" wishes to teat the thing for himself, I can put him in the way of doing it by giving him the fellowing recipe i—Let "CE" take a tithable farm, let him refuse to pay tithes, and he will get the bums. One dose of this mixture will suffice to convince "if'" that if the Church is not established by Act of Parliament she is very much bolstered up by it. Weald not "CE" think it "quite too too" near establishing our friends the Salvation Army if he was compelled by law to support them by his tenth? What better evidence of establishment could he have? His second question is:—" Whether, supposing that the payment of tithes to the above church were abolished they would cease to be payable altogether," to which I reply that Jam as anxious as he to have that point legally settled. I want this question to be discussed in the full light of modern thought and feeling. I object to the living being ruled by the dead. Why should money be extracted from the pockets of the living by the lies of dead and gone bigots who were ignorant enough to think of making folks religipus by act et Parliament? Let the present generation weigh this matter and decide if it be jest and right that these taxes should remain on the spade and the plough ; and if so. let them remain—if not, remit them. For a solution of " CF. s " third query heading "Tithe imposition" are my composition, I must refer him to you, sir, as the guardian of that dead secret, knowing that you will be provided with a fitting answer, though you ought not satisfy his Eve-like priesity and thirst for forbidden knowledge. In conclud- rag, allow me to ask "CE " to drop these quibblings and impertinences and reply to the broad questions of right and wrong spoken of in my first letter. If he can throw any new light on this dark subject let him do so and no one will rejoice more than yours truly, JOHN PEERS. Oreenbank, Penketh, February, 1884.

div.head: "LEATHER-HUNTER'S NOTES."
div.p: "LEATHER-HUNTER'S NOTES."

Sir.—l notice in your issue for Saturday last, that "Leather-hunter" in his football notes says Vulcan first and second teams were "sat upon" last week. This, I beg to say is not not correct as far as the'second team is con- cerned, for I believe they (Vulcan 2nd) fairly "sat upon" Pagefield 2nd, as at tbe call of time the score was as fol- lows: Vulcan, 6 tries and six minor points to Pagefield nil. The first team, I believe lost, the ground being so bad that no strangers to it could play on it. I think it would be a goad thing for "Leather-hunter " to obtain correct state- ments before inserting them in the paper. A SPECTATOR.
TEETOTAL LODGE ROOMS VERSUS BAR PARLOURS. .

Sir,—After reading and re-reading A Ratepayer's" letter, which appeared in your issue of the 9th inst., I am wholly at a loss to account for the bitter feeling against e teetotalers manifested by Mr. H. Whitham in his letter in ',liner of the 16th inst. I cannot for the life of me see what" A. Ratenaver's" letter has to do with teetotalism ; for there is not a stogie expression in it which would lead ,a,nHy.o nwe .t"ostehemi nsk tyoohn ar vceo rtar eits po ta dent was an abstainer. But payer" is such an one and stoirtufiworttattglrahnetehdutrblsath'i'sApußeAttiele- sarcasms at the whole body of teetotal suppose "A Ratepayer" is a teetotaller, would H d tboavitefver justify the use of such silly, jargonconventienal whatever.ahVv ; ' has given utterance to without any discrimination I think that the utmost your correspondent ought to done, was to confine his remarks to the individual who had e given him offence. I do not endorse "A Ratepayer's " expression towards O.H. w..„ and had it been my own case I should have treated it with silent contempt, coming as it did from an anonymous correspondent. Neither should I have taken any notice of "H. W.," had be not signed his name; but knowing "H. IV ,"as I do, to be in many respects a sensible and sterling man, and one worthy of my steel, I cannot for- bear to utter my protest against this tirade of abuse towards such an earnest body of reformers as teetotallers are, aud have been, long ere "H. W. " had seen the light. I also 44.7 him to prove his assertion that teetotallers are as a body '3it narrow-minded lot of abusive despots ; " his asser- tion that he has "very rarely met with teetotallers who understood temperance " may be taken for what it is wo-th. Certainly his own example won't help us, if his latest epistle is a sample of what temperance in writing means. No," H. W.," take the mote out of thine own eye, /cc., &C. There is a proverb that speaks of what the conduct of those should be who live in glass houses. Ponder it tie thou pen thy next letter to the public. "A narroimainded lot:of abusive despots pushing the tea-

pot down everyone's throat." . . . "His teetotal hobby- horse." . . . "Everything that does not emanate from the pop bottle" . . . " The ranting and raving of fanatical men." . . . "Their watery nostrums.' le , such the language that should emanate from "men of temperate habits who know how to control the appetite as well as the tongue." Do "moderators who wilt have to regenerate society" accustom themselves to the use of such discourteous language? Will the above "leaven proceed- ing from a temperate townsman" . . . "in the end have a beneficial effect?" The italics are mine, and I leeve your readers to judge how far "H.W.' may be considered to stand within the temperate zone in us- ing the language above quoted towards teetotallers. "If. W." goes on to say "I am sure that men of temperate habits, who know how to control the appetite as well as the tongue "—why not include the pen—" are much superior to men Iwho have to pledge themselves to a rule of conduct in con- sequence of their weakness." What about life teetotallers? —a goodly number—and also those who have joined the Imovement, and who have never been addicted to habits of intemperance? Many like myself have simply signed the pledge in order to work in the good cause of reclaiming the fallen, and prevent others from falling. Would it not have been wise on " Ll.W.'s " part if he had qualified his expres- sion rather than run a tilt against a noble band of workers, whose sole aim has always been to elevate their fellows to a higher platform than that upon which a large, very large, number have always stood. But take a reclaimed drunkard's case, who has taken the pledge to eustaim him in his weakness. Does he not at least show a superior spirit—aye, and caurage too—to the man "of temperate habits" who casts a taunt and a sneer at a so called weak brother? Again, the oracle has said "As noble actions and good solid work can come from the midst of smoke and beer as ever came from a teetotallers' lodge-room." lain happy to announce, sir, that Dal 7 experience is very limited as to what goes on "midst smoke and beer," and, therefore, cannot contradict " 11. W." on that point; but, on I the other hand, I have had a fair experience of what has 1 taken place within "teetotal lodge-rooms," and have wit- nessed the" noble actions" and have seen the "good solid work" that has resulted from the attendance at such places, and we shall be happy to balance the good results of work performed in our lodge-room, with the good resulting "midst smoke and beer." Will "11. W. accept the challenge? Again, we are informed that "it is the influence of moderators that will have to regerate society." Had a Whig thus spoken, no notice need have been taken; but for " H.W." to utter such a sentence ! Surely your correspondent is not about to join the club now being erected in Sankey-street. No, " H.W." is trying to pass off a joke as a kind of parenthesis. "11.,W.' won't "vote for a man pledged to float the teetotal plank to the front." Just so; certain men of bye-gone days did not like to see Others Caeting out evil, because the other's ipsit dixit was not according to their creed. We are told that a certain class of publicans are dying out, and this we have upon the authority of the bar rooms. 'Tis there the jury have sat and tried the delinquents, and their verdict is "they are not the fittest, therefore they do not survive." And now it only remains for an enlightened public to execute judg- ment. "I have more than once, aye, more than a dozen times, rectared publicans on the desirability of keeping their houses free of bad language and clear of licence. Where is the teetotaller in this town who does this? Not one." What a triumphant flourish from the "Olympus heights, dm." In order to lecture publicans, I presume we should have to visit their homes. Now, should a teetotaller venture to enter a public-house for such a purpose, I fear he would ' soon be ordered off the premises; because a teetotaller can have no right in such a house, except for purely business purposes; therefore, not being a customer he would be guilty of gross impertinence to the proprietor. "U. W. being a customer, the proprietor may only treat him as joking. No, sir, a teetotaller has other and more important work to perform, work that will be far more effective than insulting a publican in his own house. The quotation given from St. Matthew in connection with "It. W.'s " argument is rather absurd, as we are constantly obliged to witness the defilement that follows hard upon the drinking of intoxica- ting liquors.—Yours, dm.' W. H. CHAPMAN. Warrington, February 19th, 1584. MR. WHITHAM AND :POT-HOUSE ARRANGE- MENTS.

Sir,—One is accustonieciibeeS letters in your columns ; from the pen of Mr. Whitham so frequently that I am con- vinced many of them are entirely overlooked, which would not be the case if they were fewer and far between. Mr. I Whitham so seldom says anything about the pot-house that this must be my apology for troubling you with this episge. I have often wondered how it was that Mr. Whithain, who professes to take sach a profound interest in what he con- siders to be for the benefit of workingmen, should never i raise his voice in denunciation of that which all must I admit is the greatest enemy to the working classes of our country; but I am annoyed to find him becoming what he claims to be, "the friend of the publican." Doubtless finding himself in being such, he goes out of his way to make an unwarrantable, and I must say bitter, attack upon the teetotallers of Warrington; nay more than this, Mr. Whitham makes a charge which is positively untrue. lie tells us that a certain section of the Liberal party want to force their watery nostrum to the front, and that the party will split upon such despotic notions. Mr. Whitham cannot prove a single occasion when the temperance people of this town have ever done what he asserts, and I chal- lenge him to do so. The fact is, upon all occasions this section of the party have been most loyal, and have always worked most heartily to secure the success of the Liberal candidate. Can Mr. Whitham say the same ? because I am given to understand that no member of the party so frequently tries to "force his nostrums" upon the party as Mr. Whitham, or that at any rate Mr. Whitham should not throw stones. If Mr. Whitham will stand by the Liberal party as the teetotallers have always done in Warrington, we shall ever have a united party, which must ensure success at any future election. lam glad to hear from Mr. Whitham that he has " mat than a dozen times" lectured publicans on the desirability of keeping their houses free of bad language and clear of license, but Mr. Whitham wants to know where is the teetotaller in this town who does this ? Surely Mr. Whitham forgets that the narrow-minded lot of abusive despots which he terms us are constantly doing the very thing he tells us nobody does but himself. I fear Mr. Whitham must treat the speeches of our local temperance orators as many I fear do his letters—not taking the trouble to read them. Con Mr. VVhitham point out the house where intoxication is unknown, or even rare? I fear not; and such being the case you must have the accom- paniments of bad language and license. We say remove the cause of intoxication and the other evils will disappear as a natural consequence. I never remember a single occasion when Mr. Whitham has either by his voice or pen publicly denounced those vices he now claims to have lectured . publicans for permitting in their houses, of ' which houses he admits being a frequenter. Mr. Whithans also makes a serious charge against a certain • political club for permitting drinking and gambling. If • Mr. Witham is neither a shareholder or member who has • given him this information ? Surely it must be " mere idle gossip," heard, perhaps, in the pothouse. If Mr. Witham ; is at cli friendly towards this club, whichever it may be, why not favour its committee by proving his charge or I withdrawing the slander. In conclusion, I would advise i Mr. Witham to leave out his scriptural quotations, because, coming from one who professes to care little for the good old book, the words enshrined upon its sacred page cannot be to him either a lamp to his feet or a light unto ha path.—Yours, &c., NEMO.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. I The fortnightly meeting of this Board a Guardians was held in the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday morning, Mr W Tyrer presiding. There were also present Messrs W Newsome,J T Hall, J Jackson, J Buckley, J Griffith,J Ken- wright, J Leatherbarrow, W Gerrard, W G Ashton, J Pen- keth; J Lowe. J Fidler, W Gilbody, J Matthew, T F R Tuson, J Fisher, W Swift, R Leigh, IV A Meadows; the Revs T Chambers, J Barnacle, and T Finegan; and Mr S H Hartley (clerk). WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT.

The Workhouse Master reported that there were at present 473 inmates in the workhouse, as against 463 in the preceding week, and 566 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 170 boys and girls in the Kirkdale schools. Thirty-fire vagrants had been relieved daring the past week, as against 56 in the corresponding week of last year.

PLAYING AT PITCH AND TOSS LONG, LONG AGO —A sailor named John Oates was charged on a warrant with not answer- ing to a summons for playing at pitch and toss in October. 1881.—The Chief Constable said that the summons for the offence was served in due course but defendant did not appear, and since that time be hsd been across the seas several times. They did great things in before anyone could see him, those days, and he was not at all disposed to think that the great things which they had accomplished were in vain. (Hear, bear.) If he remembered rightly some 10,0001elue ribbons were donned in connection with that mission, and, when he considered that, he sometimes wondered as he Walked up and down the streets of Warrington what had become of all those blue ribbons. He could certainly say that he had always retained the blue Pibbon from that time to this, although it had got worn and dirty, but he was disposed to think that a great many of their friends who were as good teetotallers as himself, and perhaps better, had left off blue ribbons when the material got dirty and old, and forgot to have new. , (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He had said on numerous oc- casions like the present, and as time went on nothing had altered his opinion that the bit of blue had a great deal, to do with the revival ef temperance throughout the country. Some people had a prejudice against the blue ribbon, be- cause they said it was an American invention, but be hoped that that would be done away with, and that they would consent to wear the ribbon as long as they lived. (Ap- plause.) Is did not at all think that because many bad. dropped the blue ribbon, and perhaps it would be impossible to find the 10,000 blue ribbons that night, that therefore the 10,000 who took the pledge two years ago bad forsaken it, tie knew it was true in connection with that Blue Ribbon Mission that a great many took the pledge who had' not the slightest intention of keeping it. He had heard of some boys and girls taking the pledge half a dozen times over just for the sake of the fun. of thine and they had got their names inscribed half a dozen different times—(laughter)—but making a liberal die- count for that he believed Warrington as a town and people were unspeakably better to-day than they were previous to the Blue Ribbon Mission. (Hear, hear.) He believed it 'told very powerfully on the drink traffic. He had heard of certain diinking shops being closed owing to theeffects of that mission, and he had not heard of them being'opened again. The landlords had been. complaining very bitterly of the Blue Ribbon Mission—(Mr. Murphy: Amen)—and although they (the temperance people) did not wish to do anybody harm, yet they meant to diminish the drink traffic and to do away with it as far they could. (Applause) At present, the temperance cause in this country was unspeak- ably higher than ever it had been before, and a wondrous spirit had been given to it during the last few years. Mr. Murphy, although he had come from Edinburgh that day, had, however, been spending nine or ten months in Ireland, and they would be glad to hear that the work which he had been privileged to do in that country had been exceedingly successful. He (the chairman) had the pleasure of meet- ing him in Belfast in September last. He found Mr. Murphy bad addressed 200 meetings, the direct result being that 100,000 persons had signed the pledge. The chairman read an extract from a temperance journal showing how uniformly successfal Mr. Murphy's work had been, and I said he was sure the meeting would congratulate him heartily on that glorious success. He should like all of them to feel what he hoped they did, that there was great room in that town of Warrington for more earnest temper- ance work to be done and they needed to do it, not in sec- tions and with little sectional jealousies, but hand in band and shoulder to shoulder, all sects of Christians working to- gether, their object being the raising up of the fallen and the rescuing of the perishing. When they read in their local newspapers of the terrible whiskey drinking going on in Warrington, and the acts of violence which weee com- mitted, it called on Christian temperance people to perform their temperance work more heartily than ever, making Warrington what it could hardly be called at present, but what it would be with God's blessing—a sober town. (Ap- plause.)
FIGHT ON A TRAMCAR: ASSAULT- ING A DRIVER.

Walter Lillev, a young men, was on Friday charged at the St. Helens Police Court with having assaulted Charles Albion, a tram.car driver, in the employ of the St. Helens and Districts Tramways Company. Mr. J. 0. Swift prosecuted. —lt appeared from the evidence given that on the night of the 9th instant the tramcar of which Albion is driver left St. Helens terminus at 10 o'clock for Prescot. When the tram-car got to the top of Cropper'S Hill the bell was rung and the driver consequently drew up. As soon as be had done this he heard a struggle going on on the top of the car, and also someone call out to him by name. He went to the top and there saw two men fighting, one of whom he got hold of, the conductor laying hold of the other. The defendant, who was sitting on the opposite side of the car, interpoaed, however, and after the exchange of a few words, struck ' Albion and knocked him down ou the seat. lie then, it was stated for the prosecution, tried to put Albion over the side of the car, and also bit nis hand in a very vicious manner. —The defendant, in defence, denied that he had used any great violence, and said he had mistaken APaion to be some one who had come up to take part in the fight.—The Chair- man (Mr. W. Pilkington) asked if anything had been done towards punishing those who commenced the fight on the tramcar. He theught something ought to have been done in the interests of the public.—Mr. Swift said the whole case had been reported by the conductor, but they had been unable to identify the man who commenced the fight or he would have been summoned.—The Chairman said there might be some slight doubt in the case, or they would cc,- , tainly have sent the defendant to gaol without the option of a fine. As it was they would fine him £1 and costs for the assault. Defendant was also fined ss. and costs for , having been drunk and disorderly the same night, shortly after the above occurrenca. THE STRIKE AT GOLBORNE. SETTLEMENT OF THE DISPUTE. It is with great pleasure that we announce to-day a settle- ment of the dispute which for the past six weeks has been existing between the firm of Messrs. John Brewis and Co., of the Parkside Cotton Mills, Golborne, and the hands em- ployed by them. The commencement of the dispute will be fresh within the recollection of our readers. 'Owing to the continued depression of the cotton trade, the firm gave notics of their intention to make a reduction of ten per cent, in the wages of the whole of their werkpeople, bet as the hands maintained that they were already much under- paid in comparison with other districts they decided to op- pose the reduction by coming out on strike. Since that time several attempts have been made to bring about a settle- ment, but the hands would only consent to resume operations on the old terms, and at several meetings pledged them- selves to adopt this course. Various incidents in connection with the dispute have been chronicled in this journal as they have occurred—the most remarkable of which is the thoroughly unanimous spirit which appeared to pervade the minds of all the operatives. On Wednesday and :yesterday (Thursday) a report was rapidly spread throughout the town that the masters had consented to withdraw the notices of ten per cent reduction; and a notice, of which the fol- lowing is a copy, was posted on the mill gate:—" Notice. These mills and sheds will commence working at 8-30 on Friday morning at the old rate of wages. , By order. Parkside Mills, February 20th, 1884." This gave great satisfaction to everyone in the town, and it was freely expected that the hands would return to work. Yesterday afternoon (Thursday) a well-attended meeting of the operatives was held at Ashton Heath. The speakers warmly congratulated those present upon the success which had attended their efforts, and'it WAS maintained that the defeat of the masters was due to the unity which had existed among the men. A. resolution was submitted and unanimously passed that the whole of the hands should resume work at breakfast time on the following morning, in accordance with the terms of the notice.

Mr. MILNER, the secretary of the Gospel Temperance movement at Sale, spoke of the success of Mr. Murphy's mission there some time since, when 1,300 pledges were taken and over 2,000 blue ribbons distributed. Persons had signed whom he had never dreamed would do such a thing. In some interesting remarks Mr. Milner spoke of the gutter children and waifs of our large towns, whose condition ha ascribes to the parents, who, instead of looking after them properly and fulfilling their high duties of father and mother, spent their money in the publiebouse for the little helpless souls. He concluded by asking the meeting to dh all they could to get rid of the terrible drink. Rev. ADAM SCOTT followed, and in the course of his ob- servations said there was more virtue in the little bit of blue than many of them dreamt of, and he was sure it was the wearing of the piece of blue thathad kept many of their work--1 ing men out of the public-house. 90 per cent, of the work- ing people who took the pledge off Mr. Murphy when be was in Lancaster had kept it, and of those who had been persuaded to don the piece of blue and had attended God's.. House regularly he did not know a single instance of fail- ure in connection with such people. (Applause.) Rev. T. RIPPON retnarked that a word or two had fallen I from the speakers that evening suggesting that they Eng- lishmen did not love America. He was there as an English- man to say that they did love Americans, and that was one reason why he entertained such an admiration for Mr. Mur- phy. He hoped and trusted that nothing would occur to disturb the good feeling that at present existed between the old and new countries. (Applause.) With reference to the blue ribbon work inaugurated in the Public Hall two years ago, Mr. Yonge had said rightly that they did not see in the town of Warrington so many blue ribbons to-day as they were wont to see, bat that did not mean the temperance sentiment was any lower than it was two years ago, as he believed the temperance sentiment in Warrington was highei• to-day than it had ever been, and. the Blue Ribbon Mission put new life into the old temperance societies connected with their different churches. As a temperance reformer he was glad to know that the temperance question was now advocated from the pulpit. 'the time was that to preach a temperance sermon from their pulpits and even their dissenting pulpits would mean showers of reproof being showered down on their heads, but times had changed. Sir Wilfrid Lawson stated the other day that the Duke of Albany was a teetetuller, and.he (Mr. Rippon) expected the Queen herself would sign the pledge next. (Applause.) Mr. MURPHY (who was loudly applauded) then.addressed the meeting in an eloquent speech. Hr first expressed his warmest thanks to Mr. Yonge for giving him that privilege of being with them and saying good-bye before he left for his own mother country, which he expected to.do on the 2511 or 29th of March. He was glad to hear the testimony regarding their work in Warrington. True it had not been all that they would wish it had been as some had fallen away, but he noticed in every town he visited. that it was not difficult to hear of the man who had broken the pledge, • as there were any number of people who were willing to tell L them that fact, but there were few who would stand by and point to those who had kept it faithfully, but there were men who two years ago had signed the pledge who came to the house of God and who had remained true up to the present. (Applause.), He say a man in the church that night with his wife and child whom be prevailed to take .the pledge 5 two years ago, and he (Mr. Murphy) thanked God for that L living testimony of the permanency of their Gospel Tem- perance Mission movement. (Applause.) As Mr. Yonge had stated, he had been in Ireland. That was a grand country and a noble people, and he only wished it was pos- sible that the English people should become better, acquainted with the good people over there. They heard plenty ef the people who were not very good, but he would, say that there were as loyal subjects in the north of Ireland as there were in England, and as much reverence was evinced for Her Gracious Majesty in Ulster and Munster as in Lan- cashire. (Applause.) He thanked God that a better day had dawned upon Ireland, and that peace and happiness had permeated that country. Mr. Murphy attributed the whiskey drinking in Ireland as accessory to, the crimes which had been committed, for he believed that if the drink had not been • sold the crimes would nbt have been committed. Over 15,00 e people signed the pledge and donned the blue ribbon, and that was why the country had been so quiet lately. ' (Hear, bear.) Of course there was opposition tommet in • their work, but the fact that they had opposition wasa proof ' that they were right. The Duke of Albany, speaking at ' Liverpool a short time since, made this declaration, that the drink wall the only terrible enemy England had to fear. (Hear, hear.) That mevement reached • the highest as well as the lowest class in the United Kingdom. Mr. Murphy alluded to the Duchess of ' Sutherland and other members of the aristocracy taking such a great interest ia the temperance cause, and when they saw the grand and noble work they were accomplishing it would be most convincing to the most sceptical that it was a great reform.. They were told that they were struggling ' with a minority, but so was Christianity. He urged total abstainers to throw off any lethargy in their work. Ha -poke at some length on individual enterprise in the tem, perance movement, and in concluding his address asked them to infuse a new inspiration, a new courage, into their • work, and they would be rewarded by the golden gate of • liberty being thrown open, and England would be free from that terrible sin. (Applause.) • Rev. E. MOORE was sure that the public conscience of ; Warrington was sound on the question of temperance. If ti,ey could get their measures before the House of Com- ment be should be hopeful of the result. The meeting was shortly afterwards brought to a con- clusion. Several appropriate temperance hymns were sung
NEWTON-LE-WILL) w CHORAL SOCIETY.

Linder the auspices of this society a concert, consisting of Sullivan's cantata "On shore and sea," with miscellaneous songs, duetts, and glees was given in the Newton Town Hall on Monday evening, before a large and appreciative audience. The hall had been tastefully decorated for the occasion, under the direction of Mr. E. T. Evans, of Earles- town, the extended platform being covered with red cloth and the windows draped with long curtains. The choir was under the efficient conductorship of Mr. P. Fairclocigh ; and Mr. J. H. Greenwood, or Manchester, executed the piano- forte accompaniments in a brilliant manner. In the cantata the principal solos fell to Mr. J. Owen, who succeeded fairly well; and his singing was duly appreCiated. In her ffirst appearance before an audience,Miss Roberts (Newton) showed a little nervousness, but gained her confidence as the e-en- ing wore on. She possesses a sweet voice of average com- pass, and gives promise of future improvement. She was warmly applauded. In the opening chorus the singers were not quite together, but the succeeding pieces were effectively given, so much so as to draw forth commendable applause from the audience. The miscellane- ous part of the programme was opened with a humourous song, entitled "Fair Rosamond," by Mr. J. H. Greenwood, who, it is needless to add, created much merriment. He however, did not respond to the encore wliich followed. Mies Rees, Miss Turner, and Miss Atkin sang with taste Donizetti's "Over meadow, over mountain," which was succeeded by "Our sailors on the sea" (Le), a song by Mr. Howard, who received a recall. Miss Grace rendered Caroline Lowthian's song, "The gates of the west," with considerable sweetness and a clear enunciation of the words, and well merited the hearty encore which she received. The choir gave Pinsuti's glee, "The watchword," and Brinley Richards' "Let the hills resound," after which Miss Rose was warmly received in her song "The old lock" (Well- inge), of which she gave an excellent rendering, her efforts being rewarded with a recall. The duet, "Sweet evening hour" (Smart). was well interpreted by Miss Grace and Miss L. Grace; and Mr. Stone's song, "Down in the deep" (Harding), was encored. The amusing and lively glee, "Three Doughtie men" (Pearson), was given with much effect by the choir: Mice Liptrot prettily sang "Wild flowers " (Gounod), and received a recall ; as did also Mr. W. Haskell for his song, "On deck" (Jude). Mr. J. H. Greenwood's humorous "Re- miniscences of a cabman" created much laughter. On being recalled, he gave "The silver wedding "—an equally amusing selection. Front's boat song," entitled " Hail to the chief," by the choir, brought the programme to a close.

STAGS PLAYS AT THE TOWN HALL—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday, Mr. W. H. Thomas- applied for a license to be granted to Mr. W. G. Foreman to hold the performances of stage plays in the Town Hall on the even- ings of the 25th and 26th inst. The plays were to be "Our Boys" and the," Waterman," and were to be performed by amateur dramatic performers for the benefit of the St. Helens Cricket Club. The application was granted. EMBEZZLEMENT BY A FRIENDLY SOCIETY SECRETARY AT PRESCOT.—A young man named Thomas- Bowstead was on Tuesday charged at the Prescot Police Court, under war- rant, with having embezzled monies the property of the i Loyal Victoria Lodge ot Oddrellows (Present), of which he had been secretary.—Mr. Mackenzie, who appeared on ba• , half of the trustees, said the trustees of this friendly society ' had applied to Mr. Evans for a warrant against the prisoner for embezzling monies belonging to the society. Since that warrant was issued it had been founfl that there would be some difficulty in proving the case ; 'there had also been some arrangement come to between the parties. His ap- plication was therefore, with the consent of the Bench, that they discharge the prisoner, and that the warrant be with- drawn.—The Clerk (Mr. Spencely) Sall the Bench would have to know what the arrangement was —Mr. Mackenzir. said he believed the arrangement was one whereby the amount of the prisoner's defalcations had been estimated, and the prisoner and a friend had undertaken to repay the money—The Chairman (Mr. W. W. Pilkington): don't chink a thing of that sott ought to be withdrawn; the case will have to go on.—Mr. Mackenzie :I quite admit that thia is an unusual application, but my instructions alit entirely withdrawn, and he was not prepared to go on with it.--The Chairman said the case had been put into the hands of the police, and in case Mr. Mackenzie did not go on with it they would have to adjourn it.—Mr. Mackenzie admitted that a criminal court ougla not to be made the means of a civil action, and he did not think it was the intention of the parties to make that applic ition, but discoveries had been made of some difficulties in the way of the prosecution. Applications of that kind were sometimes granted.—The Chairman: We think it ought not to be granted in this Ca.,e. We will adjourn the case till next session.—Mr. Mackenzie : In the meantime you will allow bail ?—The Clerk: Von said you were not instructed. Do you appear on both sides? Let him apply for himself.—The prisoner was then remanded till the 26th lust., without bail.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday. There were present: Mr. Greening (chairman), Mr. Cooper (vice-chairman), His Worship the Mayor, Rev. G. F. Roberts, Dr. Mackie, Major Cartwright, and Messrs. Foster, Blackhurst, Jolley, Jeans, Brown, Appleton, Darhyshire, Grange, Worthing- ton, Hnmphreys, Hunt, Bonnell, J. Houghton, Greenali, G,bsonv W. Houghton : Mr. J. C. Sutton (clerk), and Mr S Sutton (deputy clerk.)

FIRE OUT-RIMEL At a meeting of the Workhouse Committee on the 15th inst. tenders for a new boDer, &c., were submitted by Mr. Stephen Mose, whose tenter was £l2 10s., and Messrs. Jones and Son, whose tender was £l3 10e.—The committee recommended that new service water pipes be laid at once, and that hydrants be placed where required in case of fire. The oid pipes, it was stated, are silted up.—Major CART, I WRIGHT moved the confirmation of the proceedings of the committee, and im doing so remarked that there were 30 in- mates fewer than last year in the house now ; and also that out-relief had hem reduced by SA 10s. per week.—Mr. JOLLEY seconded the motion. Mr. BLecxturnsr bald be did not see anything to congratulate thercselves upon either as regarded the decrease in the number of inmates or_in the decrease of the out-relief. He considered it was sometimes a downright cruelty and hardship tc,compel peor people to go into the house. Every case, he said, should be considered on its merits, and as long as he was a member of that Beard be should invariably stick out fOr out-relief. Mr. Apmerrotr considered there was cause for congratulation on both heads, but thought that out-door relief, judiciously and properly administered, Wa3 the proper thing.—Mr. BROWN took it that all the relief was judiciously administered, but he was afraid a great deal of out-relief was given, which perhaps Would be better if reconsidered. He was notaware either that they usually forced people into the house;. he could not call to mind any instance where pressure had been used to send a person into the house. Be thought they were rather kind, to the people who asked. for relief, and that their conduct in that respect ' worrki compare favourably with that of any other Board of Guardians.—The Cnernmtas pointed out the necessity for providing new water service pipes and, hydrants, as suggested by the committee in case of fire.—Dr. MAREIR, thought the branches put down should be quite the size of the main with the full force.—Major CARTWRIGHT, alluding to the observations about out-relief, said he hoped it would not be oupposed he acted arbitrarlay in that matter, but he did, not wish to see out-door relief administered to worth- less people to eke out a bare existence.—The proceedings' of the committee were confirmed. THE PADGATE SCEIOOLS. The proceedings of the Schools Committee were unim- portant. The doctor reported that he had examined the children and found them all well. The minutes-were • adopted.
SCHOOL FEES.
The Fehool Fees Committee reported that they had .dis. posed of 12 new and 49 old cases—total 61.

THE VALUATION OF THE RAILWAYS. Mr t COOPER moved a motion confirming resolutions of the Assessment Committee, directing the clerk and valuer (Mr. Owen) to enquire into and report upon the accounts of the London and North-Western Railway and the Bridge- I water Canal Company, and also directing Mr. Owen to value the property of the Collins Green Colliery Campany, in the township of Burtonwood, for the purposes of assessment. Mr. Cooper observed that he hoped ths Assessment Corn- - mittee would be able to bring up the rateable value not only of the railways, but of several works, to a much higher standard.—Mr. DARETSHIRB seconded the motion. He had, he said, been a ratepayer in this Union for the last twenty years, and he had always, and still thought that he was paying a. portion of tne rates which the Bridgewater Navi- gation Company ought to pay.—Major CARTWRIGHT spoke in favour of a re-valuation of the Union, and observed that it was a. simple matter to value a farm,„ but he would be shot if they could value all the railway lines through the raion.—Dr. MACKIE cautioned the Board against being too hard on the railway companies, who, he remarked; were prepared to fight. He also stated that in a neighbouring union about 200 farmers were having the assessment of their farms raised simply because the London and North-Western Railway Company did not think they were fairly. treated.—Mr. BLACKHURST thought the railway, companies ought to bear their fair share of assessment.— Mr. Appx.wrots considered the farms in this Union were as- sessed too high.—After some further consideration, in which the CLERK, emplained the course he intended to take when appealing before the County Assessment Committee at Preston, the resolution was carried. THE MASTER'S REPORT.

The MAsirnn reported that the number of inmates in the House daring last week was 325, against 57.6 tin the corres- ponding week of last year. The number of vagrants re- lieved was 115.-01 of whom were men, 18- women, and 6 children. There were 83 imbeciles in the Workhouse. The Master further reported that on Februaryl.6 a man, named Richardson, broke into the Workhouse and put up a number of things in a bag to carry away with him, when he was disturbed and made off. The matter was reported to the police. tie is the person who got six months for a similar act at lirrescot Workhouse almost seven months ago, also six months from here over 14 months ago. Mrs. Reynolds and Friends gave an entertainment to the inmates on Monday night, at which the Rev. B. B. Present presided. All seemed to enjoy the entertainment very much. There was no other business of interest.

div.head: TELEASIIHESHIP.
div.p: THE TELEASIIHESHIP.

The CLERK read a communication from the Local Go- vernment Board, sanctioning the appointment of Mr. C. C. White as treasurer to the Union. Mr. NEWSOME moved that the balances of the several accounts of the Guardians in Parr's Bank be transferred to Mr. Wbite, and also that Mr. White be formally appointed treasurer. Mr. LEATHER- BARROW seconded this proposal, which was carried unani- msualy.—The CLERK also read a letter from Mr. White, in which he gave the names of two of the directors of the Manchester and Salford Bank who would stand his bonds for £lO,OOO.

div.head: PROPOSED ALTERATIONS AT THE WORKHOUSE.
div.p: THE PROPOSED ALTERATIONS AT THE WORKHOUSE.

Another communication from the Local Government Board was read with respect to the proposed further increase of accommodation at the Workhouse, and stating that before they sanctioned these alterations they considered it neces- sary to instruct their professional advisers to visit the Workhouse and to report thereon.

ONE-SIDED PATRONAGE. A letter was read from Mr, W. G. Dixon, cab proprietor, of St. Helens, complaining of what he censidered the unfair way in which cabs were engaged by the St. Helens relieving officer. His place of business, he wrote, was convenientiv situated, and as he waa a ratepayer he thought he had a just right to have a fair share of their patronage.—Mr. FIDLER : If it is divided amongst others he ought to have a share.—Mr. JACKSON Yes; he was born in the Union. (Laughter.)—The CH/dam/LS thought the relieving officers ought to be told to divide their patronage.—lt was agreed that this should be done.

div.head: MEI EXPENDITI7RE.
div.p: MEI EXPENDITI7RE.

The CLERK submitted an estimate of the expenditure for the half-year ending September 29th. The total amount was .£25,073.—Mr. CrILBODY asked how that amount com- pared with srevious estimates ?—The CLERK said it was much the same. There was a slight increase in the Assess- ment Committee charges. but there was a considerable reduc- tion in the out-relief. Within the past few years there had been a reduction in the item of out-relief of about £2,000.— Mr. Cueslinsits: I think that will be the most satisfactory intelligence to the ratepayers.—ln answer to a question, the CLERK said the railway assessments in the Union had recently been raised by almost £lo,ooo.—Mr. NEWSOME : That will mean that the railway companies will now pay a sixth of the rates of the whole Union.—The CLERK: More than a sixth—nearly a fifth —The subject then dropped.

div.head: VAC-ANT RELIEVING OF-FICERSHIP„
div.p: THE VAC-ANT RELIEVING OF-FICERSHIP„

The CLERK said that six applicants (out of 196 who had applied) for the vacant relieving officership at St. Helens had been requested to attend that meeting for the purpose of a final selection. These six were :-0. M. Barton, R. P. Beard, Thomas Bell, and Peter Taylor, of St. Helena; James Tinsley. Whiston ; and Joseph Tracey, Ditton. These candidates having been separately called into the room and interrogated, each of their names was voted upon. It was then found that Mr. Tracey and Mr. Barton had re- ceived the highest number of votes, the idrmer receiving nine and the latter six. The names of Mr. Barton and Mr. Tracey were again pat to the vote, when they each 'received 13 votes. The Chairman thereupon gave the casting vote for Mr. Barton, who accordingly received the appointment.

SUPPOSED DEFALCATIONS. The CLERK asked that the books of Mr. Harrison, the late relieving officer, should be referred to the Finance Com- mittee. They bad found, be said, since Mr. Harrison had ceased to be actively engaged as the servant of the Gear- dians,that he had been giving orders to persons who required relief not on the prescribed form. Owing to this it was dtterly impossible for the Guardians or himself (the clerk) to ascertain how much money had been spent in the dis- trict. He might say that over £2O was now owing to vari- ous tradesmen in the Union, and he was very much afraid that the Guardians would not be in a position to pay the greater portion of that money. He should like the matter to be thoroughly investigated by the Finance Committee, that the committee might say as soon as possible what steps should be taken.—Mr. Ham. moved, and Mr. SWIFT seconded, that the matter be referred to the Finance Com- mittee, and it was agreed to. THE PANTASAPH QUESTION. The Rev. T. FINEGAN, in abcordance with a notice of motion, moved that the resolution passed in August last, that no children be sent to Pantasaph Orphanage from the Workhouse, should be rescinded. In support of this proposal he pointed out that up to last August all the accounts from Pantasaph had been most cheering and satisfactory. Consequently he had been some- what surprised when he saw what bethought was the hasty action of the Guardians in removing the children away from that institution, and in saying that no more children should be sent there. He contended that the representatives of Father Henry, who had given so much time and trouble without fee or reward, in advancing the welfare of the in- mates of the Workhouse, ought to have some weight with the Board. He pointed out also that Pantasaph Orphanage was a public institution, and consequently to a great extent lived upon its reputation, and that the action of that Board was calculated to reflect upon the establishment. In regard to expense, Pantasaph, he said, contrasted favourably with Kirkdale, and therefore there could be no objection to rescind the resolution on that account. In conclusion he urged that if they adopted his proposal it would tend to establish in the Union a more perfect harmony and modus ivendz. —Mr. SwisT seconded the proposal. In doing so he said he had recently paid a visit to Pantasaph, and found the people there very much hurt by the action of the Guar- dians. In regard to the charge that children had been kept in the orphanage longer than the Guardians thought they ought to be, there were none kept there over 13 years of age, with the exception of one who was an im- becile.—Mr. LEATHEREARROW opposed the proposal. He said that although children only cost 4s. 3d. a week at Pantasaph, while they cost 4s. 101 at Kirkdale, the cost of sending them to the former place was so much greater as to almost reduce the difference. Besides, more people who wanted children went to Kirkdale, which was a more con- venient place.—Mr. JACKSON thought they ought to "obey the prayer" of Father Henry, and adopt the proposal of Father Finegan.—Mr. FIDLER thought that in sending the children away the Guardians were simply shirking the responsibility of building, schools of their own, till the Local Government Board stepped in and compelled them to build. , —Mr. MEADOWS, while speaking favourably of Pantasaph,

thought it was the duty of the Guardians to getthe children situations as soon as they possibly could, and thus relieve the ratepayers of their maintenance.—Mr. HALL admitted that Fantasaph was a splendid institution, but they could not expect people to go there for children. He pointed out that when 19 children were brought away to Kirkdale 18 were placed in suitable situations within a fortnight —The Rev. T. CHAM- BERS supported the proposal. He considered that any the- advantage which Pantasaph suffered owing to its distance was overbalanced by the advantages which the children bad in being educated at that Place. He took it that if any childrenthad been kept longer than they ought to have been it was as much the fault of the Guardians and their officials as of anyone else.—Mr. NEWSOME, who opposed the proposal, said it seemed to have been forgotten that of the 34 children brought from Pantasaph no fewer than 19 were of an age between 12 and 18.—Father FINEGAN, in reply, said there had only been four of the children over 14 years of age. He believed there were quite as many in Kirkdale Bchools —On the proposal of Father Finegan being voted upon 7 hands were held up in its support, and 12 against. It was consequently lost. THE PROPOSED WELL AT THE WORKHOUSE.

From the report of the Visiting Committee it appeared that the further consideration of the scheme for sinking a well at the Workhouse was left over to allow of inquiries being made. This was all the business.

CRUELTY TO A PONY.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday, a youth named Thomas Gilgannon, was charged with having cruelly worked a pony whilst in an unfit state; and George Moss, the owner of the animal, was charged with having allowed the same to be worked. It was stated by an officer that on the 7th inst. he saw the first named defendant driving the pony near Greenbank Alkali Works. One of the animal's hind legs.was in a shocking state, being I almost rotten. Inspector Keighley corroborated this state- ment, and superintendent Jobnson said the pony bad been since destroyed. Moss was fined 10s, and costs, and Gil- gannon ss. and costs. PROSECUTION BY THE ST. HELENS CORPORATION.—John Hogan, tubmaker, St. Helens, was on Friday, summoned befure the St. Helens Bench on two charges, viz., of having erected a building without previously having given the Corporation the requisite notice in writing; and of having covered the same building with a combustible material. Defendant pleaded guilty, and Mr. J. 0. Swift, who prosecu- ted on behalf of the Corporation, said that as Mr. Hogan had pleaded guilty the Corporation were that the case should be adjourned for a fortnight in order to allow Mr. Hogan an opportunity of complying with their require- ments, which he had expressed a desire to do. The case was accordingly adjourned for a fortnight.

SAVAGERY AT Sr. HELENS.—A young man named Wm Naughton was on Monday charged, at the St. Helens Police Court, with having done grievous bodily harm to Thomas Butler by biting off a tiortion of his ear. Both men' it seemed, lodged together at the house of. John Harris 36, Langtree-street, Parr. On Saturday night, about 11 o'clock, Butler was sitting in the house when the prisoner came in drunk and accused him of having said something about him. After some words had been exchanged, they both went into the yard to fight, but before any blows had been struck the prisoner got hold of Butler and, after they had both fallen to the wound, got hold of his ear with his teeth. Butler cried out that his ear was being eaten off, upon which a man named Lacey separated them. After the blood had been washed away from Butler's face, it was seen that nearly , half of his ear was gene. The piece of ear was afterwards picked up by tlse landlady's daughter. The prisoner was ceoacaitted to the Sessions for trial.

div.head: DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT HAYDOCK LODGE ASYLUM.
div.p: DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT HAYDOCK LODGE ASYLUM.

£3,000 DAMAGES. Haydock Lodge Lunatic Asylum, of which institution Dr. Beaman is the proprietor, was the scene of a most destruc- tive tire on Wednesday evening. The establishment is situated in its own grounds, about midway between Newton. le-Willows, Ashton, and Haydock, and the main building is a commanding and palatial looking structure, formerly occupied as the seat of the Legh family. About ten years ago this was destroyed by fire, but fortunately, on the present occasion the devouring element was confined to an extensive block of two storied buildings at the rear. This block is utilised by the laundries, sculleries, ser- vants' rooms, engineer's house, bakehouse, &c, and mea. sured about 30 or 40 yards square. It was here that the outhreak occurred, and before the flames were extinguished the whole building was reduced to ruins, while the Asylum proper for a considerable time was in imminent danger of falling a prey to the flames. How the fire originated is at present a mystery, but it was discovered in the drying-room attached to the laundry, after it had been locked up for the night. About nine o'clock, Miss Kate* Cahill, the head-laundress, saw that all was safe, but a little later a smell ot burning timber was detected, and on a search being instituted smoke was noticed to be issuing from the dre log-room. On the door being opened a dense volume of smoke came out of the room, and it was seen that the clothes suspended for drying purposes were on fire, and the flames had also reached the wood work adjoining. An alarm was instantly given, and the Asylum tire bell was rung. The members of the fire brigade quickly turned up, and immediately made a determined effort to suppress the outbceak with buckets of water, fire extincteure, &c., while under the directions of Mr. D.Robinson,engineer, several hose pipes were affixed to the hydrants about the grounds. The flames cmickly spread, however, and other portions of the building were soon ablaze. In the meantime a mounted messenger had been despatched to Ashton for the Ashton Volunteer Fire Brigade; another-was sent to Newton for the engine and brigade from Messrs. McCorquodale and Co.'s printing works; while a third proceeded to the, Hay- dock Collieries for Messrs. Richard Evans and Co.'s brigade. The Ashton men immediately put in an appear- anceelmt the lack of an engine was soon manifest. How- ever, with the means at their disposal they bravely strove to cope with the flames until Messrs. McCorquodale's engine and men turned up—which they did about an hour after the outbreak, the engine and men from Messrs. Evans' appearing on the scene a few minutes later. By this time, however, a portion of the roof had fallen in with a loud crash, and as the flames shot high in the air the reflection was observed many miles away, hundreds of persons being attracted to the spot from Earlestown, Givelborne, Newton, and Ashton, while the sounding of the various fire-alarms announced the fact to many others. Seeing the danger which menaced the whole block Dr. Beaman gave orders for the roof connecting it with the Asylum to be destroyed, and this, ass matter of precaution, was duly carried out by members of the fire brigades. The latter continued, to battle ' with the flames, but one room after aaother fell a prey to the fire, and as the flumes continued to shoot out of the roof and windows the spectacle was "awfully grand." The utmost efforts were exerted to prevent the fire spreading to the main building; and we are pleased to be able to say that, thanks to the assistance ren- dered by the various brigades and other willing helpers, this object was achieved. Fortunately, the almost hurri- cane of wind which was blowing came from over the Asy, I lum, for lilt had been blowing in the opposite direction the task of saving the principal structure would have been a most difficult and dangerous one. Up to about two o'clock on the following morning the lames burned fiercely, but after that hour they gradually declined, as they had burnt out all the contents of the block in which the conflagration had occurred. At four o'clock nothing but the smouldering ruins remained, and many of the firemen were able to return to .their homes—but a few were kept on guaret in case another outbreak should take place. The various brigades deserve praise for their hard and persever- ing efforts to extinguish the fire, but undoubtedly especial praise is due to the Newton men, who were under the effi- cient command of Captain Wood. The engine they bseught with them came in eminently useful, and rendered good set- vice. The damage is estimated at about £3,000, which is coveredpay insurance. The machinery and engine house was also destroyed, and as the building was fitted up with the best Modern machinery great damage was caused. A large body of police constables, in charge of Police-sergeants Savage (Ashton), D.avlin (Haydock), and Comninas (Newton) were in attendance to preserve order, and they also rendered valuable assistance. During the course of the fire P.C. Ratcliffe, of Gulborne, met with a mirachaus escape from serious injury, if not death. He was in one of the rooms directing a hose pipe when a chimney stack fell, and seeing this coming he just stepped back beforethe bricks alighted in front of nim. Ho was knocked to the floor, and so surpris- ing was his escape that the falling bricks tore the bottons off his coat as they descended. We are informed that every precaution was taken

for the due safety of the inmates of the Asylum in case the fire should have spread. As it did not do so, none of the patients will be interfered with, and barring a little incon- venience which the servants will temporarily have to put up with, the establishment will be carried on as usual. A large number of persons paid a visit to the Asylum, en Thursday, in order to see the destructive effects of the fir e

CHESHIRE DAIRY FARMERS' - ..ASSOCIATIOic. meeting of the Cheshire Dairy Farmers' Association was held on Saturday afternoon, at the Golden Lion Hotel, Chester. Mr. Feorge Barbour, chairman of the Council of the Association, presided. The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings explained that the present was the first meeting of the gisiety since the show held in Chester last October. That show was a most successful one. The association seemed to be making headway, and he believed it was, doing good bene- ficial work both for the landlords and the tenant farmers of Cheshire. Mr. J. CARTER BELL, the county analyst, then read a Paper on milk, in which he said :—lt is all important for farmers to understand that it is more profitable to produce rich milk than poor; as in Cheshire alone, if the milk is only a few degrees above the standard it would make a dif- ference in money value to the amount of £5OO a day. Chemists and others have observed that the cream and fat is liable to the greatest variations; therefore in judging a milk it has been found advisable to separate the cream and to have a standard for the cream or fat, and also a standard for the solid matter without the fat. As it is difficult for the public to understand the figures belonging to a milk analysis I propose to call the milk "Standard milk, or above or below standard." We must now ascertain what standard milk should be. For my purpose I shall say that 100 parts by weight of the milk must contain twelve per cent of total solid matter; of this three per cent should consist of the fat or cream, and the remaining nine per cent consists of sugar, casein, mineral matter, 8:c. This standard milk is what would be yielded by an ordinary poor dairy. There are cases within my experience where cows have not given standard milk; thus I have found some poor cows which would only give milk containing nine per cent of solids not fat, and 2i per cent of fat. Such a milk as this would be below the standard; on the other hand, I have found cows which would give solids not fat ten per cent, and four per cent of fat, This would be far above the standard. Thus, if three per cent of fat is the standard and by some means it is reduced to two, one-third of the cream would have been removed, or the fat would be 33 below the standard. If the cow is giving rich milk and the fat amounts to four per cent, then that milk would be 33 above the standard. You may naturally ask me the question: In your experience sde you find the majority of cows give milk above or below the standard? My reply is that I find very few cows which will give milk below the standard. As an instance, I may take the county of Chester and the borough of Salford as examples. In these places the Adulteration Act is so well carried out by the inspectors appointed for the purpose, that for the year 1883 some hundreds of samples of milk were analysed by me, and taking the adulterated and the non-adul- terated samples, the average milk was considerably above the standard laid down by the Society of Public Analysts. As these samples must have represented some few thousand cows, I think it may be fairly stated that milk from a herd of well-fed cows does not fall below the standard, though some chemists say that well-fed cows will give milk as low as 15 or 20 per cent, below the standard. If such cows do exist that are in perfect health and well fed, and give milk of the above quality, the sooner the farmer removes such offenders from his stalls the better it will be for the dairy. Mr. Bell discussed the effect of different kinds of feeding upon the quality of the milk, and concluded by observing that the members of the Association would see how desirable it was to pay attention to the scientific part of milk production, and it should be the aim of each to Ran in a friendly rivalry to raise the standard of milk. The CHAIRMAN said the competition now-a-days in farm- ing was 80 very great that, while it -should be the effort of the farmer to conduct his farm on business principles, it was desirable that he should avail himself, so far as he' could, of the benefits derivable from the science of chemistry. We were yet in a state of infancy in respect of knowledge as to the feeding of cows. We were told that if cows were fed on one class of food the supply of butter would be in- creased; and if they were fed on another class of food the milk would be more adapted for •cheesemaking, but the question arose : How were we to learn which food was most adapted to increase the butter and which to increase the cheese 2 Coldnel HAMMERSLEY, chief constable of Cheshire' .re- ferred to the existence in Cheshire of many pools of dirty water, which the cattle were ,often allowed to drink while they were being driven to the fields, and asked whether the drinking of such water by the cows did not affect the quality of the milk. Mr. CARTER BELL replied that while he had no good data upon which' to bass an opinion, he could not speak too strongly against cows being allowed to drink dirty water, the drinking of such water must have an ikfluence on the milk. Mr. Thomas RIGBY, secretary to the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture, said there could be no eioutit that if dairy farmers wanted to obtain good results they must feed their cows with food rich in the constituents, which went to inake the rnatertal they wished the cows to produce. The farmers would, he thought, benefit themselves by having their milk analysed frequently. Cases had occurred and might occur again in which farmers had been,fined for adulterating their milk, whereas the poorness of the milk was not due to the use of the pail but to the thinness of the milk given by the cows. With regard to the ensilage experiments he con- sidered their importance could hardly be over estimated. It was for daily farmers to closely watch a movement from which important results might be secured. Mr. HAlLwoon, milk contractor, Manchesto, expressed his opinion that the sanitary 'condition of the farmers in Cheshire—the amount of breathing space, the drainage, be. —was far below what it ought to be. At the same time he thought that bofh in quantity and quality the milk of Che- shire was far better than that of Derbyshire. After some further discussion, a hearty vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Carter Bell for his paper.

Two men, named Alford and Collier, were apprehended at Southwell, on Saturday morning, while engaged in a prize fight. The " Druid " of Llantrissant, Dr. Price, who excited much indignation a short time ago by attempting to burn the dead body of his infant child, was discharged from custody on Saturday, at Glamorganshire Assizes, the Crown having withdrawn the charge of misdemeanour preferred against bins in respect of that proceeding. In the Queen's Bench division on Monday, a professional singer, named Harley, recovered £250 damages from Mi. Henderson, the proprietor of the Comedy Theatre, for wrongful dismissal from his employment. The dismissal was on the ground that the plaintiff did not sing "in tune." On one aide a number of professional witnesses were called to prove that the plaintiff .did sing in tune: and on the other side evidence was produced that the singing was as a rule out of tune, and that the plaintiff was not a capable first tenor. PROPOSED MINISTER FOE SCOTIAND.—Mr. Gladstone en Tuesday received a deputation appointed at a great meeting held in Edinburgh on the 16th ult, to bring under his atten- tion the general demand in Scotland for the creation of at special department of state for Scotland, with a Scotchman of personal eminence acquainted with Scotch affairs at its head, and with a permanent Under-Secretary to ensure con- tinuit, of action. In reply to the deputation, Mr. Glad- stone paid the Government were cordially in agreement with the movement which they represented. Having explained the willingness of the Ministry to introduce a measure es early as was expedient for its success, the Premier informed :he deputation that if, as practical men, they wished to , put forward this question, the best assistance they could 4ive was to use whatever influence they possessed, not to promote the acceptance of the measures of the Government —for that he had no right to ask—but to secure a reasonable rate of progress in the despatch of public business. PROPOSED RESTORATION AT ERINBUREDI CASTLE.—The members of the Edinburgh Architectural Association assem- bled at Edinburgh Castle on Saturdaf, .and-uanimously passed a resolution, pressing upon the attention of the Government the condition of the ancient hall in the castle, the associations of which are of the deepest interest to stu- dents f national history, and urging most strongly the importance of restoring the hall and other parts of the struc- ture connected therewith to something like their Original condition. It was agreed to present a memorial to the Government. HUNGRY CHILDREN.—A little boy and girl named Jos. Norman and Harriet Bates were, on Wednesday, charged at the St. Helens Police Court, with having stolen two tins of preserved salmon from the shop of Benjamin William- son, in Traverse-street. On Tuesday afternoon the two accused went to Mr. Williamson's shop to buy bread. While the bread was being sought the two were left in the shop by themselves. After they had gone the two tins were missed, and chase was given to the prisoners. The bey, while running away, droppad both the tins which were re- covered by Mrs. Williamson. When apprehended they accused each other of taking the salmon.
