div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 23. 1884,
HO RRIBLE CRUELTY TO A HEIFER.

SIX RUNCORN MEN COMMITTED. On Monday, at the Prescet Police Court, before Mr. W. L. Evans, six young men named Joseph Gaiter, James Gaiter, George Woodier, George Guy, Wesley Yarwool, and Henry Johnson, all of whom belong to Runcorn, were charged with having wilfully mutilated a heifer, belonging to Mr. John Sutton, farmer, of Spake. Mr. H. le. Riley prosecuted, and Mr. J 0. Swift defended.—Mr. Riley, in opening the case, said the prisoners were charged under section 40 of the Act consolidating the law of malicious injury which dealt with persons guilty of wilfully and un- lawfully killing, maiming, or wounding cattle, and when he mentioned to his worship that the punishment might be so high as 14 years' penal servitude, he would feel, as he did, en the one hand that no person should be put on his trial unnecessarily, but, on the othee, if there was a prima facie case made out, that they ought to be committed, and not left to be dealt with under the less severe law of cruelty to animals. On Saturday night, the 26th January, a heifer belonging to Mr. John Sutton was placed in a small field where there was a barn or shed to shelter in. On the fol- lowing morning, about seven o'clock, it was found to be unable to walk', and was bleeding from the barron. Close to where it was lying was found a long sick covered with blood and fat, apparently cut from a decaying tree in the same field. The heifer was removed on a door to the ship- pen, and though in considerable pain it was allowed to live until the Monday, when it was killed. Upon examination afterwards it was found that some sharp instrument had been pushed violently up the cow's barron. A hole had been pierced into one of the larger intestines, and also into the fat near the spine. The instrument had touched the kid- neys, and the liver was also injured, these injuries showing very pointedly that the stick had been moved rapidly up and down the animal's body. The next important point was as to whether the six prisoners were in any way connected with the injuries. On information being given to the police inquiries were at once made, and it was ascertained that all the prisoners had been at Liverpool on the night of the 26th ult. They missed the last train there, and afterwards started to vqlk home. The way home led them past the field in which the heifer was placed. On their being arrested they said they had sheltered in a barn, and four of them were separately allowed to show an officer the barn in which they sheltered, and from what they said it was evident they had been in the immediate neighbour- hood of this outrage. On the respective coats and trousers of Joseph Gaiter and George Guy were found traces of blood and fat, and these had been analysed by Dr. Camp- bell Brown who would tell them the blood and fat on the stick was identical with that on the clothing.—Evidence was then given as to the finding and removal of the muti- lated heifer by Ann Dunbabbin awl Ralph Dunbabbin, who are in the employ of Mr. Sutton.—Dr. C. J. Campbell Brown, county analyst, spoke to having examined the stick and the coats,and trousers referred to above, and having found thereon stains of the blood of a mammal, and also some fat. These stains were evidently of very recent origin.—Wm. Elitchmold spoke to having killed the heifer and corroborated the statements of Mr. Riley as to the in- ternal injurieseit had received.—Thomas Rigby, butcher at Hale Cliff, Hale. gave similar evidence to that of Hitch. mold.—Ellen Wiaapenny, who lives in Oglet-lane, Speke, I said that on the morning of Sunday the 27th January, between five and six o'clock, someone knocked at her docile and when she looked out of the window she saw four or five young enen striking matches in the road and there war another at the doer. They went away in a few minutes as she did not open the door. She could not recognise the prisoners as being any of those young men, as she had had a very imperfect view of them—Mrs. Ellen Stockton said she saw six or seven men pass Mr. Sutton's farmhouse at a 1 quarter past six on the Sunday morning in question.— Samuel McClean, ticket collector at the Widnes side of Run- corn bridge, spoke to having seen six or seven young men pass on to the bridge between seven and eight o'clock on the morning in question. He did not know any of them James Lambert, ticket collector at the other side of the bridge, gave similar evidence. The prisoners told him they had missed the last train on the previous night from Liver- pool and had had to walk. He knew only one ef the party and that was George Guy.—Police-Seegeant Robinson, of Widnes, said he was present when the prisoners were appre- hended. Guy could not account for the bloodstains on his clothing. He said he had not lost any blood himself during the past six months.—Dr. Hall said he had exam- ined Joseph Gaiter and George Guy, and could find no traces of cuts or scratches on them frnm which blood could have come.—lnspector Raymond, a Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals officer, stationed at Liver- pool, spoke to having been present when the prisoners Jos. Gaiter and George Guy roads statements. They both ad- mitted having walked from Liverpool en the night of the 20th ult. The former, however, said they had not taken shelter anywhere during the night, while Guy said they had gone into a barn for shelter. He said, however, that there was no animal in the barn.—P.S. Ball spoke to the prisoners having been charged at Prescot on the 3rd inst. They each stated, then that they had been in the shed in ques- tion, Joseph Gaiter retracting his former statement.—Evi- deuce having been given by P.S. Edgar and P.C. Davy, Mr. Swift addressed the Bench for the defence. He pointed out that all the prisoners were so far men of irreproachable character, and were at present engaged by Runcorn firma. He contended that there had been no evidence given suffi- cient to justify the committal of the prisoners for trial.— His Worship, however, was of opinion that the evidence was sufficient to commit, and consequently each of the prisoners was committed for trial at the assizes. Bail was allowed, and fixed at two sureties in £3O each, and each prisoner in £6O. ,

RUNCOR4 COMMISSIONERS AND THE SHIP CANAL. A special meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commis- sioners was held at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road, on Thursday morning, for the purpose of considering the ad- visability of opposing the Ship Canal Bill, and, if thought desirable, of affixing the seal of the Board to a petition against the Bill. Mr. Meadowcroft presided, and there were present :—Dr. Steele, R. Shaw, H. White, W. Fisher, J. Pritchard, P. Speakman, F. A. Lake, J. W. Lightburn, Tim- mins, F. Fairhurst, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), and W. Brookes (secretary). Mr. SHAW, as chairman of the Ship Canal Committee, made a statement. He said a short time ago the Manches- ter Ship Canal Company agreed to give deep water accom- modation at Runcorn. They requested that the committee should draw up clauses, and submit them. This was done, but when the committee came to discuss the details of the clauses with the company they told them that they had taken no powers under their Act for making deep docks, and they had no means to do it. This was a debateable question. Though they might not, as a Ship Canal Company, be able to spend any of the meney they were raising for a specific purpose, it was a question whether they could not as the I owners of the Bridgewater Navigation Company make any I docks that the committee required for the furtherance of that particular branch of their trade. However, the com- pany met the committee with that objection, and they thought the next best thing they could do would be to take powers to make a deep-water dock for themselves ; that was, that tile Runcorn people, in the shape of a company or any other way they liked to put, might have power to make a deep dock connected with the low water channel, and also connected with the Manchester navigation. There was a convenient place where the dock might be put, and that was at the far end of "No man's land." That dock would abut on the deep-water cutting, whence they could easily get into the present locks. A draft clause was sent down from Manchester in reference to that deep dock, stating that they would not oppose the inhabitants of Runcorn making a deep dock, but they excluded any land in their possesSion, or any land they were seeking to obtain. This reservatien, of course, entirely removed the possibility of making a dock at all except to- wards the Old Quay, where it was well known docks would be developed without auy assistance from Runcorn. The object the committee had in view was to continue in its present course the traffic now passing along the higher canal, and it was their opinion that if they got the deep water dock connected with that canal they could in spite of the Manchester Ship Canal still hold a very large propor- tion of the traffic in that direction, because it must be clear that if vessels of one or two :thousand tons could be got into the dock, and the goods then transhipped into flats, vessels would never go on to Manchester through the wind- ing canal. Runcorn would thus be put in a much better position in every way. Tne committee were mot yet without hope of obtaining this concession, but unless they opposed the Ship Canal Company they would have no locus slaudi at all, and could not make any arrangements. It did not follow because the seal was affixed to the petition that any money would be spent in opposing the Bill, because he believed if the committee placed a fair case before the company they would meet them fairly. If it became necessary to oppose the Bill the committee would bring the matter before the Board and ask the advice of the members. From the 68th clause of the Bill the Board would Sad that the company took powers to put a charge upon all vessels entering Runcorn Docks which they thought could not have 'got into the present docks. supposing the deep-water cutting were not made. The corn- mitte pointed out to the company that there would be a great amount of friction in carrying out this clause in its present loose form, as it would be very debateable ground whether vessels could or could not have entered the docks, and the only way to obtain a remedy would be to apply to the Bard of Trade for a settlement of the question. The company agreed, on this representation, that any vessels that c -mid get into the docks over the present sills should be free of charge. Of course it was self-evident that if a vessel entered the docks no charge could be made upon 4. This c incession, however, had not been embodied in the Bill, and unlees the Board opposed the Bill they could not hold the company to it. Mr. LIGHTEMRN thought more could be obtained in a friendly way than by opposing the Bill, ani he was of opinion that sufficient time had elapsed for the negotiations to have been concluded. Mr. Slaw described the steps that had been taken from the C,,ninsencemmt, and pointed out that Friday was the I last day on which petitions against the Bill could be lodged. SPEIZIAN said the committee had been twice to "Manchester, and had interviews With the promoters of the scheme; and they were as far advanced on the second in- terview as they were on the first. The committee had adopted every coursa possible. , Dr. STEELR ebjected to spending any money upon the matter, but he agreed with the Board putting themselves in

a position to oppose the Bill if necessary. He thought the the Board would be able to get what they wanted without adopting that extreme course. The Citaiantatf pointed out that Icr)g.ing a petition would cot prevent negotiations. Mr. LIGHTSITEN contended that it tended to destroy the friendly spirit. Negotiations ought to nave commented earlier.

Mr. SI'EAKMAN said if Mr. Lightburn had attended the committee meetings he had been summoned to attend be would have had no objection to raise. Mr. PRITCHARD moved" that in the opinion of this meet- ing the interests of the town of Runcorn are prejudically affected by certain provisions of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill now before Parliament.

Mr. Strew seconded the motion, which was carried unani- mously. Mr. SHAW then moved that the Commissioners petition the House of Lords against the Bill, and that the seal of the Board be affixed to the petition. Mr. SPEAKMAN seconded the proposition, will& was carried.
It was stated that no legal steps would be taken without first consulting the Board.
A PROJF,CTED PErRCHASB,

The Board then considered the advisability of acquiring the land abutting upon Waterloo-road, and lying be- tween Canon-street and the land adjoining the Town Hall. During a short discussion that took place it transpired that Mr. Farrell was about to build upon the land a row of cottages, the backs of which would be di- rectly opposite the Board-room window. It was considered by some members that this would depreciate the Commis- sioners' property, while if the Board purchased the land it could be utilised for a good purpose in the future.—Mr. SPEAKMAN suggested that it would form an excellent site for public baths.—Ultimately a committee, consisting of Messrs. Fisher, Timmins, Pritchard, Lightburn, and Lake, was appointed to consider the subject and report to the Board at the next meeting. The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

Yesterday afternoon, a special meeting of this Board was held at the Cemetery. Mr George Moss presided,and there were present Messrs W Whittaker, P Briscoe, H CoSebum, 'I: Norman, W Mellor, W Littler, and W F Salkeld (secre- tary) —On the motion of Mr T Norman, seconded by Mr Mellor, it was decided to accept Mr Savage's offer of £lB a year for the rent of the field adjoining the Cemetery. Mr Beckett, of Hartford, who is erecting the new church in Greenway-road had an interview with the Board in refer- ence to the damage done to the Cemetery rails and coping during the storm in January, by a hoarding erected by him. It appeared he had nothing whatever te place before the Board, but in a coloversation that took place his reiterated his determination not to make good the damage, as it would be a dangerous precedent. He had, he asserted, taken the best legal advice he could on the subject, and he was in- formed that such was the exceptional nature of the storm— there had not been one like it for 40 years—that there was no doubt that it was one of those acts of God, which no man could take the responsibility of.—Mr Norman asked Mr Beckett who authorised him to put the hoarding up?— Mr Beckett replied that his plans were passed, and never in his life had he got any authority to puta hoarding up. If he had pet it up illegally why did not the Commis- , sioaers' surveyor stop him P—Mr. Norman made some re- marks to show how violently the boards must have bean I hurled to break the lamp in three pieces and then smash 1 the rails and ceping.—Mr. Beckett said the violence of the storm would be an argument in his favour.—The interview then terminated, and after a short discussion the subject dropped. It will be further considered at the next meet- ing.

DEA.TH AND FUNERAL OF MR. G. RHODES, OF RUNCORN. Our readers will hear with sincere regret of the death of Mr. George Rhodes, which took place at his residence, Leinster Gardens, Runcorn, on Tuesday morning. The de- ceased gentleman, who had been in an unsettled state of health for some months past, resigned his public duties in autumn last year, and his end was not altogether unex- pected. Twenty years have elapsed since Mr. Rhodes, who was a native of Hanley, took up his residence in Runcorn as agent to the North Staffordshire Canal and Railway Co., in succession to Mr. Robinson, who was promoted to the position Of manager at Stoke. He had previously held a similar appointment at Preston Brook, residing at that time at Dutton. From the first be took an active interest in the intellectual live of Runcorn. He was to the fore in every movement that tended to the intellectual and social ad-1 vancement of the people, and his matured judgment, and strict probity of character won for him the respect and esteem of all with whom he came in contact. To young men he was ever ready to act the part of mentor, guide, and friend, and withal with a genial kindheartedness that made his advice and assistance doubly welcome_ Living in an age of wonderful scientific discoveries, he was passionately fond of scientific pursuits, and his attainments, which were of no mean order, he was always glad to use for the benefit of his fellow-townspeople. He was connected with the now defunct Literary Institute from its formation, and filled the honourable and onerous positions of president and trea- surer, while many were the delightful excursions which the members of the Field Naturalists' Club of that institution had under his guidance, his wide knowledge of botany rendering his presence invaluable Under the auspices of the Institute he frequently delivered lectures on scientific subjects, illustrated by experiments and various instruments. But his services as a lecturer, or as an exhibitor of interesting scientilic apparatus, were often in request for charitable purposes in connection with church and chapel, and be was ever ready to respond to the call irrespective of creed or denomination. In the adminis- trative affairs of the town he did not take a very prominent part, but on two occasions he was elected a member of the Board of Commissioners, and, as we have previously stated, only retired in consequence of declining health. On all subjects that were introduced for consideration he exercised an independent judgment, and gave his adhesion to that policy which promised to be most beneficial to the community at large. The deceased gentleman was also one of the first members of the Free Library Committee, in the operations of which body he took particular interest. Fur several years he was a member of the Burial Board, and at the time of his death he was the honoured chairman of that body. Although a gentleman of very broad religions views be was a regular attendant at Bethesda Chapel, and in the various undertakings of the congregation he took a prominent and responsible part. He was lor a long period the treasurer of the Sunday school, only retiring from the position two years ago. In politics he was a Conservative of wide sympathi,=B, but he numbered his friends amongst all parties and all denominations. No man stood higher than he in the estimation ef the community, and by bra death Runcorn has lost one of its foremost men of light and leading. The deceased gentleman, who was in his 05th year, has left a family of grown up sons and daughters. The mortal remains of the deceased were interred at Run- corn Cemetery yesterday afternoon, the body being followed to the grave by a considerable number of the leading gentle- men of the town. The funeral cortege, which consisted of a kearse and three carriages, left beinster Gardens at half-past twa, and the respect in which Mr. Rhodes was held was shown by the darkened windows along the route. Preceding the hearse were the following gentlemen:- T Norman, P Briscoe, E Timmins, W Fisher, 3 W Light- horn, F A Lake. M Barker, W Sutton, G Moss W Melfor, W J Shore, R Evans, W Handley, W Vil7F Sal keld, H Coleburn, W Whittaker, J Kirkham, Joseph Williams, W H Chadwick, R Hampson, T Sirnister, T Stringfellow, G Surnmerfield, T Riley, Joseph Littler, F Beck, T Hand- toy, J R Frith. John Williams, R Andrews, J Roberts, J Craig, and F Fairhurst. Walking beside the hearse were the carriers, Messrs T Lydiate, J Dobson, T Ellis, and W Ctingle. In the first carriage were Rev J D Thomas, Dr Carruthers (who had attended the deceased gentleman in his illness). Dr MacDougall, and Mr. James Pritchard; in the second were Messrs. F. Rhedes;W. Rhodes, Geo. Rhodes, Jesse Rhodes, and Harry. Rhodes (sons) • in the third were the sons-in- law—Messrs. W. H. Ringiand, R. Hall, and J. Priestland. At the last moment, Mr. J. Meadowcroft, the chairman of the Board of Commissioners, telegraphed from Manchester that he was unable to attend the funeral, and show his esteem and respect for Mr. Rhodes. The service in the church and at the grave-side was conducted by the Rev. J. D. Thomas, pester of Bethesda Chapel. Mr. F. Fairhurst, Church-street, was the undertaker; and Mr. S. Yarwood supplied the hearse and carriages. We may state that Mr. J. Pritchard and Mr. J. Meadowcroft are the executors under the will of the deceased. VOTE OF CONDOLENCE. A special meeting of the Runcorn Burial Board was held yesterday afternoon, and at the conclusion of the business Mr. G. Moss, who was in the chair, said: Before we separate I feel constrained to mention the loss which threßoard has sustained by the death of its chairman, Mr. Rhodes. I feel sure ern giving utterance to the feelings of every member of this Board when I say how deeply we regret his loss— (hear, hear)—both on account of the personal regard we had for him and hie services to this Board. Mr. Rhodes was a thoroughly straightforward, honourable, and upright man— one in whom everybody placed confidence a man, indeed, .in whom there was no guile, and as such .he was universally respected; but, more than that, he was' to a remarkable degree esteemed for his uniform amiability of charactet. Whenever you met him he was pleasant and cheerful; always ready to listen to anything that any one had to say to him; and willing to give the best of his counsel and advice. I feel sure that in losing Mr. Rhode., Runcorn has lost one of its best and foremost townsmen. It was a pleasure to meet him at this Board. His strong common sense and unerring judgment could always be relied upon whenever we got into a difficulty of any kind; and we, as members of this Board, shall feel his loss very much. I have no doubt every one sympathises very much with his family, and I have to move that the secretary write to Mrs. Rhodes ex- pressing the sympathy of this Board with her and her family in their gtest bereavement. Mr. Littler said: As a member of this Board and, a neigh- bour of Mr. Rhodes, he felt justified in seconding the pro- position that had been moved by Mr. Moss. He should feel very deeply the loss of Mr. Rhodes. He had heard it ex- oressed on all hands that he was most highly esteemed by everybody with whom he tame in contact, and as Mr. Moss had very properly said he was a gentleman it whom confi- deuce could be ploced in all matters. The motion was carried unanimously,

I , STOCK AND SHARE MARKET.
Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 1, Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (Feb. 218t):--

We have to record a week devoid of any special general fea- ture, and beyond the depreciation and partial recovery in Mexican railways exhibiting no instance at movement calling for special remark Railway traffics are fair, and prices In these investments are a little irregular, but. without great change in either direction. Foreign funds contradictory, but better on the whole. Egyptians show Unified and Detre lower and the preference higher, the alteration in all cases being but frac- tional. Peruvian, Russian, Spanish, and Italian are all better, the three first-named showing decided advance. 311131C1C&D per cents. are Ito 3-8 lower. Mexican railways have seen some quick and wide fluctuations. Standing a week ago at about 43 they were gradually put down to between 33 and 391, reaching these figures on Monday last, since which they have shown better, now quoting about 44, or a fall of about 4 on the week. Miscellaneous series producing only a very moderate amount of business and a number of changes in quotations, which evince strength In bank shares and weakness in insurance and mineral undertakings. Others about steady.

VOLUNTEER RETURNS FOR LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE. —The return of the Volunteer force of Lancashire and Cheshire, shortly to be presented to Parliament, are, on the whole, most favourable, those for the two counties showing a net increase of about 560 in efficients, and over 600 in en- rolled. over the previous returns, when the respective totals were 29,829 and 30,690. Lancashire has nearly 2,000 efficients out of 25,600 enrolled; and Cheshire 5,500 effi- ciente mit of 6,500 enrolled. Dealing first with the artillery, the eight Lancashire brigades have 5,550 efficient& out of 5,800 on the rolls, and 480 proficient officers and sergeants- the two Lancashire engineer corps, 1,170 efficient s out of 1,200; and the 22 battalions of infantry, 18,100 efficients out of 18,100 enrolled volunteers. The Ist Cheshire and Carnarvon Artillery advances its enrolled from 653 to 692, ,and its efficients from 613 to 653; the let Cheshire Engineers has lost ground slizhtly, and the five battalions of infantry sum up over 4,300 efficients and over 4,400 enrolled as Lagainst 4,055 and 4,083 respectively,

SURRENDER OF TOKAR. IMPORTANT DESPieiCil, We are indebted to the courtesy of the editor of the Daily Telegaec for a copy of the following important telegram

tiaatim, FninsY,ll-30 A.M.—Five soldiers have come from Tokar, and report that thembols ha-re been keeping up a tor/dant fire from their guns and rifles. The garrison, linable to hold out any longer, had a conference on Tuesday with the rebels. On Wednesday, Adjutant-Maibr Yacoob Effendi and Maccaiyi Effendf, the head of the police, and also a sergeant of artillery, wont to the rebels and con- ferred with them. These, upon their return, told thc Governor that they were to give up their arms on Thursday. Many of the soldiers murmured, and a large proportion escaped during the night. The five fugitive soldiers report that Tokar was thus given up yesterday.
anab;

TAT: NEWS CONYMMED, The Times third edition contains the following telegram, dated Suakim, to-day :—" Tokar has surrendered to the I rebels. Five soldiers have come in who state that the rebels , kept up a heavy fire from Krupp gunvand rides for several days, and many of thosoldiers of the town were killed. At , last, being unable to defend the 'works any longer, the I Governor sent emissaries on Tuesday tb confer with the I rebels and te make termrlbrthe surrender. On Wednesday Adjutant-Major Yacoob Effendi went out;.accourpanied by ;Maccaivi Bey, the governor ef the town. On their return they announced that the soldiers most give- up their arms. ;There Was a great commotion among the men, many of whom refused to abandon all hope of further resistance. 'Finally, however, their surrender was arranged on the terms demanded by the rebels, During the sight many of the soldiers escaped, passing through the rebel lines. These five men are the first who havararvived, but they' 'Tim': that others are straggling on the road hither. Tokar Was finwity given up yesterday..

RECEPTION OF THE NEWS IN LONDON.' The Central News says—The news rece ved in London yesterday to the effect that the garrison of Tolearhad sue- rendered caused much excitemente although it did not give. rise to such a painful sensation as that occasioned by the fall of Sinkat. In that case the garrison had been cruelly massarred, but in the present instance the surrender, as far! as is known, has been unaccompanled by any act of ' bar- I barity. The news up to the present " rests almost solely upon the evidence of native spies who have arrived at Suakim. These men state , that, being closely beleaguered by the rebels, who it is already known have for some days past been maintain- ing a warm and effective fire, the beads of the garrison opened negotiations with the enemy with the result that the fort was to have been given up yesterday (Thursday). This news was received in the course of the day at the Foreign Office, and by the naval and military authorities at head quarters; but up to a late hour this evening no intelligence, official or otherwise, has reached London that the surrender, has actually taken place. But at the War Office and the Admiralty little doubt is felt that the rebels are now masters of Tokar. Five native soldiers, who escaped from , the fort, confirm the statement of the spies so far as it goes, and report moreover that other soldiers who also got wear from Tokar safely are following them. The Central News learns that pending confirmation of the actual surrender, General Graham is continuing his preparations for an early landing of his forces at Trinkitat, with the view of an im- mediate advance upon Tokar, or at least of affording protec- tion to the fugitives. The last of the expeditionary force, with the exception of one consignment of transport animals, bee now left Sues, so that General Graham will have every- thing in readiness for a start in a day or two. AritnNl Hewiti, undertakes the defence of Suakim and the command of the i..,orptiart troops left at that place, and is also in- vested with civil authority. On receipt of the first official telegram announicng the news brought to Suakim by the spies, an informal meeting of Misieters was hastily summoned to meet at the Foreign Office at half-past two. By that hour Mr. Gladstone, Lords Granville, North- brook, Hartington, and Kimberley, and Sir Charles Duke had arrived, and were in consultation. Their deliberation lasted until four o'clock, when Mr. Gladstone left for the , Heuer, of Commons, being followed at intervals by the other ministers. Great animation prevailed in the lobbies this evening. As ministers arrived they were eagerly pressed for confirmation of the report of the fall of Tokar by those members who were on sufficiently intimate terms to enter into conversation with them. The House of Com- mons was crowded with members, and the ministerial state- ments respecting Tokar were listened to with profound attention.
Sir Bartle Frere's condition remains unchanged. A gas explosion occurred yesterday morning at a house in Dudley-road, Birmingham, causing serious injuries to persons:. _

M. BRADLAUGH.—The Central News learns that accord- ing to present arrangements the case against Mr. BradlAugh for taking his seat without having been properly sworn will be conducted by the Attorney-General, the Solicitor-General, and Mr. S. Wright. .

In response t.".; a letter Mr. J. L. Davies, head master of the Garth Board School, Bangor, North Wales, has just re- ceived from Mr. Gladstone apiece of wood, from a lime tree felled in Hawarden Park, by the Premier, which is to be utilised in training a picture of the right hon. gentlem In. THE GALE): EXTRAORDINARY DISASTER.—During the gale on Thursday the roof of a house fell in at Shotts, Lanarkshire. The roof being of thatch caught fire, and with the wind that prevailed the flames spread rapidly. In a short time other houses caught fire, and before the fire was extinguished a whole row of workmen's houses was burned to the ground.

THE CONSECRATION OF THE NEW BISHOP OF CHESTER. —Our Chester correspondent is informed that the consecra- tion of Canon Stubbs, of St. Paul's, as Bishop of Chester, will take place in the Chester Cathedral in the last week in larch. The ceremony will be performed by the Arch- bishop of York. Our correspondent adds that Dr. Jacobson, the retiring Bishop, is now infirm and hag very indifferent health.

THE DIFFICULTY AT EARL SPENCER'S COURT.—The difficulty between Earl Spencer and the medical profession has terminated satisfactorily, the Lord-Lieutenant having cancelled the recent order that the wives of the physicians i and surgeons to His Excellency should not be permitted to take their places at the drawing-rooms and state balls. along with the wives of the other official members of his stall in attendance on the Countess Spencer. The threatened re- signations are therefore averted. THE PEERAGE AND ITS DEFENDERS: THE SENSATIONAL BREACH or PROMISE CASE.—The action for breach of promise marry brought by Miss Fortescue against Lord Garmoyle came indirectly before a meeting of the Belfast Society for Promoting Knowledge on • flursday, when the , Rev. Dr. Bryce, who was a tutor of Earl Cairns when a pupil at the Belfast Academy, objected to have the World or Truth society papers on the library table, on the ground that their information about the upper classes is misleading, especially that about Lord Garmoyle's father. He strongly denied that Lord Garmoyle's grandfather was a .tradesman and the great grandson of a butcher. Everyone knew, he said. that Lord Cairns's father was a highly-accomplished gentleman living on his fortune, and that he was a highly. educated gentleman.

HOUSE OF LORDS.

THE SURRENDER OF TOIKAR.—EarI GIUNVILLE read two telegrams from Suakim relating to the surrender of Taker. Colonel Baker, telegraphing at noon. said fugitives and spies had reported the surrender of Tokar. The married half of the garrison had submitted to Osman, the rest attempted to reach Suakim. A telegram received half an hour later stated the report et the actual surrender was not confirmed. Preparations for landing troops at Trinkitat were therefore being pressed forward.

OVER-CROWDING OF THE POOR—The Marquio of SAMS- Butts moved for a Royal Commission to inquire into the over-crowding of the poor.—The PRINCE of WALES was gratified at being placed on the Royal Cemml.ssion. He took a great personal interest in the housing of the poor. As a landed proprietor in Norfolk he had pat the dwellings of his labourers in such condition that none can't' say that they were ill-housed. He trusted the Commission would do much towards the amelioration of the condition of the poor in the country.—Earl Shaftesbury and ths Bishop of Lon- don followed —The Royal Commission was agreed to. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

LOCAL TAXATION.—Mr. R. YORE.. Rave notice on an early day to move a resolution with regard to local taze- tion.—Mr. RYLANDS postponed his intention of bringing under the attention of the House the sub;ect of local taza- tion.

THE 'BELFAST OBANGEMEN.—Mr, THETELYAN, replying to Mr. Sexton, said there were no grounds for prosecating Mr. Cobain, grand master of the Orangemen of Belfast for the speech delivered at Belfast on Saturday. Churchill's question as to the intentions of the aovernment with regard to the Eradlaugh prosecution, said he must wait to see what was the judgment of the Court of first instance before saying whether the case woula be car- ried to the Court of Appeal and, HOWE) of Lords. The report of Tokar being actually sur- rendered has not yet been, received, and preparations for • landing at Trinkitat are therefore being pressed forward."--- In reply to Sir S. At the Warrington Police Court, on Thursday, before: Captain Litton, James Richardson, alias Green, 52 :yeses af age, a collier belonging to Newton, but last from Prescoef• was brought up on a charge of breaking and entering. the' Warrington Workhouse, and stealing therefrom-five loaves' of bread, Clbs. of bacon, a sack, and a glass sloth, value 'lee or thereabout, the property of the Guardians, also a raa,er and case, value la, the property of Ralph :obisnson, an en" mate.—Mr. A. Browne prosecuted on behalf si the police. --- The prisoner, it seems, is getting notoriously krrown-tothe Workhouse authorities, having been sentenced some time last year to three months' hard labour for msaling.propertt from the Warrington institution, and to sin ,months for breaking in the Union Workhouse at Whiston, neat", Prescotar-With regard to the present charge,i,:appearod that between one and two o'clock OD the morn- ing of Cot/inlay last, Ralph Jobnsem, an old man, who acts as assistant cook at, the. Workbouse,got up as usual to look after the heating appap' tus, drc.,*arKl.on going into the kitchen he hoard a noise. On striking a match he observed what he thought to be a bag of rubbish, and he kicked it, baths foni-gl it contained the prisoner. The latter prayed to 190 allowed to go awl, but Johnson not being inclined to grant this request a struggle took place been them; but the prisoner, who OW' powered the-old man and gave him a partinghick, managed to make hia.escape into the yard by forcing.the frame of ' a swing window, through which he jumped. Johnson then raised an alarm by shouting "Murder," and called tan Mrs.' Langley, the assistant matron, who in turn, apprised.the master, M:, C' Mackey. Mrs. Langev, o going to the kitchen, missed a quantity of bacon which :sung across the place, and also five loaves of bread. On looking into the bag he foul& the five loaves-of bread, the bacon, the glass, cloth produced. P.C. Neil received prisoner into his mistody from the ' county police at Prescot, on Wednesday., Juld he 'produced the razor and case, which was identified :)sy Johnsen as longing to to him. In reply to the charge, prisoner told the officer it was foar loaves of bread, and nat five, although it' did not matter =Oh, and he admitted stealing the razor- Prisoner was not an inmate of the Worthouse-al: the tiros. • Everywhere was fastened up at nine o'cl)ck on Friday night, and he must have made his entry hefora that time. —Prisoner, who had nothing to say and no witnessesta" call, was committed for trial to the Liverpool Asatzes. _
